ideas.title: Paid Exit Capture: Layoffs Become Agent Evals
ideas.one_liner: Pay departing employees a completion bonus to turn their tacit exception-handling know-how into the eval sets and edge-case playbooks the employer's AI agents need, before that knowledge walks out.
ideas.customer: Head of AI, COO or CHRO at 1,000-20,000-person companies running AI-justified headcount cuts in ops-heavy functions (claims, support, finance ops, procurement), plus PE operating partners doing portfolio-wide cuts.
ideas.problem: Companies cut the people who know the long tail, then find their agents fail on it. Reversals are now reported (Klarna rehiring humans in 2025, Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversing 45 cuts, CNBC's Jul 2026 'regret' headline). Exit interviews are HR theatre, and angry leavers have no reason to document anything.
ideas.solution: A 2-3 week 'capture sprint' inside the notice or severance window. A consented, paid interview agent plus a domain reviewer walks each person through their 50 hardest cases. Output is a graded eval set (inputs, gold decisions, rubrics, 'when I'd escalate') and a playbook the employer owns. Workers get a bonus scaled to eval quality (measured by held-out agent accuracy), a signed contribution credential and optionally a recall or contract-rights clause.
ideas.why_now: AI was the top-cited layoff reason in Challenger data for five straight months through Jul 2026, and enterprise agent rollouts are now bottlenecked by evals and edge cases rather than by models. Reversal stories are giving CFOs a fresh fear. Interview agents are cheap enough to run the sprints at scale.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40k fixed fee per role-cluster capture sprint (roughly $1.5-4k per captured employee after bonuses), plus an annual eval-refresh retainer once the agent is live.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: To the employer a laid-off worker is a depreciating liability, but for the agent rollout they are the only source of ground truth on the long tail. You can only get it by paying, and paying on eval quality fixes the incentive. The data is worth far more than the severance delta.
ideas.first_30_days: Use public WARN filings to list 40 companies mid-layoff and pitch 15 HR/AI leads a free 5-person pilot at cost. Have an employment lawyer draft the consent, IP-assignment and NDA carve-out template. Deliver one eval set and show before/after agent accuracy as the case study.

ideas.title: Retrain Displaced Managers for Data-Center Builds
ideas.one_liner: A 10-week bridge program that turns laid-off program managers, analysts and ops leads into project-controls, cost-estimating, commissioning-paperwork and permitting roles at data-center and grid builders.
ideas.customer: General contractors, EPC firms, data-center developers and utility contractors pay a $12-25k placement fee or staff-augmentation margin. Learners pay little, or the cost is covered by workforce-board funds.
ideas.problem: Everyone tells displaced office workers to 'learn AI', the most crowded direction. Meanwhile AI's own physical build-out has a shortage of schedulers (P6), cost engineers, document controllers, commissioning coordinators and interconnection or permit analysts. Contractors can't hire them, and mid-career office workers face 6-13 month searches.
ideas.solution: Cohort training on scheduling, cost control, contracts, commissioning documentation and site-safety basics, taught by retired project-controls leads. It includes a paid 4-week job-shadow on live projects, certification prep (OSHA 30, PMI-SP, AACE) and guaranteed interviews with partner contractors.
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler capex on data centers and grid work is at record levels and contractors openly cite labor shortages. Big-company cuts of managers ('anti-bureaucracy' layoffs like Amazon's ~16,000) are pushing experienced coordinators onto the market. Stanford data shows the pain concentrated in AI-exposed office roles.
ideas.revenue_model: Placement fee of 10-15% of first-year salary (about $12-18k) from contractors, plus paid corporate cohorts and optional deferred tuition.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The AI boom creates a shortage of non-technical, non-AI office roles in the physical world. The displaced manager's scarce skill (vendor wrangling, org navigation, documentation discipline) is exactly what construction lacks, and nobody is training for it.
ideas.first_30_days: Call 20 mid-size mechanical and electrical contractors in hot markets (Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona) and get their unfilled-role lists. Sign 3 pay-per-hire LOIs. Recruit 15 laid-off PMs from layoff communities. Run a 4-week evening pilot with a retired scheduler and place the first 5.

ideas.title: Shared Apprentice Pools for Office Work
ideas.one_liner: A group-training organisation (the Australian trades model) for white-collar work. It employs new grads, trains them to supervise AI output, and rotates them across several mid-size hosts that share the cost and get first pick.
ideas.customer: Mid-size (100-2,000 employee) accounting firms, insurance brokerages, property managers, logistics and healthcare-admin employers pay host fees. The new grads are W-2 employees of the pool.
ideas.problem: Each employer rationally stops hiring juniors because AI absorbs junior tasks and trained juniors get poached. Collectively that empties the 3-5-year-experience pipeline around 2029. Stanford finds 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend, and 42% of recent grads are underemployed.
ideas.solution: The pool hires 25-40 juniors per cohort and gives 8 weeks of workflow-specific training (AI-assisted bookkeeping, claims triage, contract abstraction). It then places them 2-3 days a week across up to three hosts for $38-50/hr as supervised AI-assist analysts with QA metrics. Senior mentors get stipends, and hosts pay a fixed conversion fee at months 12-18. The pool handles payroll, insurance and HR.
ideas.why_now: The freeze is widening (Aug 2026 Stanford revision), and AI tools make a trained junior productive from week two. Employers are stuck in a prisoner's-dilemma on training. Pooled employment is a proven fix in Australian trades and in Germany's dual system.
ideas.revenue_model: Host fees at 25-35% gross margin, plus conversion fees of $8-15k per hire.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The junior freeze is a coordination failure (a training externality), not a technology fact. Hosts are buying a cheap call option on the scarce 2029 mid-level hire, and pooling removes the poaching fear that blocks individual employers.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one vertical with retiring owner-operators (independent insurance brokerages or small CPA firms). Sign 6 hosts at a pilot rate through a state society or trade association. Hire 10 grads via college career centres. Use a PEO for payroll so you build no HR infrastructure.

ideas.title: Alt-Data From AI-Training Gig Workers
ideas.one_liner: A worker-owned pay-transparency panel for expert data contractors. Its aggregated signals on which domains are hiring, what they pay and how many hours exist become a leading-indicator dataset for investors and rival platforms.
ideas.customer: Hedge funds, VCs and AI-lab competitive-intelligence teams pay $30-150k a year for the index. Workers get the basic tier free or for $9-15 a month.
ideas.problem: Mercor's reported gross run rate went from about $0.5B to $2B in nine months, and the category claims millions of contractors, yet nobody outside the labs can see which skills are in demand or when a domain saturates. Workers complain of falling pay and have no rate data, while investors price a $10-25B category on anecdotes.
ideas.solution: A browser extension plus web app where contractors log, or auto-capture from their own dashboards, pay rate, hours offered, rejections and coarse project category (never confidential content). There is a public 'Levels.fyi for AI gigs' leaderboard by platform and domain, and a paid weekly index of hours availability and pay by domain, with saturation early-warnings.
ideas.why_now: The human-data market went from niche to multi-billion in a year, contractors are publicly vocal (HN, Verge, Wired coverage) and investor appetite for AI-adjacent labor data is high. No panel exists.
ideas.revenue_model: Institutional data subscriptions ($50-150k a year), a premium worker tier ($9-15 a month) and possibly sponsored placements from challenger platforms recruiting supply.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Gig workers are usually treated as supply, but here they are a sensor network that reads the frontier labs' priorities weeks before any press release. Workers will join because it helps them negotiate and avoid saturated domains. Platforms can't easily object to workers sharing their own pay data, provided the design avoids NDA-covered project details.
ideas.first_30_days: Seed 300 members from data-annotation subreddits and Discords with a pay-rate survey. Publish a 'State of expert AI gig pay' report. Pitch 10 funds and 3 VC platform teams a sample weekly index, and land one paid pilot.

ideas.title: Independent Inspections for AI-Built Software
ideas.one_liner: A third-party inspection-and-certificate service, staffed by displaced senior engineers, that tells buyers, lenders and insurers what is really inside AI-generated apps before money changes hands.
ideas.customer: Buyers of micro-SaaS and small apps on acquisition marketplaces (deals $20k-$2M), SMBs whose apps were built by vibe-coding freelancers, seed investors doing diligence and lenders financing software purchases.
ideas.problem: Insiders say AI made software cheap, but the cost moved to trust. Marketplaces are filling with prompt-built products of unknown security, licensing and maintainability, and misconfigured database rules in AI-generated apps have been reported. Traditional code audits cost $10-50k and take weeks. Meanwhile senior devs sit unemployed for many months.
ideas.solution: A fixed-price 48-hour 'app inspection': automated scans (secrets, dependency licences, database access rules, auth and PII flows) plus a 2-4 hour senior human review. The output is a standardised graded report like a home-inspection report, with repair-cost estimates and a maintainability score. Inspectors are paid $500-900 each, and an optional badge can be accepted by escrow agents.
ideas.why_now: The vibe-coding boom in 2025-26 flooded acquisition marketplaces with AI-built listings, agentic scanners make the first pass nearly free, and unemployed senior engineers are abundant.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-4k per inspection at 40-50% gross margin, recurring contracts with portfolio buyers, and referral fees from repair shops.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When production cost collapses, value shifts to attestation. Every asset that became cheap to produce (1970s housing, used cars, diamonds) spawned an independent inspector class. Nobody has yet set the trusted standard for AI-built software, and the inspectors' seniority is the moat, the same people the market calls redundant.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer discounted $500 inspections in acquisition-marketplace buyer forums and Indie Hackers. Recruit 6 laid-off senior engineers and run 10 inspections on live listings. Publish anonymised findings ('7 of 10 exposed user data') and sign one escrow or broker referral partner.

ideas.title: Rights-Request Engine for Rejected Applicants
ideas.one_liner: A consumer tool that files legally formatted data-access and automated-decision requests to employers' hiring systems, turning silent rejections into scores, reasons and evidence.
ideas.customer: Job seekers, starting in the UK and EU under GDPR Art. 15/22, then Illinois and California. They pay $12 a month or $29 per request pack. Secondary buyers are plaintiff-side employment firms and researchers who license opt-in aggregate data.
ideas.problem: Applicants send dozens of applications, get almost no replies and never learn why (HN: 65 applications, 3 phone screens, 0 interviews). New laws give people rights to see and contest automated screening, but nobody uses them because finding the right contact and format is a hassle.
ideas.solution: A browser extension logs each application (company, ATS vendor, date). After 30 days of silence it files a data-access and automated-decision request, tracks the one-month deadline, escalates to the regulator, and parses the response into a structured 'why I was screened out' report. Opt-in aggregate stats show which employers and ATS vendors auto-reject which profiles.
ideas.why_now: California's automated-decision regulations start binding in Jan 2027 and Illinois' AI-in-employment notice law took effect Jan 2026. The Mobley v. Workday collective action is live and AI resume screening is ubiquitous. Job-search desperation is at a peak, and EU/UK rights already work today.
ideas.revenue_model: Consumer subscription or per-pack fees, plus opt-in anonymised data and insight licences to labor economists, unions and employment plaintiff firms. Employer-side compliance-readiness upsell later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Regulators created rights but no practical channel, and that friction is the enforcement gap. The service converts individual rights into aggregate leverage: an employer receiving 500 requests per role starts giving candidates real feedback, and the request-and-response dataset becomes the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a GDPR-only MVP (templates, deadline tracker) for UK/EU applicants in two weeks, with a UK data-protection solicitor reviewing the templates. Seed it in UK and EU job-search communities and HN at £9 per pack. Measure response rates and refine.

ideas.title: Moonlighting and IP Clearance for AI Experts
ideas.one_liner: A concierge that checks and files the employer-disclosure, IP-assignment and confidentiality paperwork professionals need before moonlighting as AI-training experts, and issues clean-provenance certificates that labs and vendors can rely on.
ideas.customer: Employed lawyers, bankers, doctors, consultants and engineers doing expert-data gigs pay $79-149 per clearance. Data vendors and lab legal or procurement teams pay for an annual B2B license.
ideas.problem: Millions of experts have signed up, many still employed at banks, law firms and hospitals with outside-activity approval rules (e.g. FINRA-registered staff), IP assignment and confidentiality duties. Some platforms even solicit prior work that former employers may own (HN Apr 2026). One trade-secret suit could freeze a vendor's programs, and workers risk termination or licence discipline.
ideas.solution: (1) A contract reader flags moonlighting, IP and confidentiality risk in the worker's agreement and handbook. (2) Templates for the employer disclosure or approval request. (3) A scanner for confidential markers in submitted work. (4) A 'clean-room certificate' per contributor. (5) An onboarding API vendors can require. A partner attorney covers the advice.
ideas.why_now: The Mercor breach and class actions have made vendor risk teams and lab counsel nervous. Reports of labs asking contractors for real past work samples raise provenance stakes. The scale of professionals moonlighting for AI companies is unprecedented.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-clearance fee for workers plus $50-250k annual vendor licences and per-contributor API fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer with money is the vendor's general counsel, not the worker, but the worker channel gives distribution and data. A database of moonlighting and IP policies for the top few thousand employers, built from worker submissions, becomes the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 20 moonlighting experts. Hand-build 50 employer-policy profiles (big banks, Big 4, large law firms, health systems). Run a manual $99 concierge clearance service. Pitch two mid-tier data vendors' compliance leads a paid pilot.

ideas.title: Layoff Early-Warning for Credit Unions
ideas.one_liner: Turns public WARN notices and layoff signals into member-level outreach lists, so lenders can offer hardship plans about 60 days before payments are missed.
ideas.customer: Credit unions (roughly 4,400 in the US), community banks, mortgage servicers and auto lenders pay $1.5-6k a month, often via credit-union service organisations.
ideas.problem: White-collar layoffs are lumpy and local (information-sector employment fell 23k in one Aug 2026 month, Amazon cut ~16,000 corporate roles). Lenders learn about them from missed payments, when charge-off risk is already high and members are hardest to help. Hardship programs exist but outreach comes too late.
ideas.solution: Ingest state WARN databases, news and layoff trackers. Match employers to the lender's book using payroll ACH descriptors on member accounts. Rank members by exposure, then supply compliant outreach scripts, pre-approved skip-a-pay or modification offers, and uplift measurement.
ideas.why_now: Layoffs are steady and concentrated in higher-balance, AI-exposed white-collar borrowers. Payroll descriptors and open-banking data make the join easy. Small lenders have no data teams, and the low-hire market makes re-employment slow (7-13 months in practitioner reports).
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-6k a month per institution, or a performance fee on avoided delinquencies.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The layoffs are public. The scarce piece is the join to the lender's book via payroll descriptors. Employees of a laid-off employer often bank at the same local credit union, so the risk is concentrated, and the ROI is stated in avoided charge-offs rather than charity.
ideas.first_30_days: Normalise 50 state WARN sources. Backtest with a friendly credit union on two past layoff events to show missed payments 45-90 days later. Get two credit-union service organisations to run a paid $1k-a-month pilot.

ideas.title: AI-Aware E&O Cover for Solo Consultants
ideas.one_liner: A specialty insurance agency for laid-off professionals turned solo consultants whose errors-and-omissions cover may quietly exclude AI-assisted work, with premiums discounted for logged verification workflows.
ideas.customer: Solo and 2-10-person consultancies (fractional CFOs, marketing and analytics freelancers, dev contractors, HR and ops consultants) pay $400-1,500 a year in premium. The agency earns roughly 15-20% commission.
ideas.problem: Large carriers have reportedly sought AI-liability exclusions, so a freelancer who used AI on a deliverable can find a claim denied. Client contracts increasingly demand E&O plus AI-use reps. Newly independent laid-off professionals never read the policy language.
ideas.solution: A retail agency that places policies with carriers offering affirmative AI coverage (an MGA program later). A lightweight verification log (source checks, review sign-off) yields an underwriting-friendly attestation that lowers price. A contract clause checker flags indemnities, plus a template AI-use disclosure for clients.
ideas.why_now: Carrier AI-exclusion filings surfaced in late 2025, layoffs are creating a wave of new independents, and enterprise procurement now asks vendors for AI-use attestations. AI-liability startups target enterprises, not solos.
ideas.revenue_model: Commissions of 15-20%, MGA fees later, and a $10-a-month verification-log tool.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The gap is one of underwriting information: how AI-assisted work is actually verified versus what the policy assumes. A logged verification workflow is data an insurer will pay for with lower prices. Premiums are too small for big brokers to chase, so a new insured class goes unserved.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a licensed E&O producer (or get licensed). Read the AI language of 10 carriers and publish a 'Does your E&O cover AI?' checker and newsletter for laid-off and freelancer communities. Bind the first 20 policies.

ideas.title: Escrow and Tax Rails for Agent-Hired Humans
ideas.one_liner: The compliance and payment layer that lets software agents legally hire humans for judgment and real-world tasks: owner KYC, task-legality screening, escrow, worker classification and tax forms.
ideas.customer: Agent-framework developers and companies whose agents need on-call humans (verification, phone calls, notarisation, in-person checks), plus the workers doing the tasks. Take rate is 8-12%.
ideas.problem: Agent-to-human marketplaces are appearing (47jobs, Hirenewtalent.ai in the brief, and viral 'rent a human' sites in early 2026), but nobody is the clear payor, employer or liable party. Who issues 1099s, who is responsible if an agent sends someone to do something illegal or never pays, and how do workers avoid scams?
ideas.solution: An API plus MCP tool ('ask_human'): agents post tasks against funded escrow tied to a KYC'd human or company principal. A legality and safety classifier rejects risky tasks. Automatic tax forms and classification, dispute arbitration and two-sided reputation follow, with optional injury insurance for physical tasks.
ideas.why_now: Agent frameworks and MCP matured in 2025, agent-payment standards and stablecoin rails are being rolled out, and agent-run marketplaces are going viral. Regulators will demand a principal of record after the first scandal.
ideas.revenue_model: 8-12% take rate on tasks plus an insurance margin for physical work.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The marketplace is cheap to clone. The moat is the principal-of-record and liability layer, which is what regulators and enterprise buyers will eventually require, so building the compliant rails first wins the boring middle.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a minimal escrow API and MCP tool with 200 vetted workers in one niche (phone verification calls, document notarisation, local checks in 3 cities). Onboard 10 agent builders through Discord and HN and complete the first 500 paid tasks.

ideas.title: Layoff Compliance Autopilot for Mid-Size HR
ideas.one_liner: Software plus expert review that generates every notice, filing and adverse-impact analysis a reduction-in-force needs, including a documented record of whether AI or restructuring drove each decision.
ideas.customer: HR and legal teams at 200-5,000-employee companies and the boutique employment law firms advising them pay $4-15k per event or $12-30k a year.
ideas.problem: RIF rules are fragmenting by state. New York's WARN form asks whether layoffs stem from AI or automation, New Jersey mandates severance, and OWBPA requires age disclosures for group terminations. Remote workforces span 20+ states. Mid-size firms rely on $500-an-hour outside counsel or spreadsheets while age-bias and AI-washing scrutiny (Mobley v. Workday) rises.
ideas.solution: Upload the roster and selection criteria. The tool maps each jurisdiction's rules, generates notices, separation agreements and OWBPA disclosures, runs adverse-impact statistics (age, race, sex, disability, leave) with remediation suggestions, and builds an AI-attribution record of task-level evidence for each decision. It includes a filing calendar and a lawyer-in-the-loop review queue.
ideas.why_now: Cuts are steady even though Challenger totals are down 41% year on year, AI is the leading cited reason, and NY added an AI checkbox in 2025. Age-discrimination class actions are live, and LLMs now make document generation cheap while lawyers still sign off.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-event fee ($4-15k), annual subscription, and revenue share with reselling law firms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The pain is not 'AI layoffs' but the compliance combinatorics of remote-first firms. The economic buyers (law firms and HR) either bill by the hour or bear the risk, and steady low-volume cuts mean repeated use.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a state-by-state rule matrix for the top 12 states plus federal rules. Sell $2,500 'RIF readiness packs' to 10 boutique employment firms. Run three live RIF events with friendly firms.

ideas.title: W-2 Employer-of-Record for AI-Training Experts
ideas.one_liner: A task-metered payroll, benefits and contract layer that lets data vendors and labs engage expert contractors as short-term employees without the misclassification and breach exposure of 1099 mass onboarding.
ideas.customer: Second-tier human-data vendors (challengers to the Mercor-scale players) and enterprise AI teams running expert-evaluation programs pay an 8-12% margin over payroll.
ideas.problem: A class action alleges Surge AI misclassified annotators, Mercor's reported breach exposed about 40k contractors' voice samples, and contractors report declining pay and stress. Enterprise buyers in banking and healthcare won't sign vendors lacking employment and security controls. Standard EOR services can't handle 2-40 hour micro-engagements.
ideas.solution: Instant W-2 onboarding across 50 states, with per-task hourly pay, automatic state paid-sick-leave accrual, workers' comp and unemployment tax handled. A data-security wrapper (SSO, ephemeral biometric handling) and portable pay stubs for the worker's income verification round it out.
ideas.why_now: Misclassification suits and breach fallout landed in 2025-26, enterprises are now buying expert data and demanding compliance, and a multi-million expert contractor pool has appeared with unprecedented scale.
ideas.revenue_model: 8-12% of payroll plus a per-worker admin fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Leading marketplaces prefer contractor status because they keep 30-40%, but enterprise and regulated buyers can't absorb the liability. Being the plumbing for challengers, not another marketplace, gives them the enterprise wedge against incumbents.
ideas.first_30_days: White-label an existing PEO or EOR to avoid licensing. Sign two small vendors (legal, medical or finance data) for a pilot cohort of 50 W-2 experts. Publish a misclassification-risk checklist to generate inbound.

ideas.title: Certified Coder Audit Pods for Autonomous Coding
ideas.one_liner: Displaced medical coders, organised as credentialed audit pods, provide the sampled human sign-off that lets hospitals trust autonomous coding AI to submit claims.
ideas.customer: Autonomous medical-coding vendors who need a human audit layer to close hospital deals, hospital revenue-cycle compliance leaders and physician groups. Pricing is $1.5-4 per audited chart or $15-40k a month per pod.
ideas.problem: Coding is a highly exposed white-collar job, and coders are being cut as autonomous coding reaches production. But billing compliance (False Claims Act exposure, payer and RAC audits) needs accountable, credentialed review. Vendors' own audit teams are thin or offshore and unlicensed.
ideas.solution: Pods of 5-10 CPC/CCS-certified ex-coders with a lead auditor, receiving risk-stratified samples of AI-coded charts via API. They provide error-taxonomy dashboards, monthly compliance attestations, feedback loops that retrain the model and contractual accuracy thresholds.
ideas.why_now: Autonomous coding moved into production in 2025-26, the coder job pool is shrinking, payers are using AI audits themselves and hospital margins are under pressure.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-chart fees or pod retainers at 45-55% gross margin, plus premium attestation packages.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Full automation in healthcare billing stalls at the accountability signature, and the people displaced are the ones who can provide it. The human role shifts from doing to auditing a 5-10% sample, which is recurring compliance spend rather than labor cost. The audit data is also valuable training data for the vendor.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 laid-off certified coders through AAPC and AHIMA forums. Pitch 5 autonomous-coding startups a pilot: audit 1,000 charts at about $2 each with a written accuracy report. Sign one as a design partner.

ideas.title: Program Survival Analytics for Regional Universities
ideas.one_liner: A subscription that tells provosts which degree programs will fail the new federal earnings tests and loan-cap economics as AI hollows out their feeder occupations, with a redesign playbook.
ideas.customer: Provosts, institutional research offices and deans at regional universities, master's-heavy colleges and online providers ($20-60k a year), plus state systems.
ideas.problem: As I understand the 2025 budget law (verify specifics), programs whose graduates don't out-earn benchmarks can lose loan eligibility, and Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers with new caps from July 2026. Graduate programs in cognitive fields (analytics, MBA, MS CS, communications) rely on borrowing, while entry-level demand is falling (NY Fed: 42% recent-grad underemployment). Institutions see it only when enrollment drops.
ideas.solution: A program-level model combining College Scorecard earnings, occupation-level job-posting trends, AI-exposure scores and enrollment and borrowing data. It delivers early-warning flags, a scenario tool, recommended pivots (in-degree apprenticeships, short credentials, employer co-design) backed by real employer demand signals, and board-ready compliance reporting.
ideas.why_now: The new loan and accountability rules began July 2026, the AI-driven junior hiring freeze is measurable (Stanford: 19% gap for ages 22-25), and university budgets are tight.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual licence of $20-60k, program-redesign consulting and state-system contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Universities already face compliance deadlines, but nobody has tied AI exposure to the earnings-test math. A federal deadline creates budget urgency that 'future of work' advice never gets. The first programs to fail are likely master's degrees in cognitive fields.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the model from public Scorecard data for ~200 institutions as a proof. Generate 'programs at risk' reports for 20 target universities' master's programs and email institutional-research directors and provosts. Sell three $7.5k pilot diagnostics.

ideas.title: Short-Time Compensation as a Service
ideas.one_liner: Software and admin that lets employers shrink hours instead of headcount using state work-sharing programs, where unemployment insurance replaces part of the lost wages, as an alternative to AI-driven layoffs.
ideas.customer: HR and finance leaders at 50-2,000-employee firms in states with work-sharing programs (about half of US states, verify) planning 10-30% reductions in AI-exposed teams. PEOs and payroll providers are channels.
ideas.problem: Employers treat headcount cuts as binary, yet many states pay prorated UI when firms cut hours 10-60% rather than lay people off. Almost nobody uses it. AI-driven demand shifts are gradual and uncertain, layoffs risk rehire regret and severance costs, and workers lose health coverage and face 6-13 month searches.
ideas.solution: (1) A calculator comparing work-sharing to layoff, including severance, recruiting and regret costs. (2) Plan-filing automation per state. (3) Weekly claim administration integrated with payroll. (4) A training-hours module for reduced-hours periods. (5) Tracking of approvals and caps. (6) A glide path to natural attrition.
ideas.why_now: AI restructuring is happening under uncertainty (Challenger shows AI-cited cuts small and partly narrative), reversal headlines are growing, and the market is low-fire, low-hire, so retaining talent has become valuable.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-60 per participating employee per month, or 5-10% of validated avoided severance and rehire cost, plus PEO reseller revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The subsidy already exists and is unused because nobody owns the admin burden. Becoming the 'TurboTax for work-sharing' turns a public benefit into a retention and anti-regret hedge that contradicts the 'cut now' reflex.
ideas.first_30_days: Map work-sharing rules and forms in the 6-8 biggest states. Interview 15 mid-size HR leads and 5 PEOs. Offer free feasibility analyses to companies that filed WARN notices and convert 2-3 to paid pilots.

ideas.title: Agent-Populated Simulated First Job for Juniors
ideas.one_liner: A 12-week simulated first job where new grads work inside a persistent fake company staffed by AI coworkers, clients and managers, producing an auditable work record employers trust.
ideas.customer: Employers pay $4-8k per hire or subscribe to pre-screened cohorts. Universities and bootcamps pay per-seat licences ($500-1,500), and state workforce boards fund seats. Start with RevOps, FP&A or customer-success analyst roles.
ideas.problem: The bottom rung is gone. Employers don't hire juniors because AI absorbs the tasks they learned on, and internships or apprenticeships need employer bandwidth, the very thing missing. Grads can't get the experience employers demand (Stanford: 19% gap, 42% underemployment).
ideas.solution: A persistent multi-agent world with a messy CRM or ledger, a ticket queue, stakeholder agents with hidden goals who change requirements, an AI manager giving 1:1s and an on-call incident. The junior works with their own AI tools and everything is logged. Senior humans grade a few deliverables weekly. The output is a portable 'experience ledger' (hours, artifacts, review outcomes, error-detection rates) employers can inspect.
ideas.why_now: Long-horizon agent capability and multi-agent simulation now make believable coworkers affordable (Project Vend-style and TheAgentCompany-style experiments), employers say they can't evaluate candidates in AI-permitted interviews, and the freeze is widening.
ideas.revenue_model: Employer per-hire success fees and pre-screen subscriptions, university licences and modest learner fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The cold start of apprenticeship marketplaces is employer supply. A simulation removes it: the employer is fake but the evaluation is real. Employers hire on traces of judgment rather than resumes, and the moat is a scenario library built from anonymised real incidents.
ideas.first_30_days: Build one role sim (RevOps analyst) with 4 agent personas. Run it with 20 recent grads via a college career centre. Get 5 mid-size SaaS employers to review the graduates' traces and commit to interviews.

ideas.title: Parametric Cover Against Career-Field Collapse
ideas.one_liner: Index-based protection that pays out when hiring in a specific occupation falls past a threshold, sold first to bootcamps, income-share funds and private student lenders whose job-guarantee promises are now correlated bets on entry-level demand.
ideas.customer: Bootcamps with job guarantees, ISA funds, private student lenders and university tuition-protection programs. Later, workers via employers and universities as a benefit.
ideas.problem: These institutions underwrite outcomes assuming stable entry-level demand. If CS, marketing or analytics hiring drops 30% they all fail together, and no hedge exists. The tail risk is now visible (22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend, junior tech postings down ~35% in major EU countries in 2024).
ideas.solution: Phase 1 (about 6 months): publish an Occupation Demand Index (postings, hires, claims mix by occupation and metro) plus stress-test analytics, sold as a subscription to lenders and ISA funds. Phase 2: structure parametric covers through an MGA, fronting carrier and reinsurers, triggered by the index. Phase 3: consumer livelihood cover via employers and universities.
ideas.why_now: Occupation-level posting data (e.g. Indeed Hiring Lab) is rich, AI exposure is a new correlated risk, parametric insurance infrastructure has matured, ISA funds and bootcamps are under strain, and event-contract markets are normalised.
ideas.revenue_model: Analytics subscriptions ($30-120k a year) first, then premiums and ceding commissions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Occupational risk has never been hedged because individual triggers create moral hazard. An index solves that for institutions whose portfolio effectively is the occupation, and AI displacement is exactly the correlated tail that reinsurers price.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the index from public BLS and posting data and backtest against bootcamp outcome reports. Pitch 10 ISA funds, bootcamps and private lenders a paid $10-25k stress-test pilot.

ideas.title: Royalty Marketplace for Expert Agent Skills
ideas.one_liner: Retired and displaced specialists package their procedures, judgment rubrics and worked examples as machine-loadable skill packs that companies' agents pull on demand, with per-run metering and royalties to the author.
ideas.customer: Enterprises and SMBs deploying agents in regulated or technical workflows pay $200-2,000 a month per seat or per run. Authors are displaced experts who earn royalties.
ideas.problem: Agents are competent generalists that fail on domain procedures (customs classification, prior-authorisation appeals, tax-exchange steps). Hourly expert gigs pay once, so expertise is consumed without ongoing income, and enterprises can't find vetted, tested procedures.
ideas.solution: A curated marketplace of skill packs in the open Agent Skills format (instructions, scripts and tests), each with an eval suite and author credentials, metered per invocation through an MCP gateway. Quality is scored on held-out test performance and versions update as rules change. Wedge: tariff and customs-compliance packs written by retired customs brokers.
ideas.why_now: The Agent Skills format (Oct 2025) and MCP are becoming standard across agent tools, tariff volatility since 2025 has created urgent demand for trade-compliance expertise, and experienced professionals are being displaced.
ideas.revenue_model: 25-30% take on subscriptions and per-run fees, plus enterprise private-skill hosting.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Hourly data labor turns experts into a consumable, while royalties make them asset owners. A metered gateway makes value attributable, and the moat is trusted eval suites rather than the marketplace itself.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 8 retired customs brokers or trade-compliance professionals. Build 5 tested skill packs and an eval harness. Sell to 10 importers already using agents at $300 a month and measure error reduction.

ideas.title: Worker-Owned Agentic Back-Office Cooperatives
ideas.one_liner: A franchise-in-a-box that helps laid-off finance and admin staff form co-ops running agent-leveraged bookkeeping, payroll and billing services for local small businesses, keeping the surplus themselves.
ideas.customer: Small businesses (5-50 employees) pay $600-2,500 a month. The co-ops pay a 5-8% platform fee, and are financed by cooperative-lending CDFIs, SBA microloans and workforce boards.
ideas.problem: The AI productivity dividend flows to platform owners while back-office workers lose jobs. Small businesses lack trusted human accountability (Bench's Dec 2024 shutdown stranded about 35k SMBs), and pure-AI bookkeepers still need a human on the hook.
ideas.solution: Co-op charter templates under state worker-co-op law, a shared agent stack (ledger automation, document intake, reconciliation) so each member handles 30-60 clients, a shared E&O policy, bank account and brand, client acquisition through local CPAs and chambers, and patronage dividends. Six-week onboarding.
ideas.why_now: Agentic accounting can now handle high-volume categorisation and reconciliation, finance-ops layoffs are rising, Bench's collapse left an opening, and co-op-friendly state laws and CDFI capital exist.
ideas.revenue_model: 5-8% of co-op revenue as a platform fee, tooling margin and $5-10k implementation fees per co-op.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Ownership is the lever: workers who own the margin adopt agents fully, whereas employees hide productivity gains for fear of layoff. The scarce asset is trusted local human accountability, and agents supply the cost side.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 8-10 laid-off bookkeepers and controllers in one metro through layoff communities. Form a pilot co-op with a co-op legal clinic. Sign 15 SMB clients via three local CPAs and a chamber and run the first monthly closes.

ideas.title: Vetted Remote Operators for Home Robots
ideas.one_liner: A privacy-audited, background-checked, insured pool of remote operators who take over home and warehouse robots at their hard moments, sold to robot makers as the trust layer for teleoperation.
ideas.customer: Home-robot, service-robot and warehouse-robot makers pay $18-35 per operator-hour. Operators are displaced support and ops workers earning $22-30 an hour.
ideas.problem: The first consumer humanoids (such as 1X's NEO) ship in 2026 relying on remote humans who can see inside homes, which raised a privacy backlash. Robot startups lack a scalable, vetted, insured operator workforce and would otherwise use anonymous offshore BPOs, while buyers want accountable domestic operators.
ideas.solution: Recruit and train from displaced call-centre, ops and gaming talent. A standard teleop certification, privacy protocols (blurred or avatarised feeds, no recording, no-go zones), session audit logs, background checks and E&O/cyber insurance form the service. Scheduling covers time zones and performance metrics track intervention success. Start with warehouse or delivery robots, then homes.
ideas.why_now: Consumer humanoid preorders and shipments began in 2025-26 with teleop as the fallback, warehouse and sidewalk robots are at scale, and privacy concerns make trust a differentiator.
ideas.revenue_model: 30-40% margin per operator-hour, certification fees and an insurance premium share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for robots is not hardware but trusted remote labor, and every teleop intervention also trains the policy. Privacy trust, not price, is the moat, and it reframes displaced workers as a new 'robot pilot' class.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact 20 robotics startups (delivery, warehouse, cleaning) with a pilot of 5 vetted operators for 200 hours at cost. Write the privacy protocol and audit template. Recruit 30 candidates from laid-off support and ops staff.

ideas.title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
ideas.one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
ideas.customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
ideas.problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
ideas.solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
ideas.why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.

ideas.title: Ratepayer Impact Statements for Data Centers
ideas.one_liner: An independent, quantified 'who pays' filing for every proposed data center, like an environmental impact statement but for your electric bill.
ideas.customer: Data center developers who need a credible neutral document to win zoning or PUC approval ($50-150k per project). County governments, state consumer advocates and ratepayer coalitions ($15-40k per docket) also buy it.
ideas.problem: 7 in 10 Americans oppose data centers in their community and New York imposed a hyperscale moratorium. Residential rates are up 7.3% and utilities requested a record $31B in hikes in 2025. Nobody can credibly say how much of a specific rate case or interconnection cost a given project causes, so each side hires ad hoc experts and the fight runs on vibes.
ideas.solution: An open, auditable cost-causation model built on FERC Form 1, EIA-861, large-load tariff filings, IRP capacity plans and PJM auction results. It outputs a 10-year per-household bill delta for a specific project under different tariff terms (minimum take, collateral, bring-your-own-capacity). Deliverables are a standardized Ratepayer Impact Statement and a witness-ready exhibit. A free state-by-state 'who pays' scorecard is the top of the funnel.
ideas.why_now: Affordability is a midterm issue and opposition is now bill-driven. Utilities are adopting large-load tariffs whose terms can be modeled. Capacity prices at the cap make cost shifts visible in dollars per MWh.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-project fee from developers, per-docket fee from advocates and counties, and an annual subscription for PUC staff. Independence comes from a published fee schedule and a methodology committed in advance, as with credit rating agencies.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders dismiss opposition as NIMBY, but it is really about bills, and bills are quantifiable. Whoever owns the accepted number owns the approval process. Both sides will pay for it, the way both sides accept an appraisal.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free 'Who Pays' report for three states using public filings. Email 10 state consumer advocate offices and 20 county planning departments. Offer a $12k pilot impact statement on one live docket. Approach two mid-size developers who are stuck in a zoning fight.

ideas.title: Credit Ratings and Insurance for Virtual Power Plants
ideas.one_liner: A neutral firmness rating plus a parametric shortfall policy, so hyperscalers and utilities can buy VPP megawatts they can actually count.
ideas.customer: VPP operators and installers (pay for the rating), hyperscalers and utilities buying capacity (subscribe to reports), and reinsurers and MGAs (take the risk and pay a fronting fee).
ideas.problem: Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home announced 16.8 GW of 'capacity-as-a-service' for data centers with no disclosed pricing, metering or verification standard. A 580 MW dispatch from 140k batteries on Sept 9 proves the tech works, but one event is not firm capacity. Buyers under bring-your-own-capacity rules need MW they can legally rely on.
ideas.solution: Publish a methodology that works like ELCC for distributed fleets: fleet-level P50/P90 availability by season and hour from attested device telemetry, with letter-grade tiers. Add a parametric policy, underwritten by a partner MGA or reinsurer, that pays the buyer if delivered MW falls below rated MW in a dispatch event. Start with public data from the ERCOT ADER pilot and California's DSGS program.
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler-VPP deals, PJM's curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule and real dispatch events like Sept 9 mean there is finally enough event data to rate fleets.
ideas.revenue_model: $50-250k a year per fleet rated, subscriptions from buyers, and a fee or premium share on the insurance wrap.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The VPP industry thinks its hard problem is enrollment. The buyer's hard problem is trust. Hyperscalers only pay for 'firm' if a third party is on the hook. Ratings plus insurance turn dispatch volatility into a financial product, and the standard-setter collects a toll on every MW sold.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish an unsolicited scorecard of public ERCOT ADER and California DSGS dispatch performance. Offer 15 VPP operators a free confidential rating in exchange for telemetry. Sound out two MGAs or reinsurers on parametric structure. Pre-sell a rating to one aggregator that is already pitching hyperscalers.

ideas.title: Sell Heat Pumps to Health Plans
ideas.one_liner: Sell home electrification to Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans as a cost-of-care reduction instead of selling it to homeowners as a climate upgrade.
ideas.customer: Medicaid managed-care organizations, Medicare Advantage plans (supplemental benefits) and nonprofit hospital community-benefit budgets. They pay per completed install, plus an outcome bonus.
ideas.problem: The 25C credit ended 12/31/2025, homeowners face ~$9,000 heat pump quotes, and HEAR rebates roll out unevenly by state. Meanwhile health plans pay for asthma and COPD ER visits, heat illness and gas-stove-related respiratory events that cost thousands per admission.
ideas.solution: A 'clinical electrification program in a box'. Claims data finds members with asthma, COPD or heat vulnerability. A vetted contractor network installs a heat pump, heat pump water heater or induction cooktop. The program stacks HEAR/HOMES rebates so the plan pays only the gap, tracks ER visits and medication use, and reports ROI to the plan. Billing runs through Medicaid health-related-social-needs and in-lieu-of-service pathways or MA supplemental benefits.
ideas.why_now: Some state Medicaid waivers (Oregon's climate-device benefit) and MA plans already pay for air conditioners and air filtration. $8.8B of HEAR/HOMES money needs matching demand. Federal homeowner credits are gone, so the old buyer has weakened.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-6k net per install paid by the plan after rebate stacking, a platform fee, contractor take-rate, and outcome-based bonuses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders keep trying to improve the homeowner's payback. The payer with the fastest ROI is the one who pays for ambulances. Health plans have budget lines, claims data to find the right homes, and no need for a 10-year payback.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with a Medicaid climate-device benefit or a Southwest MA plan. Find two MCO community-health leads. Build claims-based targeting analytics. Run a 25-home pilot with one contractor using existing HEAR or utility rebates, and write a one-page ROI memo from baseline ER usage.

ideas.title: Add Megawatt-Hours to Already-Interconnected Batteries
ideas.one_liner: The queue limits megawatts, not megawatt-hours, so sell cheap add-on energy blocks to existing 2-hour battery and solar sites that already own the grid connection.
ideas.customer: Owners of 2019-2024 vintage 2-hour storage and solar sites (IPPs, infrastructure funds, utilities) in PJM, ERCOT and CAISO. Storage developers and data center developers who lack queue positions are the second buyer group.
ideas.problem: New MW wait years in interconnection queues. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh and new projects average 3.5 hours. Existing 2-hour fleets are under-accredited for capacity, and their owners are not thinking about bolt-on energy.
ideas.solution: Engineer and finance duration uplift by adding DC-coupled or AC-block MWh behind the existing inverters and point of interconnection. Provide standardized BMS integration and warranty tooling. Second product: use surplus interconnection headroom at solar and wind farms to add storage MW, with a revenue share to the site owner. The company screens sites from public data, packages them and sells them or builds them.
ideas.why_now: Cell prices collapsed. Capacity prices at the cap reward accredited duration. Regulators (surplus interconnection service, MISO ERAS, PJM RRI) are openly trying to reuse existing grid connections.
ideas.revenue_model: Engineering and development fee per kWh added, a share of incremental capacity revenue, or resale of ready-to-build projects.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the interconnection agreement, not the battery. Every existing 2-hour battery is a queue position with half its energy potential unused, and it is the one capacity addition that skips the queue.
ideas.first_30_days: List ~200 US storage projects at 2 hours or less from EIA-860 and ISO data. Model uplift economics for 10 of them under PJM and ERCOT rules. Send owners a one-page 'what two more hours earns you' analysis. Sign two or three paid feasibility studies. Line up a non-FEOC DC block supplier.

ideas.title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers
ideas.one_liner: Validated dynamic load models and ride-through test packages so data centers can pass the same grid-code exams that generators pass.
ideas.customer: Interconnection teams at hyperscalers, neoclouds and colo developers, and their EPCs. Transmission owners and ISOs need the models validated, and the developer pays.
ideas.problem: About 1.5 GW of Northern Virginia data center load tripped offline together during a 2024 fault. AI training loads swing tens of MW in seconds, and xAI buys Megapacks largely to smooth them. Texas SB 6 and NERC large-load work now push for ride-through and dynamic models, but no standard model library or test lab exists for GPU cluster, power-supply and UPS stacks.
ideas.solution: Build a parametric EMT and PSS/E model library for common facility architectures (UPS topologies, PSU behavior, 800V DC). Validate it with hardware-in-the-loop tests at a partner lab. Sell per-project model packages, ride-through study reports and compliance-ready certification letters. Charge a subscription to keep models current as hardware changes.
ideas.why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
ideas.revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. Inverter-generator modeling became a consulting industry after events like the 2016 Blue Cut fire, and large-load modeling will follow. The model library is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit one or two power-electronics engineers from a utility or ISO. Publish an open primer on GPU-load oscillation. Contact interconnection leads at 10 neoclouds and 5 TO planners. Sell a $15k 'large-load model gap analysis'. Sign a university hardware-in-the-loop lab as a partner.

ideas.title: Plug-In Electrification Kits for Landlords
ideas.one_liner: Sell curated no-new-circuit kits (120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps, induction, balcony solar) to small landlords and housing authorities as an electrician-light retrofit.
ideas.customer: Small landlords (1-50 units), property managers and public housing authorities. Utilities and state HEAR programs co-fund the kits.
ideas.problem: Data centers pay electricians 25-30% more, so residential contractors cannot staff jobs. Panel upgrades cost $1,500-5,000. Renters and multifamily have no obvious product, and landlords have no reason to pay for tenants' savings.
ideas.solution: A packaged program with approved plug-in devices only (UL 3700 balcony solar in states that legalized it, 120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps). Maintenance staff or a handyman installs them. The company handles rebate stacking, a lease addendum and tenant paperwork, an insurance rider, and remote monitoring. It also sells a landlord 'plug-in policy in a box' for HOAs and condo boards.
ideas.why_now: Nine states had signed plug-in solar laws by September 2026 and UL 3700 now exists. 120V heat pump water heaters and window heat pumps arrived, and housing-authority window heat pump rollouts show large buyers exist. Labor scarcity makes no-electrician products the path of least resistance.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on $1.5-4k kits, a per-unit administration fee from utility and state programs, and SaaS for portfolio managers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The electrician shortage is the binding constraint, so design products that do not need one. Renter electrification will run through plug-ins, and whoever writes the landlord's compliance and insurance paperwork controls distribution.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two plug-in-friendly states. Assemble a three-SKU kit from existing vendors. Pitch 20 small landlord associations and two housing authorities. Sell 20 kits. Get an insurer's written OK on the rider language.

ideas.title: Batteries That Pay Off Utility Arrears
ideas.one_liner: Install free home batteries in households behind on bills and let capacity payments retire the debt, which is cheaper for the utility than writing it off.
ideas.customer: Utilities, co-ops and munis in high-capacity-price regions (PJM first) that run arrears and shutoff programs. State PUCs and community action agencies co-sponsor. The utility pays from bad-debt and program budgets.
ideas.problem: 13.4M households were disconnected in 2024 and about 1 in 6 are behind on bills. Rates rose 7.3% in a year and this is a midterm issue. At the $325/MW-day cap, each kW of dispatchable capacity is worth about $118 a year, so a 5 kW home battery is worth roughly $590 a year gross, before accreditation haircuts and the aggregator's share.
ideas.solution: A no-cost 10 kWh 'bill-relief battery' for arrears households, enrolled in a utility or aggregator capacity program. Capacity and energy revenue is credited against the arrears balance for 5-7 years, after which the customer keeps it or the utility retains it. The company handles installation, financing and dispatch. The utility gets less bad debt and fewer politically toxic shutoffs.
ideas.why_now: Capacity prices hit the cap, packs cost about $70/kWh, dispatch at scale is proven, and utilities are under political pressure on affordability with few tools.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-install fee, a share of capacity revenue while the arrears are being retired, utility program payments, and project finance spread.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: At this capacity price, a battery earns more than it costs to give one away. Utility bad debt is a hidden capex budget that has never been spent on assets.
ideas.first_30_days: Get one utility's arrears distribution and model unit economics under current capacity prices. Pitch five community action agencies and three co-ops or munis on a 50-home pilot funded by weatherization-adjacent money. Line up a philanthropic first-loss guarantee.

ideas.title: Street-Level Gas Pipe Retirement Optimizer
ideas.one_liner: Software plus a turnkey block-by-block electrification crew that tells gas utilities which streets to retire instead of replace.
ideas.customer: Regulated gas distribution utilities in MA, NY, CO, MN, WA, CA and IL, and their regulators. Funding comes from pipe-replacement capex budgets.
ideas.problem: Electrification shrinks gas throughput, so fixed pipe costs land on fewer customers. Utilities still replace leak-prone mains at millions of dollars per mile. Regulators (for example Massachusetts DPU 20-80-B) demand non-pipeline alternatives, but nobody optimizes at street-segment level. Heat pump quotes run ~$9,000 and labor is scarce.
ideas.solution: GIS, billing and housing-stock analytics that score each pipe segment for retire-versus-replace, and find streets where electrifying 30-80 homes costs less than replacing the main. Then deliver the electrification block by block: group purchase, one crew per street per week, optionally networked geothermal. It is filed as a utility non-pipeline alternative.
ideas.why_now: State non-pipeline-alternative orders and thermal-energy-network laws are in force. With federal credits dead, utility-funded programs are the only scaled electrification channel. Ratepayer affordability pressure makes stranded pipe a live issue.
ideas.revenue_model: $250-500k a year SaaS per utility plus a per-home program fee ($5-12k) paid from avoided pipe capex.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Gas utilities' problem is no longer selling heat pumps. It is stranded pipe. Their pipe replacement capex is the electrification budget hiding in plain sight.
ideas.first_30_days: Model one Massachusetts or New York utility territory from public leak-prone-pipe, assessor and census data. Publish a 'retire-first streets' list for one city. Pitch a city sustainability office, a regulator and two utility strategy VPs. Sell a $60-100k pilot analysis.

ideas.title: Verified-MW Truth Feed for Data Center Load
ideas.one_liner: A probability score and satellite-plus-permit verification of every large-load request, so planners and investors can tell the real 42 GW from the 201 GW of paper.
ideas.customer: Utility load-forecast and IRP teams, ISOs, state PUC staff and consumer advocates. Hedge funds, infrastructure investors and equipment makers buy the same feed as alternative data.
ideas.problem: About 36.6 GW is under construction versus about 201 GW 'in planning'. Developers file duplicate requests at several utilities, utilities over-forecast, and ratepayers fund the generation and wires built for load that never shows up. Even xAI's Memphis battery is '2.8 GWh counted versus 3.3 GWh claimed' and nobody verifies it.
ideas.solution: Fuse interconnection filings, zoning and permit records, tax abatements, transformer and switchgear procurement signals, construction imagery (SAR and optical), thermal signatures of cooling plants and tariff deposits into a per-project probability of energization by date and MW online. Ship it as an API, quarterly reports and exhibits usable in regulatory proceedings.
ideas.why_now: Large-load requests are exploding, utilities are adding deposit rules, and cheap satellite data plus LLM document parsing lets a three-person team do this.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-500k a year per investor subscription and $75-300k per utility or ISO, with discounted licenses for consumer advocates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The most expensive number in the grid is the load forecast, and it is built from self-reported requests. Hedge funds already want the same data for AI-capex tracking, so they can fund a public-interest product.
ideas.first_30_days: Build datasets for Virginia, Ohio and Texas. Publish a 'phantom load index'. Sell three alternative-data subscriptions at $30-50k. Offer free trials to two consumer advocate offices.

ideas.title: Warm-Backup Servicer for Orphaned Solar
ideas.one_liner: Be the standby operations-and-maintenance contractor for lenders and securitization trustees holding portfolios of systems whose installer died.
ideas.customer: Trustees and servicers of solar loan and lease securitizations, tax-equity and debt holders, and buyers of distressed portfolios. Homeowners can buy direct as a secondary channel.
ideas.problem: Sunnova, Titan, ADT Solar and Freedom Forever failed. Manufacturer warranties survive but nobody supplies the service labor, and monitoring clouds die. Customers with dead inverters stop paying, which erodes the cash flows lenders depend on.
ideas.solution: A backup-servicing contract. Onboard the portfolio's asset data, replace dead monitoring clouds with a local gateway, dispatch vetted local technicians through a roll-up network, handle manufacturer RMA and warranty claims, and upsell battery retrofit and VPP enrollment.
ideas.why_now: The bankruptcy wave of 2024-26 has portfolios sitting in trustees' hands. With 25D gone there are fewer new installers. A 46% storage attach rate means more complex systems in the field.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-15 per system-month standby retainer, a $250-450 margin per truck roll, an RMA handling fee, and referral fees for battery and VPP enrollments.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Lenders do not care about kilowatts. They care about payments, and a homeowner with a dead inverter stops paying. Service is a credit-protection product, and its buyer is the party with the balance sheet and the pain.
ideas.first_30_days: Identify three distressed portfolios from trustee reports and call the servicers. Sign a 1,000-system pilot in one metro. Onboard two local service shops. Build the gateway on vendor APIs and local Modbus.

ideas.title: FEOC and Cyber Passport for Batteries
ideas.one_liner: A serial-number-level ledger of material-assistance content and firmware and comms attestations for storage projects, built for tax-credit buyers and insurers.
ideas.customer: C&I and utility-scale storage developers and integrators, tax-credit transfer buyers (banks and insurers), and lenders.
ideas.problem: FEOC rules require 55% non-FEOC content for storage starting construction in 2026, rising to 75% by 2030. About 80% of US cells are Chinese and non-compliant projects run about 43% pricier. IRS cost tables are not due until 2027, so nobody can prove compliance. Buyers of tax credits and insurers need evidence, and concern about undocumented radios in imported inverters adds a cyber layer.
ideas.solution: A workflow and ledger that captures the bill of materials at cell and module level with supplier attestations and cost tables, then computes the material-assistance ratio conservatively. Each project gets an audit-ready evidence packet. Optional teardown, RF and firmware attestation runs through a partner lab. The 'passport' is what transfer buyers and insurers accept.
ideas.why_now: FEOC applies to 2026 construction starts, the tax-credit transfer market is doing diligence at scale, and tariffs are rising.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-50k per project, $2-5k a month SaaS per developer, verification fees from transfer buyers, and cost-plus lab attestation.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The burden is evidence, not sourcing. With IRS guidance missing, the first firm whose conservative methodology gets accepted becomes the de facto standard, and insurers will only underwrite recapture cover against that record.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free MACR calculator with conservative assumptions. Interview 10 developers and three tax-credit transfer buyers. Sell three paid compliance-file builds at ~$15k for 2026-start projects. Pre-agree terms with an attestation lab.

ideas.title: Transformer Buying Co-op for Small Utilities
ideas.one_liner: Pool the orders of hundreds of rural co-ops and municipal utilities into one standardized spec so they can get in line together.
ideas.customer: Roughly 900 electric distribution co-ops and 2,000 municipal utilities, plus solar and storage developers. They pay a procurement fee.
ideas.problem: Power transformer lead times average 128 weeks, distribution transformer prices are up as much as 95%, and over 40M units are past service life. Small utilities order in dozens with bespoke specs and go to the back of the line. One contrarian says standardized units can ship in 12-14 months, so procurement, not manufacturing, is the bottleneck.
ideas.solution: Pre-negotiated framework agreements with two or three manufacturers (including offshore) for a small menu of standard units, for example pad-mount 25-167 kVA and 5-10 MVA substation units. Add a predictive replacement list built from age and AMI loading data, a financed rotating stock pool, and slot reassignment among members.
ideas.why_now: Data centers outbid utilities for manufacturing slots, lead times are at 128 weeks, and co-ops and munis are scrambling with no purchasing leverage.
ideas.revenue_model: 2-4% procurement fee, a stock-pool financing and storage spread, and $10-30k a year SaaS for replacement planning.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Part of the shortage is fragmentation. Manufacturers prioritize buyers who commit to standard specs and volume, and small utilities are collectively huge but individually invisible.
ideas.first_30_days: Collect 30 co-op and muni transformer spec sheets. Propose a common spec at a state co-op association or APPA event. Get five utilities to sign LOIs for a 200-unit pilot order. Talk to two mid-size manufacturers with open 2028 slots.

ideas.title: Independent Battery Safety Review for Counties
ideas.one_liner: Sell counties and fire marshals a developer-funded third-party plan review, hazard analysis and first-responder plan for every battery project.
ideas.customer: Storage developers pay the fees, usually through a county-controlled escrow. Counties and fire authorities contract the reviewer, and insurers use the dossiers.
ideas.problem: US storage installs hit a record 18.9 GWh in Q2 2026. After the January 2025 Moss Landing fire, hearings turn hostile and local moratoria spread. Fire departments lack expertise, NFPA 855 and UL 9540A data are hard to interpret, and developers lose 6-12 months in permitting.
ideas.solution: An independent safety dossier: hazard mitigation analysis, interpretation of large-scale fire test data, an emergency response plan, a thermal and off-gas monitoring plan and training for local responders. Sell it as fixed-price packages with an annual inspection option, plus a model county ordinance and review checklist.
ideas.why_now: Record installs are moving into populated areas, moratoria and insurer repricing are active, and code cycles are updating.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-80k per project via the county escrow, $5-10k a year for inspections, and training contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is trust, not technology. A reviewer the county chooses but the developer pays, like a planning consultant, speeds approvals and removes the NIMBY veto.
ideas.first_30_days: Draft a model BESS review ordinance and checklist. Offer free reviews to three counties with pending applications. Get two developers to pay for pre-application dossiers. Retain a fire-protection PE and a retired fire marshal.

ideas.title: Arc-Flash and Protection Studies Factory
ideas.one_liner: Deliver PE-stamped short-circuit, coordination and arc-flash studies in days rather than months, using AI to turn photos and one-lines into models.
ideas.customer: Electrical contractors and EPCs building C&I storage, EV depots and data center electrical rooms, plus facility managers facing five-year label refreshes.
ideas.problem: Power-systems engineers are scarce and studies gate energization and permits, with 8-12 week backlogs. A delayed 60 MW site costs about $3M a week. NFPA 70E requires reassessment every five years, and small C&I storage projects cannot afford $30k custom studies.
ideas.solution: Studies as a productized service. The contractor uploads single-line diagrams, nameplate photos and the utility fault-current letter. AI extracts the equipment and builds the ETAP or SKM model, a licensed PE reviews and stamps it, and the customer gets labels and coordination settings on a five-business-day SLA at a flat price per switchboard.
ideas.why_now: Vision and language models now parse one-lines and nameplates well enough to draft models. The data center and storage boom, and the engineer shortage, make throughput the scarce resource.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-15k per small C&I study, $30-100k per data center study, and recurring five-year renewals plus label printing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody lacks software. They lack stamps and turnaround time. PE-supervised throughput with AI drafts is a labor arbitrage that stays unglamorous enough to avoid heavy competition.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit two retired power-systems PEs. Build the extraction pipeline on 20 anonymized one-lines. Sell five C&I storage installers a $4k fixed-price study with a five-day SLA. Measure margins.

ideas.title: Compute Boilers: Servers That Heat Buildings
ideas.one_liner: Install liquid-cooled inference servers in the boiler rooms of hotels, dorms, pools and laundries, sell the compute, and give the building cheap hot water.
ideas.customer: Hotels, university housing, municipal pools and YMCAs, multifamily buildings with central hot water, and laundries. They get cheaper heat. Inference providers buy the compute.
ideas.problem: Large AI sites wait years in interconnection queues, yet buildings already have continuous thermal loads, existing 3-phase service and unused headroom. Sub-MW loads avoid large-load studies. Owners face pressure to electrify hot water and building-emissions fines such as NYC's Local Law 97.
ideas.solution: Sealed 30-100 kW direct-to-chip liquid-cooled modules plumbed into building hot-water loops that capture most of the heat. The company owns and operates the hardware and sells GPU-hours to inference customers through a neocloud partner. The host gets heat at a discount to its gas or electric cost. First product: 20-40 kW pilots at about 10 hotels and pools in one metro.
ideas.why_now: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling is now standard, AI demand exceeds grid supply, small-model inference fits ordinary fiber, and UK pool and hot-water-cylinder server projects prove the model.
ideas.revenue_model: Compute revenue share, heat sold to hosts at 50-70% of their current fuel cost, and GPU-lender financing of the hardware.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The grid is not short of electrons. It is short of interconnection at big sites. Sub-MW building sites already have service and a thermal sink, and heat reuse lowers hosting cost below any standalone data center, so the queue is bypassed.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign LOIs with five hospitality or pool operators in a state with cheap power and good fiber. Run heat-load audits. Spec a module with a liquid-cooling OEM. Get a GPU-lender term sheet. Deploy a 10 kW test unit at one site.

ideas.title: Battery-Islanded Feeders Instead of Undergrounding
ideas.one_liner: Sell utilities islandable rural feeders powered by enrolled home batteries as a cheaper alternative to undergrounding and repeated wildfire power shutoffs.
ideas.customer: Wildfire-exposed utilities and co-ops (California, Pacific Northwest, Colorado, Hawaii), funded from wildfire-mitigation capex. Tribal and community microgrids are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: Undergrounding costs roughly $2-3M or more per mile, and public safety power shutoffs cut power to thousands of homes for days. Home batteries are common (46% storage attach), but each only serves its own house, and utilities cannot use them to keep a whole feeder alive.
ideas.solution: A feeder-level controller, smart switch and grid-forming coordination software that lets a segment island when upstream is de-energized, with enrolled home batteries powering critical loads. The same software runs normal VPP dispatch to pay for itself. The utility contracts it as a non-wires wildfire alternative.
ideas.why_now: 140k batteries delivered 580 MW on Sept 9, grid-forming inverters are now standard, wildfire budgets are large, and affordability limits undergrounding.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per customer-year availability payment from the utility, a controller lease, and VPP revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The battery is already in the house, and the missing pieces are coordination and a switch. Utilities cannot earn a return on efficiency, but they can on wildfire mitigation capex, and you are competing against $3M per mile.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach small co-ops and munis in fire-prone areas. Pick a 200-home feeder with at least 30% battery attach. Propose a paid $40k feasibility study and a pilot using existing devices. Partner with a microgrid-controller vendor.

ideas.title: Delay Insurance for Data Center Energization
ideas.one_liner: Parametric insurance and pricing data that pay developers and lenders when the utility misses its committed energization date.
ideas.customer: Data center developers, construction lenders and hyperscale tenants with delivery-date penalties. Reinsurers supply the capital.
ideas.problem: A delayed 60 MW site costs about $14M a month. Utilities commit to dates that slip, standard delay-in-start-up cover excludes utility delay, and developers cannot hedge the largest schedule risk in the AI buildout.
ideas.solution: Build a database of utility energization performance (committed versus actual dates) by utility and substation type. Write parametric cover with the trigger set at the utility's committed date plus N days, under an MGA or coverholder structure with a Lloyd's or reinsurance backer. Also sell a 'time-to-power index' to lenders and developers.
ideas.why_now: The hyperscale pipeline is huge, waits reach years, and new large-load tariffs formalize committed dates, so the risk is finally observable in public filings.
ideas.revenue_model: Premium of roughly 2-5% of limit a year, with 15-20% MGA commission, plus data subscriptions from lenders and developers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Delay looks uninsurable only until you notice it is parametric. The trigger is the utility's own date, which the developer cannot move, and it is currently priced by gut.
ideas.first_30_days: Compile a dataset from ~200 public PUC and utility large-load filings. Publish a free 'Time-to-Power Index' teaser. Meet three MGAs or coverholders. Pitch 10 lenders. Land one design-partner letter of intent.

ideas.title: Beneficiary-Funded Dynamic Line Ratings
ideas.one_liner: Skip the utility's missing incentive: let the data center or generator that needs capacity pay for dynamic line ratings and take a slice of the capacity released.
ideas.customer: Data center developers and congestion-constrained renewable, storage and merchant generation owners. The utility is a passive partner.
ideas.problem: Dynamic line rating adds 30-50% capacity at about a tenth of the cost of reconductoring, but utilities earn no return on operating savings, so adoption is stuck. Projects held back by a few constrained lines lose years or revenue.
ideas.solution: A special-purpose company funds and deploys DLR (sensors plus weather-model virtual ratings) on the specific lines limiting a beneficiary's project. A three-party agreement has the utility accept ratings with a safety margin and keep the reliability data, the beneficiary gets earlier energization or less curtailment, and the company earns a capacity-uplift fee for about 10 years.
ideas.why_now: Automated study tools (Tapestry ran ~220 GW of PJM applications in under an hour) show speed is possible. FERC's ambient-adjusted ratings rule and GETs consideration laws mainstream the concept. Cost of delay is enormous.
ideas.revenue_model: Cost-plus up-front sensors and analytics, plus an annual $/kW capacity-uplift fee or a share of avoided curtailment.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for the utility's incentive to change, and it will not. Contract the incentive from the customer instead. That is structurally a customer-funded upgrade, which utilities already know how to accept.
ideas.first_30_days: Use public congestion and rating data to find the 20 lines most limiting renewables and large loads. Sell three $25-60k congestion and rating audits to constrained project owners. Recruit one utility engineering champion. Resell sensors from an existing DLR vendor.

ideas.title: Transformer-Level VPP That Defers Replacements
