ideas.one_liner: Orchestrate home batteries, water heaters and chargers under each overloaded transformer, and get paid by the utility for every replacement you delay.
ideas.customer: Rural co-ops and municipal utilities facing 128-week transformer lead times, with investor-owned utilities later. The utility pays per transformer-year of deferral.
ideas.problem: Over 40M distribution transformers are past service life and new EVs and heat pumps overload them. Lead times are long and prices are up sharply. Today's VPPs dispatch at system level and ignore which transformer is constrained.
ideas.solution: Join each enrolled device to its transformer using AMI and GIS data, forecast loading, and dispatch flexible devices to keep every unit under its thermal limit. Guarantee performance with a penalty, and offer participating homes discounted batteries or controllers. Start with cheap loads (thermostats, water heaters, EV chargers) before batteries.
ideas.why_now: Transformer lead times, a 46% storage attach rate, proven large-scale dispatch, wide AMI deployment and mature DER standards (IEEE 2030.5, OpenADR 3).
ideas.revenue_model: $1-3k per transformer per year deferral fee versus $15-40k replacement cost, plus SaaS and VPP energy revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: VPPs are sold on system capacity, but the utility's scarcest asset is local: the pad-mount unit. Flexibility at the right node beats megawatts at the wrong one.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one co-op with AMI data. Analyze it to find ~50 near-limit transformers. Propose a 90-day pilot with about 200 homes starting with thermostats, water heaters and chargers. Use measured loading reduction as the success metric.

ideas.title: Independent Robot Bake-Off and Acceptance Lab
ideas.one_liner: A neutral test cell where warehouse buyers watch robots handle their own SKUs and pallets before signing, with published, verified throughput numbers.
ideas.customer: Mid-size 3PLs, grocers and retailers (roughly 50-500k sq ft) evaluating palletizing, picking or humanoid pilots. Robot vendors are a second payer (for certification), and lenders and insurers are a third.
ideas.problem: Vendors control the demo. Buyers cannot verify throughput on their own product mix, and pilots eat 6-12 months. Funding is running far ahead of proof: Maven raised a $100M Series A with about 8 robots deployed, Agility booked $1.8M of revenue against a $2.5B SPAC valuation, and early 1X NEO demos were largely teleoperated.
ideas.solution: Rent a 20-30k sq ft cell in a logistics hub. Buyers ship 200 pallets or 500 SKUs. Vendors run their robots under a standard protocol. The lab logs picks per hour, error rate, human-intervention minutes, teleop minutes and mean time between failures, then issues a 'Verified Throughput' report. Buyers pay per bake-off, and vendors pay to list certified results and retest after software updates.
ideas.why_now: In 2026 procurement teams face a flood of unverifiable claims: about 22k humanoids shipped in H1, nine-figure rounds go to companies with a handful of deployed units, and buyers want outcome pricing. Nobody independent sits between vendors and buyers.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40k per buyer-commissioned bake-off, $25-75k a year per vendor for certification and retests, and data licensing of failure-mode datasets to insurers and lenders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The industry's binding constraint is trust in claims, not capability. Vendors will pay for independent verification because their real bottleneck is a 9-12 month sales cycle (compare UL, J.D. Power, Wirecutter). The failure-mode data becomes an asset that insurers, lenders and model developers all want.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent demo floor space inside a friendly integrator's or 3PL's idle mezzanine. Sign 2 mid-size 3PLs to paid bake-offs of 3 vendors each, and give vendors a free first test in exchange for the right to publish. Release the public methodology and a first leaderboard of 'intervention minutes per hour'.

ideas.title: Delivery Robots for Gated Communities
ideas.one_liner: Buy the sidewalk-robot fleets that failed on public streets at a discount and run them inside senior-living, campus and large apartment communities as a subscription amenity.
ideas.customer: Operators of senior-living and continuing-care communities, hospital campuses, student housing, military bases and large HOAs. They pay a monthly amenity fee.
ideas.problem: Sidewalk delivery fails on demand density, not on technology. Serve built about 2,000 robots but booked $2.65M of 2025 revenue, roughly $1.3k per robot by my arithmetic. Meanwhile private communities are labor-squeezed and struggle to get meals, pharmacy items and packages to residents.
ideas.solution: Closed-loop robots on private paths deliver dining-hall meals, pharmacy pickups, mail and supplies within one campus. Use secondhand hardware, a light fleet-management layer, and teleop backup for edge cases. Price as a fixed monthly amenity fee plus a small per-delivery charge.
ideas.why_now: Sidewalk-delivery unit economics visibly broke in 2025-26, so hardware is cheap and experienced operators are available. Vision-language navigation cuts per-site mapping cost, and last-mile contractors are closing (4XH and Ardor), which shows how expensive human delivery labor has become.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-8k a month per community platform fee, plus $1-2 per delivery. Hardware is bundled or financed. Target 8-12 robots per community at about 60% gross margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A subscription amenity decouples revenue from order volume, which is exactly what killed the public-street model. A private campus also removes the permit, ADA and pedestrian-liability problems and guarantees density.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 3 continuing-care or student-housing campuses in one metro. Buy or lease 3-5 used robots from a fleet operator raising cash. Run a teleop-assisted pilot delivering meals to about 20 residents, and convert one campus to a signed LOI at about $4k a month.

ideas.title: Humanoid Rentals for Events and Retail
ideas.one_liner: The first profitable humanoid job is spectacle: rent Unitree-class robots plus a trained show operator to brands, malls, arenas and trade shows.
ideas.customer: Experiential-marketing agencies, retail flagships, stadium and arena marketing teams, trade-show exhibitors, casinos and theme venues. Universities renting lab time come second.
ideas.problem: Everyone else pitches humanoids as factory workers, where reliability, safety and ROI are unproven. Brands want a 'robots are here' moment now but cannot buy, program and insure a $16k robot themselves.
ideas.solution: Own 6-10 units. Sell packaged experiences (greeter, product demo, dance or boxing, photo-booth persona) with an operator, choreographer, safety marshal and event insurance. Every event doubles as a demo funnel for enterprise pilot inquiries, and later as controlled data capture.
ideas.why_now: Unitree's August 2026 IPO (about $9B) and G1 pricing near $16k make fleet capex trivial, so a robot pays back in roughly 10 event-days at $1.5-2.5k a day (my estimate). Humanoid hype is at its peak and marketing budgets are chasing it. China's robot-rental-for-events market is a proof point.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-6k a day per robot with operator, $25-60k custom activations, and sponsorship fees. Add an enterprise-pilot lead-gen fee from robot vendors later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Entertainment tolerates a 70% success rate and teleop, because a stumble is content. The buyer pays for attention, not productivity, so humanoid economics work here years before they work on a factory floor. Note: tariffs or restrictions on Chinese robots are a risk, so keep a non-Chinese unit option.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy 2 G1s (about $32k) and build 3 scripted 10-minute acts. Cold-pitch 40 experiential agencies, minor-league teams and mall marketing managers. Book 5 paid weekend events and film content for social proof.

ideas.title: Trusted Firmware for Chinese-Made Robots
ideas.one_liner: A security-audited, network-isolated software and attestation layer that lets US labs, utilities and cities legally buy and run cheap Unitree-class robots.
ideas.customer: US universities and research labs, utilities, municipal fleets, critical-infrastructure operators, and integrators reselling Chinese quadrupeds and humanoids.
ideas.problem: Chinese makers hold 86% of humanoid shipments and their robots cost a fraction of US alternatives, but security teams block procurement over cloud telemetry, remote access and radio vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025. There is no neutral, certified 'clean' stack, and barriers are going up.
ideas.solution: A replacement software stack and wrapper: local-only operation, cloud services removed, wireless interfaces locked down, signed OTA updates under customer keys, an SBOM, and a continuous-audit attestation report that security auditors accept. Add an optional network-quarantine gateway appliance.
ideas.why_now: Tariffs, the FCC's DJI action and expected legislation are tightening. Unitree's IPO signals the supply will keep coming, so buyers with budgets are stuck between the price advantage and compliance.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-1,500 per robot a year for the license and updates, $10-30k per security assessment, and about $800 per gateway appliance.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Each time the US restricts a Chinese hardware category, a trust layer becomes the only route for legal buyers. Everyone bets on which hardware wins, but the money sits in the compliance gap. Risk: an outright ban would kill the market, so design for a pivot to open-source or allied hardware.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy a Go2 and a G1, reproduce the publicly documented vulnerabilities, and publish a hardening guide. Offer free audits to 5 university robotics labs' IT security officers and convert 3 to paid assessments at $10-15k.

ideas.title: Royalty Co-op for Expert Robot Demonstrations
ideas.one_liner: A worker-owned data cooperative where master tradespeople record their skilled work and earn ongoing royalties when robot makers license the demonstrations.
ideas.customer: Payers are robot foundation-model teams and manipulation or humanoid startups that buy data. Suppliers are skilled tradespeople such as tire techs, electricians, welders and HVAC technicians.
ideas.problem: Data platforms pay flat hourly rates for average people making coffee. Robots need expert-quality demonstrations, and experts will not sell their edge for a one-time $20 an hour or train their own replacement without control and upside.
ideas.solution: Partner with a union local or trade school. Members use standardized capture kits (head and wrist cameras, gloves) with quality scoring. They get a guaranteed hourly rate, 30-50% of licensing revenue, and a veto over use cases. Buyers pay per curated dataset plus a royalty per training run.
ideas.why_now: Robot training data is the humanoid bottleneck. XDOF reached about $50M annualized revenue within three months of stealth, and Mecka projects $100M ARR by end-2026 on a roughly $500M valuation. Willingness to pay is proven, while worker anxiety about being trained out of a job is rising.
ideas.revenue_model: $50-500k per dataset license, with a 20-30% cooperative fee on royalties and licensing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Data quality follows expert willingness, and willingness follows ownership. A cooperative with collective pricing power is a supply moat that flat-wage crowd platforms cannot copy, and it turns worker fear into the product's selling point.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one trade school and one union local in tire and auto service or EV-charger installation. Recruit 20 masters and capture 200 hours of one task family. Sell a pilot dataset to 2 robotics startups at $30-80k.

ideas.title: 90-Day Bridge Power for Robotaxi Depots
ideas.one_liner: Containerized battery-buffered charging stalls leased per stall per month so AV fleets can open depots years before the utility connects them.
ideas.customer: Robotaxi fleet operators and depot managers, autonomous-truck terminals, and electric delivery-van fleets that need charging capacity fast.
ideas.problem: Depot power is the scaling choke point. California lead times run about 6 months for a standard charging site, 1.9 years for a new circuit, 2.8 years for a substation upgrade and 8.9 years for a new substation, and depots compete with data centers for powered industrial land. Waymo alone has 3,871 vehicles and is aiming much higher.
ideas.solution: Modular systems combining second-life EV battery storage, a small grid tie (200-500 kW) and charging software that schedules vehicles around available energy. Sell 'stalls online in 90 days' as power-as-a-service. When the full grid connection arrives, the same assets convert to peak shaving and grid-services revenue.
ideas.why_now: Waymo, Tesla and Zoox (charging fares since August 10, 2026) are all scaling at once, and interconnection queues now outrun vehicle deployment. Data-center bridge power has proven that customers will pay a premium for time-to-power.
ideas.revenue_model: $600-1,000 per stall per month, or $0.30-0.45 per kWh delivered, on 3-5 year contracts, with asset financing behind them.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For AV scale-up the binding constraint is interconnection time, not vehicles or software. Turning 'megawatts in two years' into 'kilowatts now, megawatts later' beats the utility's queue, and buffered assets keep earning after the grid arrives.
ideas.first_30_days: Get an LOI for a 20-stall pilot from one depot operator or delivery-van fleet. Source used battery modules through a reseller and integrate an existing containerized storage vendor's hardware rather than building your own. Target first revenue in month 4.

ideas.title: Drone Hub Siting and Permit Intelligence
ideas.one_liner: Parcel-level zoning, noise and neighbor-risk scoring, plus done-for-you permit filing, for retailers and drone operators expanding launch hubs.
ideas.customer: Real-estate and expansion teams at retailers (Walmart, Lowe's, grocers, pharmacies), drone operators and delivery platforms such as Wing, Zipline and DoorDash, and regional chains entering drone delivery.
ideas.problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can regulate launch hubs. Northglenn, for example, requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and no more than 65 dB at the property line. Walmart and Wing plan 270+ sites by 2027 (about 150 stores added in a year), and each is a separate local land-use fight.
ideas.solution: An LLM-parsed database of municipal zoning codes and drone ordinances, an acoustic model of hub operations, and parcel scoring (buffer, noise, neighbor density, HOA covenants) that outputs a go/no-go and a permit dossier. Add concierge filing and hearing prep. Also sell a model-ordinance toolkit to city planners.
ideas.why_now: Lowe's launched Wing/DoorDash delivery on September 28, 2026, and Walmart's rollout turns hub siting into a mass-production problem. With airspace approvals no longer the binding constraint, zoning boards are. LLMs make parsing thousands of local codes cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k per site score, $10-25k per permit package, and $50-150k a year in enterprise SaaS. City licenses for the planning toolkit are a smaller add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The sky is federally preempted but the ground is local, so the scaling constraint has moved from the FAA to the zoning board. Whoever owns the ordinance graph decides where drone networks can expand, and both sides of the table will pay.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape and structure drone-relevant ordinances for the top 150 municipalities in one high-growth state. Offer a free top-20 site scoring to a regional grocery or pharmacy chain, convert one paid permit package, and publish a model ordinance to generate city leads.

ideas.title: Loss-Curve Intelligence for Autonomous Trucking Insurance
ideas.one_liner: A benchmark and risk-scoring workbench that helps insurers, brokers and carriers price driverless-truck coverage using evidence instead of 'unknown'.
ideas.customer: Specialty insurers and reinsurers, MGAs, brokers, and large trucking carriers. AV operators such as Aurora, Kodiak, Bot Auto and Gatik also buy, to lower their premiums.
ideas.problem: Insurers price AV trucks 'slightly above' human drivers purely because of the unknown, with premiums expected to fall 15-25% a year. Werner's CIO says 'we have a gap' on pricing. Nobody has normalized exposure data by operating domain.
ideas.solution: Ingest public crash reports (NHTSA Standing General Order and state reports), published safety cases and operator-contributed telemetry. Build frequency and severity priors by operating design domain (lane type, speed, weather, time of day) and deliver a quarterly benchmark plus a route and lane risk-scoring API. Later, underwrite as an MGA.
ideas.why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and 500k+ driverless miles, the first real exposure data, and targets 30,000 trucks by 2030. Insurers must reprice yearly and need evidence to justify each step down.
ideas.revenue_model: $75-250k a year in subscriptions from insurers and reinsurers, per-policy data fees, and MGA commission (10-15% of premium) once loss data supports it.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The problem is not too few miles but the lack of a standard exposure unit. Whoever defines miles by operating domain as the accepted denominator becomes the FICO of autonomy, and operators will share data because it lowers their premiums.
ideas.first_30_days: Build an ODD-normalized frequency table from public NHTSA data. Interview 15 trucking and AV underwriters, send a free 'AV vs human benchmark' brief to 3 brokers, and close one $30k paid pilot with an MGA.

ideas.title: Robot Access Passport for Commercial Buildings
ideas.one_liner: One certified robot identity, insurance certificate and elevator/door gateway that lets any delivery, cleaning or humanoid robot enter a building, with landlords collecting a fee.
ideas.customer: Owners and managers of office towers, multifamily REITs, hospitals, hotels and malls, who pay a subscription. Robot operators pay per-robot access fees.
ideas.problem: Every robot vendor negotiates separately with building management on elevator integration, insurance, liability and hours. Buildings have no policy or tooling, and incidents have no clear owner. This gets worse as sidewalk, cleaning, security and humanoid pilots multiply.
ideas.solution: A $1-2k building-side controller integrated with elevators, doors and turnstiles through existing vendor APIs or relays, plus a registry that verifies operator, insurance, firmware version and incident hotline. A policy engine sets quiet hours, zones and speed limits, with usage-based billing. Landlords earn a share of access fees, and robot operators integrate once for many buildings.
ideas.why_now: About 22k humanoids shipped in H1 2026, delivery robots and drones are moving to multifamily, and regulators (NHTSA's July 2026 first-responder letter) are pushing for accountability. Buildings are the next permission bottleneck.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 a month per building in SaaS plus $5-15 per robot per month in access fees, split with the landlord, and installation margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in robot deployment is permission, and building owners are the gatekeepers with zero tooling. A neutral gatekeeper standard is a two-sided network, like 'ID.me plus a certificate of insurance for robots', and landlords get paid to adopt it.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach 2 property managers in one metro where delivery robots already operate. Build an integration for one elevator vendor's open API, get a certificate-of-insurance template from a broker, and charge $500 a month for the pilot.

ideas.title: Lights-Out Receiving Network for Driverless Freight
ideas.one_liner: On-demand night-shift dock crews plus remotely operable gates and dock doors so driverless trucks arriving at 3 a.m. actually get inspected and unloaded.
ideas.customer: Driverless-truck operators and their shipper and receiver customers, distribution centers with thin overnight staffing, and brokers offering autonomous lanes.
ideas.problem: Driverless trucks run around the clock, but most receivers have no dock labor, yard checks or inspectors at night. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector, and hub-to-hub handoffs leave 'hundreds of dollars' of human cost per transfer. The PrePass/Kodiak bypass integration is live only in Texas and Louisiana.
ideas.solution: Three pieces. First, a network of trained ex-driver and yard-tech turnaround crews for walk-arounds, sensor cleaning and trailer checks. Second, a $3-6k remote gate and dock-door kit so the AV can check in and get a door. Third, on-call unload crews, with everything dispatched from one app and priced per turn below the cost of a human transfer.
ideas.why_now: Aurora is exiting 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030, California's driverless-truck rules took effect on April 28, 2026, and the Teamsters sued on August 5. Hiring retrained drivers into new roles also buys political goodwill.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per truck turn, equipment lease or subscription for gate and dock kits, and a per-lane subscription for receivers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Autonomy shifts the constraint from driver hours to dock hours: the truck no longer sleeps, but the receiver does. The rent moves to whoever owns the human touch at the endpoints, and hiring displaced drivers turns opposition into a labor supply.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one corridor where driverless trucks already run (for example Fort Worth to El Paso). Sign LOIs with 2 shippers on that lane for overnight receiving, recruit 10 ex-drivers or yard techs, build a simple dispatch app and target first paid turns within 90 days.

ideas.title: Aftermarket Support for Stranded DJI Fleets
ideas.one_liner: Repair, rebuilt batteries, parts and firmware-independence retrofits for the many legally owned DJI drones that can no longer be replaced with new models.
ideas.customer: Police and fire drone units, agricultural spray operators, land surveyors, roofing and solar inspectors, and small public-safety departments with grant money.
ideas.problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in December 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in September 2026 (component tariffs follow in 2027), and China's export controls now cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Existing fleets stay legal to fly but face scarce parts and no assured US repair path.
ideas.solution: A US repair depot with stocked parts, rebuilt batteries using allied-source cells, gimbal and camera swaps, and open flight-controller retrofits (ArduPilot/PX4) as a migration path. Offer a per-drone maintenance plan with predictive service, and trade-in credits toward US-made airframes, which also become a lead source for those makers.
ideas.why_now: The December 2025 FCC action, September 2026 tariffs and export controls all landed within a year. The installed base is large and aging, and no one has a business focused on serving it.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-800 per repair, $30-80 per drone per month for maintenance plans, battery and parts sales, and referral fees from US airframe makers on trade-ins.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone debates who replaces DJI, while nobody serves the installed base for the next 5 years. Service earns higher margin than building a competing airframe, starts faster, and gives you the customer list every US-made airframe maker wants.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy 20 broken Mavic and Matrice units on secondary markets and set up a bench. Pitch fixed-price maintenance plans to 30 sheriff drone units and agricultural spraying co-ops, and sell the first 10 plans.

ideas.title: Shared Emergency Desk for Autonomous Fleets
ideas.one_liner: A neutral 24/7 first-responder interface (hotline, dispatch API, geofence directives) that small AV, robot-truck and delivery-robot operators rent instead of building.
ideas.customer: Newer and second-tier AV operators (autonomous trucking, shuttles, delivery pods, robotaxi entrants), and city and county 911 dispatch centers on the public-facing side.
ideas.problem: Regulators are asking for a human phone number, not more autonomy. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on July 8, 2026, and California's AV enforcement rules take effect in 2026 (as I understand them). Waymo alone runs about 70 remote agents per shift from two centers in the Philippines, which small operators cannot copy.
ideas.solution: A US-staffed desk trained on fire and police protocols. It offers standardized emergency-response guides, one API through which dispatch centers can stop, unlock or reroute any subscribing fleet, compliance logs, and drills for first responders.
ideas.why_now: Driverless trucking is commercial (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k driverless orders, Einride listed), new AV entrants are launching, and states are writing rules. Compliance deadlines land in 2026.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-2,000 per vehicle per year or an $8-25k monthly fleet retainer, plus training contracts with cities.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A commodity BPO with liability attached scales with vehicle count, and neutrality is a feature because cities prefer one interface for all fleets. Large operators build their own desks, so the long tail of new entrants is the market.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 10 safety and compliance leads at autonomous trucking and delivery-robot companies. Build a minimal hotline plus web console for a single pilot, co-design the protocol with 2 city or county dispatch centers, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $5k a month.

ideas.title: Safety Compliance-as-a-Service for Robot Deployments
ideas.one_liner: A standing team plus software that produces the risk assessments, safety validation and insurer paperwork every facility needs before deploying AMRs, cobots or humanoid pilots.
ideas.customer: EHS and operations directors at mid-size 3PLs, manufacturers and food or cold-storage plants, integrators without in-house safety staff, and insurers who want documentation.
ideas.problem: Deployments stall at safety sign-off. ISO 10218 was revised in 2025, standards for dynamically stable robots and humanoids are still being written, integrators are overloaded, and insurers and OSHA ask for documented assessments. Amazon's 1M-robot scale keeps injury scrutiny high.
ideas.solution: Field engineers plus templated software: site scan, risk assessment against current standards, laser-scanner zone and e-stop validation, speed-and-separation testing, training records and incident logs, with annual recertification. Offer a premium 'humanoid pilot safety case' product.
ideas.why_now: Humanoid pilots are moving into real facilities in 2026 (Figure reports about 350 units delivered, Agility has a $300M+ single-customer order) while standards lag. Insurers are starting to require paperwork, so it is a channel as well as a service.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-25k per site assessment, $3-8k a year for recertification, and software seats for integrators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For many humanoid and AMR pilots the true bottleneck is one safety officer's signature, and almost no independent practitioners exist. Insurers will steer clients to whoever produces accepted documentation, which gives you distribution.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit a certified functional-safety engineer as cofounder and build assessment templates. Sell 3 fixed-price assessments at about $10k each from integrators' backlogs, and publish a free humanoid pilot safety checklist to generate inbound.

ideas.title: Third-Party Maintenance for Orphaned Robots
ideas.one_liner: Like third-party server maintenance for IT, a spares-and-support contract for robots whose makers failed, were acquired or stopped supporting them.
ideas.customer: 3PLs, retailers, hospitals and factories running AMRs, storage systems and delivery robots that are out of warranty or whose vendors are gone, plus lenders and bankruptcy trustees holding stranded assets.
ideas.problem: Robotics funding is concentrating (Skild $14B, Physical Intelligence $11B, Figure $39B) while the long tail starves. Agility is pivoting toward wheels, and Serve's roughly $1.3k revenue per robot signals shakeout. Buyers can be left with multimillion-dollar fleets without updates or parts.
ideas.solution: Buy stranded inventory and spares from failed vendors, arrange source-code escrow or reverse-engineer key consumables, and offer annual per-robot support contracts with SLAs. Also sell certified refurbished units.
ideas.why_now: The 2025-26 funding boom is producing its first wave of failures and consolidation, while Amazon (1M+ robots, building its own robot factory) and Symbotic ($2.25B 2025 revenue) centralize the market. The orphan pool is growing now.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-4k per robot per year in support contracts, refurbished-unit sales, and escrow and trustee fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In every hardware boom the durable second-derivative business is keeping the losers' machines running. Buyers pay to avoid stranded assets, and your spares moat grows with each vendor that fails.
ideas.first_30_days: Identify 3 wound-down or struggling robot vendors, get trustee quotes on inventory (often pennies on the dollar), and approach their 5 largest customers. Sign 2 support contracts and open a small depot near Memphis or the Inland Empire.

ideas.title: Operator-of-Record for Enterprise Drone Flights
ideas.one_liner: A licensed BVLOS operations team-as-a-service that files the waivers, runs the safety case and supervises the flights for utilities, solar developers and pipeline owners.
ideas.customer: Mid-size utilities and co-ops, solar and wind developers, pipeline and rail operators, ports, mines, and their insurers.
ideas.problem: BVLOS technology is ready, but organizations lack the capability: waiver applications, safety cases, ops manuals, remote-pilot staffing and data pipelines. The final status of Part 108 (the FAA BVLOS rule) could not be verified, which adds uncertainty. Meanwhile the DJI ban forces fleet refreshes.
ideas.solution: A reusable safety-case library and remote-pilot center (one pilot supervising 5-10 drone docks) running US-made drone-in-a-box fleets. Price per line-mile or per site, with data delivered into the customer's GIS and maintenance systems.
ideas.why_now: The December 2025 DJI restrictions force fleet replacement decisions in 2026, and Wing's 1M deliveries show BVLOS operations working at scale. Whatever Part 108's final form, operators still need documented safety cases and waivers.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-20k per month per site retainer or per-line-mile pricing on multi-year MSAs, plus waiver and safety-case consulting fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Regulation is a one-time cost that vendors avoid, but the operator-of-record that accumulates waivers, flight logs and accepted safety cases builds a moat that compounds with every approval.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one region (for example co-ops in Texas or Colorado) and partner with one US-made dock vendor. Get one co-op to sign a pilot covering 20 substations, file the waiver, and aim for the first inspection within 60 days.

ideas.title: Micro-Bounties for Humans to Rescue Stuck Robots
ideas.one_liner: An on-demand app where robots and AVs post 30-second physical tasks (close a door, plug in a charger, move a cone, lift a robot over a curb) and nearby humans get paid instantly.
ideas.customer: Operators of sidewalk delivery robots, robotaxi and AV fleets, drone hubs, cleaning robots and warehouse AMRs, paying about $3-15 per task.
ideas.problem: Autonomy fails at the last physical one percent. Only 54% of Waymo's first 86M miles carried a passenger and each reset cycle takes about 2 hours. Dispatching a staffer or tow costs far more than the fix, and each fleet builds its own field-ops team.
ideas.solution: An SDK in which the robot emits a help request with location, photos and a vision-language-model task description. Nearby vetted people accept it, the robot's own sensors verify completion, and payout is instant. Strict safety rules prevent anyone touching moving machines. Start with door-ajar, debris and stuck-at-curb tasks.
ideas.why_now: Robot fleets are scaling faster than field crews (Waymo about 500k rides a week, sidewalk fleets in the thousands), and AV firms have reportedly begun paying gig workers for simple physical fixes. Vision-language models can now write the task description automatically.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-30% take on each task plus a monthly platform fee per fleet.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every robot fleet needs a thin, geographically spread hands-and-feet layer that scales with robot count. A two-sided micro-labor network is cheaper than dedicated field teams, and because the robot is the buyer, demand is programmable and grows with every deployment.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro with a delivery-robot or campus-robot operator, recruit 50 local gig workers, and dispatch manually by SMS. Sign a $2k a month pilot with a small fleet, run 500 tasks, and publish resolution-time data.

ideas.title: Remote-Piloted Robot Workcells for Returns Processing
ideas.one_liner: Two-arm teleoperated stations in US returns centers, piloted by trained remote workers in low-wage regions, priced per item and generating the data to automate each task over time.
ideas.customer: Reverse-logistics processors, e-commerce returns centers, refurbishers and 3PLs handling apparel and consumer electronics in high-wage regions.
ideas.problem: Returns are high-variance and every item is different, so they are labor-heavy, high-turnover and hard to automate. Pure autonomy is not ready and pure teleop is too slow: early stations may run at only 30-50% of human speed, so hourly pricing fails.
ideas.solution: Deploy open-source dual-arm stations (ALOHA-class, about $30k each) where remote pilots handle exceptions and supervise learned behaviors on routine items. Price per item processed, guaranteed 20-30% below local labor, and let one pilot cover 3-5 stations as autonomy improves. Every pilot hour becomes licensable training data.
ideas.why_now: Cheap arms, open-source teleop rigs and robot-learning models are good enough for supervised autonomy. XDOF's $50M annualized revenue shows the teleop-data market pays, and 1X's teleoperated NEO shows buyers already accept a human in the loop.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.40-1.20 per item processed, with data licensing to model developers as an additional revenue stream.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The teleop-versus-autonomy debate is a false dichotomy for buyers who pay per outcome. The economic robot today is a pilot-supervised robot whose human share falls every month, so the transitional business earns money while producing the data rivals pay for. It only works if you price per item and measure interventions per hour honestly.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one returns processor. Deploy 2 open-source stations on 2 tasks (test and grade electronics accessories, re-bag apparel), recruit 6 pilots through a Philippine BPO partner, and sell a 90-day pilot at a per-item price.

ideas.title: Physical-Properties Index for Every SKU
ideas.one_liner: A shared 'Gracenote for grasping': weight, center of mass, deformability, best grip points and packaging traits for millions of SKUs, sold to pick-robot makers and brands.
ideas.customer: Pick-and-pack robot vendors, 3PLs running robotic induction, CPG and retail brands (for robot-ready packaging certification), and humanoid developers.
ideas.problem: Picking robots fail on the long tail because they meet every SKU cold, and brands change packaging without notice. Amazon knows internally, but everyone else relearns per site.
ideas.solution: Fill the index from two sources: a scanning rig at partner 3PLs (3D scan, mass, center of mass, slip tests) and give-to-get contributions from robot fleets reporting grasp outcomes. Serve it by GTIN through an API with recommended grasp points and packing advice, and offer brands a 'Robot-Ready' grade that 3PLs reward with lower handling fees.
ideas.why_now: Robotic picking is now at scale (Amazon 1M+ robots, Symbotic $2.25B revenue, Maven-style mixed palletizing), and foundation models can use priors like these. A market of data buyers already exists.
ideas.revenue_model: API fees per lookup or per robot per month, $2-10k per SKU family for brand certification, and dataset licensing to model labs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Robots will not scale on smarter grasping alone. The world's goods need a machine-readable physical spec, and brands have a direct incentive because 3PLs and retailers will reward robot-ready packaging. A neutral index can become a standard the way GS1 barcodes did.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a $15k scanning rig at a friendly 3PL and scan the top 3,000 SKUs. Release a free tier, sign 2 pick-robot vendors as beta partners, and run one paid brand packaging audit.

ideas.title: Remote-Driven Tractors for the Door-to-Door Leg
ideas.one_liner: Teleoperated tractors, driven from desks by remote drivers, that shuttle trailers between autonomous-truck terminals and customers' docks within about 30 miles.
ideas.customer: Autonomous-truck operators that need a handoff solution, carriers with hub networks, shippers with private yards, and ports and rail ramps.
ideas.problem: Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves door-to-door legs with 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff, yet most freight is door-to-door. Short-haul and drayage driver turnover is high.
ideas.solution: Start on private yards, where no on-road rules apply, with retrofit teleop kits, multi-carrier connectivity and automatic safe-stop on link loss. A remote driver handles moves back to back with no deadhead, and automation covers straight segments. Extend later to short, permitted public-road hops at low speed. Price per move below a local yard driver plus deadhead.
ideas.why_now: Aurora (about 200 driverless trucks, 30,000 planned), Einride and Gatik are scaling the hub model, and the handoff economics are unresolved. Remote driving has been operating commercially in Europe and Las Vegas, and multi-carrier bonding makes latency manageable. Public-road legality for teleoperated heavy trucks in the US is unclear and needs checking.
ideas.revenue_model: $/move pricing, a monthly retainer per terminal, and equipment lease on the retrofit kits.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The industry frames the last leg as an automation problem, but it is a utilization problem. One remote driver can serve several times more moves than a local driver who deadheads between yards, so teleop can beat both a human and a full autonomy stack on price for the next several years.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign a private yard (a rail ramp or DC with 20+ yard moves a day), retrofit one tractor with a rented teleop kit, and run a week of shadow operations. Price the pilot at about 20% below the current yard-jockey cost.

ideas.title: Peak-Season Exchange for Idle Warehouse Robot Hours
ideas.one_liner: A marketplace and price index that moves idle AMRs and robots-as-a-service capacity between 3PLs and retailers to cover seasonal peaks, priced per robot-hour.
ideas.customer: Mid-size 3PLs and retailers needing Q4 peak capacity, and owners of idle fleets (integrators, RaaS providers, seasonal retailers, lenders holding repossessed units). Lenders and investors buy the index.
ideas.problem: Peaks force 3PLs into premium temp labor, while fleets sized for average load sit idle for half the year at seasonal operators. There is no market price for a robot-hour, so lenders cannot value the assets either.
ideas.solution: Standardize robot-hour listings (AMR class, payload, WMS integration) with a 48-hour commissioning kit (mapping, WMS connector) and escrowed insurance. Seed supply from idle demo pools and seasonal owners, and publish a weekly Robot Rate Index by class and region. Add forward contracts for peak later.
ideas.why_now: Robot pricing is becoming public and recurring (Figure's planned $600 a month lease, 1X at $499 a month, Agility's $300M+ order), and buyers want outcome pricing and 48-hour product-mix changes. Peak season 2026 is starting now, so the first rentals can be tested against real labor premiums.
ideas.revenue_model: 12-18% take rate on rentals, a commissioning fee per deployment, and $10-30k a year for index and benchmark subscriptions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Robots are sold as capex but bought as capacity. Once tens of thousands of units exist, capacity will trade like trailers and rail cars, and whoever runs the exchange sets the price benchmark (DAT, Drewry) and owns residual-value data.
ideas.first_30_days: Source about 50 idle AMRs from 2 integrators' demo pools and 2 seasonal retailers. Sell 3 emergency Q4 peak rentals to 3PLs paying temp-labor premiums, and publish Robot Rate Index v0 from about 40 collected quotes.

ideas.title: Playable-Until Guarantees for Online Games
ideas.one_liner: Sell publishers a pre-funded shutdown trust plus an escrowed server kit, so a dated playability guarantee becomes a selling point for $70-80 online games instead of a legal risk.
ideas.customer: Indie and mid-size publishers (10-300 staff) of co-op and live-service titles on Steam and console, and premium online games priced at $70-80.
ideas.problem: Publishers treat any end-of-life promise as a liability admission, so buyers get none. Anthem shut down on 2026-01-12, and of 738 tracked shutdown games 68% are unplayable or at risk. The EU Commission declined a mandatory rule on 2026-06-16 but wants a voluntary code by end of 2026. UFC-Que Choisir sued Ubisoft over The Crew, and a suit against Sony followed in Aug 2026.
ideas.solution: A 'Last Light' package with three parts. (1) Escrow of a server-emulator kit, builds and docs, verified by a clean-room restore drill we run. (2) A small per-title trust funded at launch (1-2% of gross) that pays a hosting partner to keep a minimal community server up for N years. (3) A store-page badge with a date, plus a public verification page. If a sunset trigger fires, the kit is released to the community.
ideas.why_now: The EU voluntary code of conduct due by end of 2026 will set a de facto standard that needs an auditor. The Stop Killing Games petition has 1.29M verified signers, a ready-made audience. $70-80 pricing needs a value story, and the Ubisoft and Sony suits show the cost of staying silent.
ideas.revenue_model: Certification and restore-drill fee of $8-40k per title, 15-20% admin retention on trust contributions, and $3-5k annual re-certification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A bounded, dated, funded promise caps liability, while silence leaves it open-ended and now litigated. Most online games reduce to stateless auth and matchmaking, so the guarantee is cheap to keep. Publishers also get a marketing asset that the Stop Killing Games community will actively promote.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit volunteer engineers from the Stop Killing Games community to draft a reference escrow spec. Pitch 30 indie co-op publishers with launches in the next 12 months. Run a free restore drill on one willing title and publish it as a case study. Presell 3 pilots at $5-8k, and get a hosting-partner letter of intent and a lawyer-reviewed template.

ideas.title: Shelved-Game Rescue Exchange
ideas.one_liner: A broker that packages cancelled and orphaned game prototypes and licenses them to laid-off veteran teams on revenue-share terms, with reversion rights if the game stalls.
ideas.customer: Publishers, closing studios and insolvency administrators holding unreleased builds (they get a recovery instead of a write-off). The paying counterparties are veteran-led small teams and the funders behind them.
ideas.problem: Ubisoft cancelled six games in Jan 2026 and cut headcount from 18,666 to 16,590. EA's owners closed a $55B LBO with $20B of debt and a stated plan to cut costs with AI. Cancelled projects sit unused with teams disbanded, while laid-off veterans have skills but no IP or prototype budget.
ideas.solution: Build a 'prototype data room' per project: build, design docs, and a third-party licence and music clearance audit. Add a standard rescue licence (revenue share, milestone reversion, credit terms) and a registry of veteran team leads. Match the two, and offer milestone-funded finishing through a small fund or partner investors. Start with insolvent and small publishers, which move faster than Ubisoft or EA legal.
ideas.why_now: The 2023-26 layoff wave left an unusually deep bench of finished-quality talent. The EA LBO and Ubisoft restructuring guarantee more shelved work. Steam distribution and Epic's 0% fee on the first $1M make a 10-20 person finish economically viable.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-15% of the licensee's revenue share, or a success fee at signing ($10-50k), plus a data-room packaging fee paid by the rights holder.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A shelved game's cost to its owner is legal and opportunity overhead, not the code. A zero-upfront licence with reversion beats a write-down and avoids a public fire sale. Insiders assume cancelled means bad, but many projects die for portfolio or budget-cycle reasons, not quality.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a public 'orphaned prototypes wanted' page. Call 20 insolvency administrators and mid-size publishers found through recent studio-closure announcements with a one-page offer. Have a games lawyer draft the rescue licence. Recruit 10 veteran-led teams from layoff communities on Discord and LinkedIn. Aim for one signed rescue by day 60.

ideas.title: Memory Budget CI for Game Studios
ideas.one_liner: CI tooling and fixed-fee audits that enforce RAM and VRAM budgets per target device, because the assumption that hardware gets better each generation just broke.
ideas.customer: Mid-size PC and console studios (30-300 staff) shipping in 2027 to Steam Deck, Switch 2 and 8-16GB PCs.
ideas.problem: AI data centers are absorbing the RAM supply. Valve's Steam Machine launched at $1,049 against an early target of about $800, Xbox prices rose, and Switch 2 goes to $499.99 on 2026-09-01. The installed base will stay at today's memory ceilings for years, but studios budget memory as a fixed cap and find regressions in late QA.
ideas.solution: An Unreal, Unity and Godot CI plugin that builds against device memory profiles, snapshots per-level memory, attributes growth to specific assets and pull requests, and suggests fixes (texture format changes, streaming pool sizes, audio bank downsampling). Sold alongside a 3-week 'memory diet' audit that finds duplicated and unstripped assets.
ideas.why_now: Memory vendors now quote a monthly price and a yes-or-no on volume, per a Valve engineer. Console and handheld price hikes in 2026 mean players will not upgrade into new game requirements. Studios are planning holiday 2026-27 lineups now.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40k per audit, $400-2,500 per month per studio for CI, and later a subscription to a device-profile and min-spec benchmark database.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The industry's optimization culture is about frame time. When hardware gets pricier over its life, the cheapest way to grow the addressable market is to shrink footprint, and most footprint is asset-pipeline waste that can be found and fixed automatically.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish an analysis of Steam minimum-spec trends versus the Hardware Survey to get inbound. Ship a free open-source memory snapshot diff tool for Unity and Unreal. Offer free audits to 5 studios in exchange for case studies, and convert 2 into paid engagements.

ideas.title: Hallmark-Style Microdramas for Women 45+
ideas.one_liner: A genre studio making 60-episode vertical dramas (cozy mystery, faith-and-family, second-act romance) for the older female audience the romance-and-revenge apps under-serve, sold through web checkout.
ideas.customer: Women aged 40-65 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia paying via coin packs or weekly subscriptions. Aggregator apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox are a second customer as licensees.
ideas.problem: Microdramas are a roughly $11B global market, with about $1.3B a year of US spend, mostly women 30-60. Supply skews toward billionaire-romance, werewolf and revenge tropes. Genres this audience already pays for on Hallmark, Lifetime and faith networks are thin.
ideas.solution: Shoot 60-70 episode series for $50-90k on 8-day schedules with real actors, and use AI only in post (subtitles, cleanup, ADR), not for performers. Test three genres with $3k of Meta ads per pilot, license winners to aggregators for minimum guarantees, then push loyal viewers to your own web-checkout app.
ideas.why_now: Epic's April 2025 ruling stopped Apple charging fees on purchases made outside its store in the US, so a vertical-drama app can keep most of the margin on web checkout. Series cycle times are under two weeks, and the market has proven willingness to pay.
ideas.revenue_model: Coin and subscription revenue via own app (LTV-driven), plus aggregator licensing fees and minimum guarantees, plus brand integrations.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The leaders optimized for early-adopter tropes. Viewers 45+ already pay for TV subscriptions, have cards on file, are cheap to reach on Facebook, and churn less. Scarcity of content for them is a supply gap, not a demand gap.
ideas.first_30_days: Shoot a 10-episode pilot for about $12k. Run a $3k ad test on three genres and pick the winner by cost per paying viewer. Pitch two aggregators for a minimum guarantee, and stand up a web paywall using an off-the-shelf subscription funnel tool.

ideas.title: Fandom Events in Empty Cinema Auditoriums
ideas.one_liner: A rights-plus-ticketing agency that fills weekday auditoriums with VTuber concert viewings, esports finals and game-reveal nights, splitting the box office with cinema chains.
ideas.customer: Fandom promoters and community organizers, VTuber agencies, esports and game publishers wanting fan events, and regional cinema chains as venue partners. Fans pay $15-30.
ideas.problem: Overseas viewers are about 30% of Hololive viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet have no communal way to attend, while Sphere-scale venues cost hundreds of millions and Live Nation controls arenas. Independent organizers rent bars with poor AV and no rights.
ideas.solution: Package a dark room, great sound and a projection booth with the rest of the event: sublicensed rights, a licensed live feed, all-in-price ticketing, cosplay contests and merch tables. Start with regional independent chains and a fixed menu of event formats.
ideas.why_now: Hololive concert revenue grew 18.7% and overseas fandom is underserved. The FTC's all-in-pricing rule and the Live Nation verdict make promoters and fans look for alternatives to arena ticketing. Cinemas still need non-Hollywood content for off-peak seats.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-25% of ticket revenue plus $2-8k per event for rights and technical fees, with cinemas taking a box-office split and concessions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in experience-economy fandom is not a $2B dome, it's a room with audio and projection, which cinemas already own and leave empty midweek. Everyone is chasing IP-in-space capex while the arbitrage is empty seats.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch 5 independent cinema owners on a revenue split. Sign one rights-cleared event, such as a fighting-game grand finals viewing or a licensed VTuber concert screening. Run three test events by day 45 and measure fill rate and concession spend.

ideas.title: Ticketmaster Exit Kits for Independent Venues
ideas.one_liner: A contract-audit and migration service that tells venue owners exactly when and at what cost they can leave exclusive ticketing deals, then moves them safely.
ideas.customer: Independent venue owners and operators of 500-3,000 capacity rooms in the US, and promoters who run pre-sales through those venues.
ideas.problem: A jury found Live Nation liable for illegal monopolization on 2026-04-15, and remedies remain unclear (a separate DOJ settlement dates from 2026-03-09). Venues with exclusive contracts do not know what leaving costs (liquidated damages, advance repayment, loss of fan data), and fear a botched on-sale day more than the contract.
ideas.solution: A contract analyzer that reads exclusivity, term, advance-repayment and change-of-law clauses and returns an exit date and cost sheet. Add a migration playbook (fan data export with consent, fee structure compliant with the FTC all-in rule, verified-fan pre-sales), white-label integrations with 2-3 alternative ticketing platforms, and pooled negotiation for groups of venues.
ideas.why_now: The April 2026 verdict, the FTC's all-in pricing rule (effective 2025-05-12), the state suits, and Ticketmaster's June 2026 placement inside Spotify all raise the stakes of lock-in. Venues suddenly have leverage but no capability.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k audit, $5-15k migration, and 10-20% of alternative platforms' fee share on the venue's tickets for three years.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Antitrust wins create optionality, not capability. The bottleneck after a verdict is the GM's fear of a broken on-sale, so the product to sell is reduced fear, plus data ownership the venue never knew it lacked.
ideas.first_30_days: Mine the public trial exhibits for venue-contract terms and publish an exit map. Reach 10 venue GMs through independent-venue trade groups. Run three paid contract audits at $1.5k and line up two alternative ticketing partners.

ideas.title: Release-Date Congestion Map and Collision Cover
ideas.one_liner: A wishlist-overlap model and anonymous date-slot registry that tells indies where launch windows are crowded, later backed by parametric cover if a mega-title lands on top of them.
ideas.customer: Self-publishing indie developers and small publishers with 20k+ wishlists, and later insurers and MGAs underwriting launch risk.
ideas.problem: GTA VI launches 2026-11-19, and other publishers are rescheduling around it. Silksong (about 5.2M wishlists, 7M+ sales by Dec 2025) pushed several indies to delay after its date was announced. Devs lock marketing spend, then a giant date shifts. When everyone dodges the same date, they pile into the same safe windows, creating new collisions.
ideas.solution: Ingest public Steam wishlist ranks, release calendars and creator schedules to produce a congestion map and a per-title collision score based on audience overlap. Add a confidential slot registry where publishers submit intended dates and get congestion feedback. Once loss data exists, add parametric cover paying out if a listed mega-title moves within +/-14 days of a locked date.
ideas.why_now: GTA VI is the largest release-calendar shock in years and its ripple lasts months. Q1 2027 herd behavior is forming now, and no one measures collision risk.
ideas.revenue_model: $49-299 per month SaaS or $500 per date report, plus a 15-25% MGA commission on parametric premiums (3-6% of cover).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Collision is treated as luck, but it is measurable through audience overlap and tradeable as a parametric risk. The herd effect, everyone avoiding the same date, is a coordination failure a neutral registry can fix.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape Steam release calendars and wishlist ranks. Publish a free Q1 2027 congestion map on Discord and Reddit dev communities. Sell 20 paid date reports and speak to 3 MGAs about a pilot cover.

ideas.title: Asset Provenance Ledger for AI Disclosure
ideas.one_liner: A plugin for Blender, Photoshop, Unity and Unreal that logs where each asset came from (human-made, AI-generated, purchased) and exports evidence for Steam disclosure and award eligibility.
ideas.customer: Indie and mid-size studios (5-100 staff) shipping on Steam, and awards and festival organizers who must adjudicate AI use.
ideas.problem: Clair Obscur lost two Indie Game Awards over AI placeholder textures removed before shipping. Eurogamer scored ARC Raiders 2/5 partly over AI voices. Valve requires AI disclosure on Steam. Accusations arrive after launch and the accused have no evidence trail either way.
ideas.solution: A local-first logger records per-asset origin (DCC commit hooks, generative-tool API logs, asset-store IDs) into a signed hash chain. It exports an AI Disclosure Report for Steam, award submissions and press, and offers a verifier portal for juries and a public provenance page.
ideas.why_now: Award controversies and press scoring now turn on AI use. Steam's disclosure requirement is in force. EA's owners plan AI throughout operations, which will multiply cases.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-49 per seat per month, $2-5k per event for awards verification, and $3-10k for forensic audits of accused studios.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The dispute is not AI versus human, it is evidence asymmetry: accusers need no proof and the accused have none. A provenance log protects studios that use AI legitimately (placeholders, disclosed tools) as much as those that do not.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a minimal Blender, Photoshop and Unity logger. Offer it free to awards-eligible entries. Talk to organizers of two indie awards about a verifier pilot, and onboard 20 studios.

ideas.title: Settlement Claim Autopilot for Ticket Buyers
ideas.one_liner: A privacy-first app that reconstructs a fan's ticket purchase history and files claims in ticketing settlements and refund orders, paid per validated claim by administrators and plaintiff firms.
ideas.customer: Settlement administrators and plaintiff firms, who pay per validated claim because they are judged on claim rates. Consumers use it free or pay a success fee.
ideas.problem: The FTC alleges $3.7B in resale fees from 2019-2024. Live Nation was found liable on monopolization in April 2026. In June 2026 the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers, and World Cup ticket failures triggered class actions in New York and British Columbia. Claim rates in consumer settlements are typically low because buyers cannot reconstruct old purchases.
ideas.solution: Fans forward receipt emails or upload data exports (avoiding restricted Gmail scopes at launch). Local parsing rebuilds each purchase (event, price, fee, date) and matches it to open claim windows and prefilled forms. Sell it to administrators as a claims-acquisition channel, and keep watching for new live-events settlements.
ideas.why_now: A wave of ticketing liabilities is landing at once, and cheap models can parse messy receipts. Individual recoveries of about $30 are uneconomical for lawyers but work in batch.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-15 per validated claim from administrators and law firms, optional 10-15% consumer success fee, and later expansion to other settlement categories.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the administrator or counsel measured on claim rate, not the consumer. Email receipts are better proof than memory, and automation turns tiny per-person recoveries into a scalable business.
ideas.first_30_days: Launch a landing page around the CMA StubHub refund order. Pitch 5 administrators and pilot one active claim. Test the receipt-forward parser with 500 users and negotiate a per-claim bounty.

ideas.title: Insider-Trading Watchdog for Entertainment Announcements
ideas.one_liner: Sportradar-style integrity monitoring for game publishers, studios and awards bodies whose announcements and results now trade as prediction-market contracts.
ideas.customer: Legal and compliance teams at game publishers, film and TV studios, awards bodies, esports leagues and streamers. Prediction-market exchanges are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: Kalshi valuation went from about $11B to $22B between Dec 2025 and May 2026, and entertainment and awards are already about 11% of activity. Employees, agencies, vendors and journalists under embargo hold non-public information that now has a price. No one monitors it, and sports leagues already pay for integrity services that entertainment lacks.
ideas.solution: Map every listed contract on Kalshi, Polymarket and other venues to the client's titles, awards and announcements. Detect abnormal volume and price moves ahead of reveals, and deliver incident packets for counsel. Add embargo-tier employee policy and training, and give exchanges a restricted-list API.
ideas.why_now: Prediction markets are expanding beyond sports despite state fights, and regulators will demand integrity partners as entertainment contracts multiply.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-10k per month subscriptions for IP owners, exchange-side API fees, and forensic investigations at project rates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Publishers think prediction markets are a gambling issue for someone else. For the first time, their 5,000 employees and 300 vendors hold embargoed information worth money. Sports solved this with third-party integrity vendors, and entertainment has none.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a tracker of all entertainment and gaming contracts across major venues. Publish a report on volume spikes before announcements. Contact compliance heads at 10 publishers and awards bodies, and sell one 3-month pilot at $5k per month.

ideas.title: Age Assurance Kit for Small Game Communities
ideas.one_liner: A drop-in age-gating kit that never stores IDs, with regulator-ready audit trails, for indie multiplayer studios, mod sites, fan forums and Minecraft-style server networks.
ideas.customer: Indie multiplayer studios (5-100 staff) with in-game chat, modding and fan-wiki sites, forums, and server networks selling ranks, mainly in the UK and EU.
ideas.problem: The UK Online Safety Act enforcement deadline was 2025-07-25, and Discord announced mandatory face-scan or ID checks worldwide in March 2026. Discord's Sept 2025 breach was claimed to have exposed 2.1M ID photos, and photo checks were beaten with Death Stranding character images. Small operators have mandates with no compliance budget.
ideas.solution: An SDK and plugin set (Unity, Unreal, Discord bot, Discourse, WordPress, Minecraft servers) that routes each user through the cheapest sufficient method (on-device estimation, card check, reusable wallet attestations). It stores only a signed over-13 or over-18 token, and ships risk-assessment templates and audit logs.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement is live, the Roblox and Discord rollouts set user expectations, and a leaked-ID breach makes 'we never hold your ID' a selling point.
ideas.revenue_model: $29-199 per month per community plus $0.02-0.10 per verification, with a documentation package for regulators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Large vendors sell to big platforms, but the long tail needs self-serve pricing and paperwork, not just a verification call. The liability is holding the ID, so a token-only design is the product, not a feature.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a Discord bot and WordPress plugin on top of an existing estimation and wallet vendor. Recruit 20 forum and server operators through modding and Minecraft communities. Convert 5 to paid plans and write the regulator documentation pack.

ideas.title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Rail for Tournaments
ideas.one_liner: Payout operations for tournament organizers and esports orgs: one-time player KYC and tax onboarding, treaty-aware withholding, sanctions screening, and multi-currency payment.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier tournament organizers (regional leagues, publisher-sanctioned circuits, fighting-game majors) and esports orgs receiving club-program stipends.
ideas.problem: Prize money exploded, with $75M at the 2026 Esports World Cup (moved to Paris) and a $20M club partner program across 40 orgs. Payments go to players in dozens of countries, including minors, with tax forms, withholding and sanctions checks, and organizers run it on spreadsheets and wire transfers.
ideas.solution: A payout platform with a portable 'player payout profile' (KYC and tax forms collected once), automated withholding by treaty, sanctions screening, escrowed prize pools released on verified results, and payment on local rails. Add visa and travel letter templates and year-end tax reporting.
ideas.why_now: Sovereign money inflated prize pools, and the Saudi-Olympic Esports Games partnership ending (2025-10-30) pushes more independent circuits. The compliance burden has grown with the money.
ideas.revenue_model: 1-2% of payout volume plus $3-8 per payee, and $500-3,000 per month SaaS for orgs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Prize pools stopped being a marketing line item and became a payments-and-tax operations problem. The onboarding data is portable across events, so each player carried through one event lowers the cost for the next organizer.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 15 tournament organizers via start.gg and fighting-game communities. Run payouts manually for two events at 1.5% to learn the edge cases, and build the KYC and tax-form intake.

ideas.title: Cross-Border Clearinghouse for VTuber Merch
ideas.one_liner: A duty-paid storefront and fulfillment rail for VTuber agencies that pre-sells to overseas fans and clears unsold Japanese inventory to them.
ideas.customer: Mid-size and independent VTuber and idol agencies (not Cover or Anycolor initially), plus overseas fans buying from a duty-paid storefront.
ideas.problem: Cover Corp's FY3/2026 revenue rose 13.7% but net profit fell 45.7%, hit by 1.8B yen of unsold merch and a 3.3B yen metaverse write-off. Overseas viewers are about 30% of viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet those fans face customs surprises, region-locked stores and 30-100% proxy markups.
ideas.solution: A global storefront and fulfillment layer with duty-paid shipping, pre-order demand aggregation, and Japanese warehouse partners. Overseas pre-order counts feed manufacturing quantities to reduce overproduction. Overstock is bought or consigned and resold to overseas fans with authenticity guarantees.
ideas.why_now: The US ended its $800 de minimis exemption in Aug 2025 and the EU is moving the same way, which breaks the old cheap-parcel proxy model. Hololive's profit drop is a public case study in overproduction.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-25% commission on gross merchandise value plus fulfillment fees, and 25-40% of wholesale margin on bought overstock.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Overproduction in Japan and unmet demand overseas are two sides of one imbalance. Forecasts miss overseas demand because logistics hide it, so a clearinghouse converts waste into revenue and generates a better forecast from pre-orders.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact 10 small VTuber agencies and 3 Japanese merch producers. Launch a 50-SKU duty-paid shop for one agency. Line up a Japan-based fulfillment partner and pre-sell to an overseas fan community.

ideas.title: Monetization Compliance-as-Code for Free-to-Play Studios
ideas.one_liner: A linter that reads a studio's store and gacha configuration and flags per-country, per-age-band violations, with an auditable rulebook curated by counsel.
ideas.customer: Mid-size free-to-play mobile and PC studios and publishers (10-300 staff) selling in the EU, UK, Brazil, Australia and US states.
ideas.problem: Rules diverge fast. Brazil's 2025 child-protection law restricts loot boxes for minors (in force in 2026), the EU consumer authorities set 2025 principles on virtual currency pricing, and an EU Digital Fairness Act proposal is expected around late 2026. Roblox age tiers and Discord age checks add age-band segmentation. Studios rely on $400-600 per hour legal memos and hand-checked spreadsheets.
ideas.solution: Ingest offer tables, gacha odds, currency bundles and subscription flows from LiveOps exports or APIs. Flag violations per market and age band against a versioned rulebook, produce audit-ready evidence, and gate builds in CI.
ideas.why_now: Brazil's restrictions took effect in 2026, the Digital Fairness Act is in the pipeline, and platform age tiers force age-aware storefronts. Enforcement history (Epic's FTC settlements) shows the cost of missing this.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-3,000 per month per title, $5-15k onboarding, and a premium tier with counsel-reviewed rule updates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Games compliance is sold as legal advice, but violations live in JSON: drop tables, prices, labels and flows. That is machine-checkable, law firms sell memos, and nobody ships a linter.
ideas.first_30_days: Have a games-regulatory lawyer co-write a 4-market rulebook. Build a linter for one config format (Remote Config plus a gacha CSV). Offer free audits to 10 mobile studios and convert 2 to $1k per month.

ideas.title: Organized Play in a Box for New Card Games
ideas.one_liner: A managed service that gives new and crowdfunded trading card games tournament software, judge training, local-game-store onboarding and prize logistics.
ideas.customer: New TCG publishers with funded campaigns (for example the Cyberpunk TCG, which raised $28.35M on Kickstarter in April 2026), and their distributors.
ideas.problem: Pokemon has sold 85B+ cards, and new TCGs live or die by weekly events at local game stores. First-time creators have big print-run budgets but no rules-aware tournament engine, judge program, store network or prize support. Kickstarter success does not equal retention.
ideas.solution: Rules-aware tournament software (decklist validation, banlist updates, Swiss pairing), a certified judge program, store onboarding kits (demo decks, promos, shipping), an event calendar and reporting, and results-integrity tooling.
ideas.why_now: The TCG boom and $28M crowdfunding raises create a wave of well-funded first-time publishers. Stores will only stock games with events.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25k per month retainer per game plus $10-30 per event and margin on store kits.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Kickstarter funds the print run, but retention is in weekly events, and store owners only back games that have them. The infrastructure is game-agnostic, so it amortizes across many small TCGs.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch 20 creators of funded TCG campaigns above $250k. Run a pilot kit at 20 stores. Assemble an open-source tournament engine and sell the first two retainers.

ideas.title: Whisper Director for Immersive Theatre and LARP
ideas.one_liner: Beacon badges plus an AI conductor that whispers real-time cues to human actors so a 100-guest immersive show feels individually authored.
ideas.customer: Immersive theatre companies, escape-room chains, LARP organizers, corporate murder-mystery producers, and Meow Wolf-style venues.
ideas.problem: Immersive magic depends on actors responding to each guest, but no actor can track 100 people. Guests get generic loops, and shows stay small and unprofitable. Meow Wolf's Los Angeles and New York venues and Sphere's $420.5M gross show the demand.
ideas.solution: Version 1 is a stage-manager console. Guests wear BLE or UWB badges, software tracks paths and story flags, and an LLM plus rules engine produces cue whispers for performers via bone-conduction earpieces. There are no AI actors, only human performers with better information. Start with 40-person murder-mystery dinners and LARPs.
ideas.why_now: Low-latency LLMs and voice models, cheap beacons, and a live-experience boom make this feasible now, and the market is pushing toward permanent immersive venues.
ideas.revenue_model: $300-1,500 per production week, $5 per guest hardware rental, and licences for permanent installs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: AI in entertainment is aimed at replacing performers, but the constrained resource in immersive theatre is coordination bandwidth, not talent. Human performers plus a conductor scales what audiences pay for.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 3 immersive producers or LARP groups. Rent BLE tags and run a 15-person cast pilot at a Halloween or winter event. Sell paid pilots at $2-4k per event.

ideas.title: Volumetric Concert Replays for Small Venues
ideas.one_liner: A multi-camera Gaussian-splat capture rig that lets attendees of 200-2,000 capacity shows buy a free-viewpoint replay of their favorite songs.
ideas.customer: Independent venues, promoters and mid-tier touring acts, with ticket-holders as end buyers at $5-15 per replay.
ideas.problem: Small acts earn only from tickets and merch, and concert film needs a crew. Sphere grossed $420.5M in 2024 but is for superstars. Fans want to relive the night from where they stood, and no affordable product delivers it.
ideas.solution: A 12-24 camera synced rig hung on lighting truss, cloud splat processing, and a phone and headset web viewer. Attendees unlock replays via a ticket QR code. Start with one or two songs with static cameras and add motion later, with revenue shared with the venue and artist.
ideas.why_now: 4D Gaussian splatting hit practical quality and cost in 2025-26, web viewers are mature, and headsets are common enough to matter.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k capture fee per show or free capture with 50% of replay sales, plus venue subscription for archives.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the film but the fan's own position. Selling 'the replay from where I stood' to the 300 people who attended targets a captive small market with high willingness to pay.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a 12-camera rig for about $8k. Capture 3 local shows in exchange for rights. Test QR-code replay sales at the merch table and measure conversion.

ideas.title: Actual-Play Sessions Turned Into Animated Episodes
ideas.one_liner: A pipeline that turns a tabletop RPG stream's audio and character art into a condensed animated episode using the cast's own voices, with human review.
ideas.customer: Actual-play shows and TTRPG creators with 3k-50k Patreon patrons, and TTRPG publishers wanting marketing series.
ideas.problem: Fans want animated adaptations, but animation costs millions. Creators have hundreds of hours of audio and no way to give patrons a visual product.
ideas.solution: Ingest the session audio and each creator's character art bible. An LLM editor condenses a 4-hour session into a 12-20 minute script. Video generation uses per-character references trained only on the creator's own art, with consenting voices and lip-sync, and a producer reviews each cut. Output includes premium-tier episodes and short clips for growth.
ideas.why_now: Video models now generate consistent characters with synced audio, and creators can use their own art and voices with disclosure, which sidesteps most of the AI-slop backlash.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-5k per episode or 20-30% of new patron revenue for 12 months, plus a licensing fee for publishers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The output is not cinema but the recap format, the 'previously on' fans share, and the same pipeline produces shorts that grow the channel. Consent and disclosure are the differentiators.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 mid-size actual-play creators. Produce one 90-second pilot for each from public sessions, and refine. Sell 3 paid episodes at $1.5k.

ideas.title: Live Lyric Captions for Concerts
ideas.one_liner: Setlist-conditioned real-time captions of sung lyrics and banter, delivered to phones and smart glasses with translation, sold to venues as an accessibility service.
ideas.customer: Venues, festivals and touring promoters with accessibility obligations, plus artists wanting international fans served.
ideas.problem: Deaf and hard-of-hearing fans get no lyrics, because speech recognition fails on singing over a loud PA. Human captioning exists for spoken theatre but not concerts, and overseas fans lack translation.
ideas.solution: Load the artist's setlist and lyrics ahead of time. Align the sound-desk audio to lyrics with tolerance for improvisation and run speech recognition only on banter. Distribute via a QR-code web page and smart glasses with per-language translation, with a human captioner supervising deviations.
ideas.why_now: Display-equipped smart glasses started shipping in late 2025, on-device translation is good enough, and venues face growing accessibility pressure.
ideas.revenue_model: $300-1,500 per show for venues plus a paid translation tier from artists' fan clubs, and sponsorship from device makers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Lyrics are the one thing known in advance, which turns an impossible speech recognition problem into a tractable alignment problem. Accessibility budgets exist but nobody sells a concert-native product.
ideas.first_30_days: Test at 3 local shows with two Deaf community groups. Partner with one venue for a free pilot, gather testimonials, and sign 2 venues at $250 per month.

ideas.title: Rent-a-Robot Creature Actors for Haunts and Events
ideas.one_liner: A rental troupe of costumed quadruped and humanoid robots, with operators and safety systems, for haunted attractions, festivals, conventions and immersive shows.
ideas.customer: Haunted attractions, seasonal theme-park events, festivals and conventions, immersive theatre producers and brand activations.
ideas.problem: Haunts struggle to hire and retain actors, and scares repeat. Fans love character robots (Disney's droids), but building one is expensive and risky, so small producers cannot offer them.
ideas.solution: Buy off-the-shelf sub-$5k quadrupeds and $6-16k humanoids and fit them with fabricated creature shells. Add a director's tablet for scripted and remote-driven behaviors, geofencing and e-stops, and insurance. Rent at $800-2,500 per night with an operator.
ideas.why_now: Cheap quadrupeds and humanoids with open-source locomotion are available, entertainment robots are already common in China, and Halloween is five weeks away.
ideas.revenue_model: Nightly rental plus operator fee, then creature shell and kit sales and character licensing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The hard part is not the robot, it is the show: safety envelope, character design, logistics and insurance. Amortizing hardware over 100+ nights a year makes this a creature-troupe service business, not a robotics company.
ideas.first_30_days: Lease 2 robots for about $6k and build two creature shells. Book 3-5 haunts and one convention for October and November at about $1,000 per night. Get event insurance and a written safety protocol.

ideas.title: Widow-First Retention Drills for Wealth Advisors
ideas.one_liner: Sell independent advisors an annual 'if one of us dies' rehearsal for couples, because the defection risk sits at the first spouse's death, not with the kids.
ideas.customer: Independent RIAs and small wealth teams ($150M-$2B AUM) whose median client is 65+. The buyer is the firm principal or COO.
ideas.problem: The industry spends on next-gen events with heirs. Cerulli says about $54T of the transfer is spousal and about $40T of that goes to widowed women. The survivor is grieving, holds a house full of logins and unknown accounts, and has to decide whether to keep the advisor. Advisors are commonly said to lose most widows within a year (widely cited, verify). The cause is usually friction, not performance.
ideas.solution: A 90-minute 'Survivor Fire Drill' run by the advisor's team with a software kit. Each spouse's death is simulated in turn. The tool builds a First-90-Days playbook: who to call, which accounts exist, which autopays must keep running, and where the documents are. It audits titling and beneficiaries from the survivor's point of view and flags single points of failure, such as only one spouse knowing the passwords.
