ideas.solution: The UK community-pub playbook, using US tools: a Reg CF offering (up to $5M a year), an LLC or co-op with member voting, a pre-launch pledge drive to prove 300-800 neighbor investors, a professional general manager, and a shared back office (bookkeeping, permits, POS, purchasing) across all venues in the portfolio. Community shares replace acquisition debt so the business isn't forced to service a loan.
ideas.why_now: Peak-65 owners are exiting in volume, Reg CF and its platforms are mature, and retail vacancy plus loneliness make the case politically easy. In the UK, community pubs have raised about GBP 35M from 37,500+ shareholders, but the US has no equivalent operator.
ideas.revenue_model: Success fee of 3-5% of the raise, a monthly management-services contract ($1.5-3k) per venue, and vendor rebates from pooled purchasing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Community ownership doesn't sell returns, it sells guaranteed regulars. 500 shareholders who each show up twice a month are a customer base that exists before the doors reopen, and that is why these businesses survive at much higher rates than buyer-owned ones. The moat is the repeatable legal and marketing kit and the shared back office, not any single deal.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose one metro and phone 25 owners over 60. Find three with positive cash flow willing to sell at roughly 2-3x seller's discretionary earnings. Launch a pledge page ('would you put $250 into saving X?') to prove demand, and retain securities counsel for a templated Reg CF filing. Charge a small engagement fee up front, with the balance due on close.

ideas.title: Camera-Free Certified: No-Record Spaces for Smart Glasses
ideas.one_liner: A certification, signage, staff-training and radio-detection service that lets gyms, spas, clinics and bars credibly promise 'no recording devices here' as camera glasses go mainstream.
ideas.customer: Owners of boutique gyms and pilates studios (especially women-focused), salons and spas, therapist and medical practices, schools, coworking spaces and event organizers. Their insurers are the eventual channel.
ideas.problem: Camera glasses look like ordinary eyewear. Researchers and journalists have documented men covertly filming women in gyms, workplaces and beaches. New York State courts banned them from all 1,240 courthouses in July 2026, and the Air Force, DEF CON 34 and UK Comic Con have banned them too. Yet as of July 2026 no major US gym chain had a formal smart-glasses policy, and staff have no acceptable way to check.
ideas.solution: Three tiers. (1) A policy kit with signage, member-agreement language and staff scripts ($29-49/month). (2) A 'Camera-Free Certified' badge with mystery audits, listed in a consumer directory of no-record places. (3) A discreet front-desk appliance or app that passively scans for the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals glasses emit and quietly alerts staff. Start with the kit and badge, and add detection once there are customers.
ideas.why_now: Smart-glasses sales climbed after Meta's Ray-Ban Display launch in late 2025. In 2026 scandals reached the mainstream, Meta bricked units with tampered recording LEDs, and institutions began banning them in a burst. Venue owners now face the liability question first.
ideas.revenue_model: $39-299 per month per venue by tier, plus one-time detection hardware, audit fees, and later insurer referral fees for certified venues.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Bans fail without enforcement, and enforcement fails without a socially acceptable way to check. The moat is the certification norm, like 'smoke-free' or 'kosher', not the detector, which is a commodity. Women-only gyms and studios are the beachhead because 'safe to change here' is a direct marketing hook, and once one studio in a town is certified its competitors have to follow.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship the policy kit and printable signage in week one. Pitch 30 boutique studios, spas and therapist offices with a 'be the first certified venue in your city' offer. Aim for 10 paying at about $39/month. Build a Raspberry Pi or phone-based BLE scanning prototype with one pilot studio and launch a simple map of certified spaces.

ideas.title: Frozen Models: Long-Term Support for AI Deployments
ideas.one_liner: A 'Red Hat for AI models': host specific model versions with a written 5-7 year availability guarantee, reproducibility pack and migration diff-testing, for companies that cannot let their AI change under them.
ideas.customer: Model-risk, compliance and QA leads at mid-size banks, insurers, health-tech and pharma-adjacent firms, and legal-tech teams that have validated an AI workflow. Later, AI-companion products and their users, who care about persona continuity.
ideas.problem: Frontier labs retire models on 12-18 month cycles. Every retirement forces re-running evals, re-validating prompts and re-documenting for auditors. When OpenAI retired GPT-4o from ChatGPT on Feb 13, 2026, it set off the #Keep4o backlash, proving people and firms treat model behavior as something they depend on.
ideas.solution: Pin and host frozen snapshots of open-weight models (and customers' own fine-tunes), with contractual availability through a stated year, a fixed and documented inference stack (versions, quantization, seeds), and a change-control pack (model card, eval suite, audit logs). Add a migration service that replays your real traffic through old and new models and produces a behavior-diff report when you choose to upgrade.
ideas.why_now: Deprecation cycles have shortened and the 2026 GPT-4o episode made instability visible outside engineering teams. Regulators and auditors increasingly ask for documented change control on AI systems, and open-weight models are now good enough for many bounded enterprise tasks. Nobody is selling stability itself as the product.
ideas.revenue_model: Monthly hosting subscription plus per-token usage, one-time change-control pack fees, and per-migration diff-testing engagements.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Enterprises don't buy the best model, they buy the model that won't change. Each frontier release is a validation event for regulated buyers, so a vendor whose product is boring stability (like Ubuntu LTS or RHEL) has a natural niche, and the cost side is cheap because old open weights run on modest GPUs. The consumer angle (keeping a beloved persona alive) adds emotional stickiness that pure infra players can't match.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 20 model-risk and compliance leads in banks and insurers. Publish a one-page 'frozen model SLA' with pricing. Host three open-weight snapshots on rented GPUs with a documented inference stack. Close two design partners at $2-5k/month and produce the first reproducibility pack.

ideas.title: Play Yards: Phone-Free Adventure Clubs for Tweens
ideas.one_liner: Membership 'junk playground' clubs staffed by trained playworkers for ages 9-14 (tools, timber, fire pits, no phones, no lessons), launched first in four-day-school-week districts where Friday is a childcare hole.
ideas.customer: Parents of 9-14-year-olds paying $150-250/month for after-school access or $45-60 per full Friday, plus landlords with vacant retail or barns. Some state child-care subsidies and school-choice funds may help later.
ideas.problem: Schools are banning phones and governments are restricting youth social media, but kids have nowhere to go for unstructured, semi-supervised time with peers. Structured enrichment (coding camps, leagues) is oversupplied, while true adventure playgrounds are rare, nonprofit and mostly for younger children.
ideas.solution: A leased warehouse, church hall or barn plus a yard, stocked with loose parts, real tools and a fire pit, with a 1:12 playworker-to-child ratio. Ship an insurer-approved risk-benefit policy, playworker training, a phone-locker rule and flexible memberships. Anchor demand with full-day Fridays in four-day-week districts, then add weekday afternoons and holiday camps.
ideas.why_now: More than 2,100 public schools in 26 states now run four-day weeks and the number is growing, mostly in rural districts with few child-care options. At the same time school phone bans and the 'anxious generation' movement have made parents ask for offline peer time.
ideas.revenue_model: Monthly memberships, per-day Friday fees (about $50 x 35-40 Fridays is roughly $2,000 per child per year), birthday parties, holiday camps, and later franchise or license fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not activities, it is unsupervised-feeling time with peers, and what makes it sellable is liability engineering: an insurance-approved risk policy and playwork training that let a for-profit offer what municipalities avoid. Four-day weeks give a ready anchor customer (working parents with an empty Friday) that funds the more interesting weekday model.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose a four-day-week district with a supportive superintendent and rent a church hall or barn for about $1k/month. Hire two playworkers, secure a youth-program insurance policy, and pre-sell 25 Friday memberships through school newsletters and Facebook groups. Run four pilot Fridays, gather parent and kid feedback, then add after-school hours.

ideas.title: Forever Guardian: Lifetime Care After Parents Are Gone
ideas.one_liner: A prepaid, life-insurance-funded successor-care plan in which a named team becomes the lifelong advocate, money manager and care coordinator for an adult with a disability after the parents are gone.
ideas.customer: Parents in their 60s-80s of adult children with intellectual or developmental disabilities (nearly one million US households have adults with I/DD living with an aging caregiver). Referred by special-needs planning attorneys and financial planners.
ideas.problem: Parents dread 'who will look after them when we're gone.' Siblings are often unavailable, state Medicaid waiver waitlists are long, pooled special-needs trusts manage money but rarely relationships, and no single accountable person exists for decades. The current autism generation is about to become adults, and the adult cohort will surge.
ideas.solution: A tiered plan. (1) While parents are alive: a named care manager, annual home visit, a living 'letter of intent' binder (routines, medications, preferences), and monthly check-in calls, so the person already knows the successor. (2) At transition: the team acts as advocate or guardian-of-record where allowed, coordinates services, audits group-home quality, and works with a partner trust company holding a pooled special-needs trust. (3) Funded by a paid-up second-to-die life policy or an upfront fee plus a monthly retainer.
ideas.why_now: Peak-65 parents are hitting the age where the successor question is urgent, Medicaid home- and community-based services are under financial pressure, and adults with I/DD are living longer than any prior generation. It is a large, emotionally urgent market with no scaled, for-profit successor-care provider.
ideas.revenue_model: Upfront enrollment ($5-15k or insurance-funded), a monthly care-management retainer ($100-200), trust administration fees through the partner, and insurance commissions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real product is a relationship that starts before the parents die. The annual home visit is both the moat and the sales funnel: by the time a parent passes, the guardian is already someone the adult knows and trusts. It converts a frightening legal product into a service with visible value every month while the parents are still alive to judge it.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with three special-needs planning attorneys and one trust company. Sign 15 families to a $1,500 'Shadow Year' (assessment, letter-of-intent binder, quarterly visits, monthly calls). Hire one care manager and validate the guardianship, trust and licensing requirements for a single state before promising the full lifetime plan.

ideas.title: Skill Rooms: Proctored Work-Sample Studios for Hiring
ideas.one_liner: Walk-in, device-free testing studios where candidates take a 90-minute employer-designed work sample under ID-verified proctoring, with a portable score that many employers honor.
ideas.customer: Staffing firms and mid-size employers hiring entry and mid-level roles (customer support, analysts, junior developers, paralegals, sales development) who are drowning in AI-written applications and AI-assisted interview cheating. Employers pay $75-200 per sitting, candidates pay nothing.
ideas.problem: Resumes and cover letters are now noise. In a dataset of about 19,000 live interviews from mid-2025 to early 2026, over a third of candidates showed signs of AI-assisted cheating (close to half in software engineering). Google, Cisco and McKinsey have brought back in-person rounds, but each employer improvising its own on-site test is expensive.
ideas.solution: Studios in 10 metros, rented after hours from coworking spaces and community colleges. Fixed-time sittings with ID checks and locked-down machines, and standard job-family work samples (writing under time limit, spreadsheet modeling, code on an air-gapped machine, mock client call), scored by rubric with human review and AI assistance. Candidates get a 'Verified Work Sample' credential valid for 12 months and portable across employers, and employers receive pre-screened slates.
ideas.why_now: AI cheating in remote interviews is now measurable and widely reported, in-person verification is returning at large employers, and entry-level applicant floods make cheap, trustworthy screening valuable. Existing proctoring vendors (OnVUE and similar) focus on certification exams, not hiring work samples.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-sitting fee from employers, premium pricing for custom work samples, per-hire placement fees through staffing partners, and optional paid practice tests for candidates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When signals get cheap, standardized proctored tests win, which is how the SAT displaced recommendation letters. The portable score, not the room, is the business: every additional employer that honors it lowers each candidate's cost of proving skill and raises its value, and it gives displaced or credential-less workers a way to prove themselves without a degree.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent a 12-seat room in one city and sign 5 staffing agencies hiring for three roles. Design three work samples and rubrics, then run a first cohort of about 40 candidates. Charge employers $125 per candidate who passes, and use the results to sign the next 10 employers on the same score.

ideas.title: Notary Network for Human-Verified Hiring
ideas.one_liner: Bonded local human witnesses (mostly mobile notaries and loan-signing agents) sit with a job candidate for a phone-free live work sample and sign an attestation the employer can rely on.
ideas.customer: Remote-first companies of 20-2,000 people hiring for roles that touch code, money, patient data or production systems (fintech, health-tech, cybersecurity, engineering, back-office BPO), plus staffing and recruiting agencies placing remote workers. The first buyer is a 30-person startup that cannot fly candidates to HQ.
ideas.problem: Video interviews are no longer trustworthy evidence of who is doing the work. Real-time face-swaps, proxy test-takers and AI feeding answers are common: a 2026 Greenhouse survey reportedly found 91% of US hiring managers had encountered or suspected AI-generated answers, and Gartner projects that by 2028 one in four candidate profiles will be synthetic. Google and McKinsey reportedly reintroduced in-person verification steps, but a small remote employer cannot fly every finalist in, and detection software is an arms race the defenders keep losing.
ideas.solution: A marketplace of vetted, insured, background-checked local witnesses. The candidate meets one at a library room or coworking space. The witness checks government ID in person, hands the candidate a locked-down laptop or a paper packet, and stays through a 60-90 minute live work sample or technical interview run by the employer over the employer's own video call. No phones are allowed in the room. The witness signs a notarial-style attestation (ID match, unbroken presence, session log, photo) that goes into the employer's applicant file. Sold as a $150-250 per-session add-on to the final-round interview. The same primitive later extends to bootcamp and university oral exams, licensing bodies, and witnessed authorship for authors and artists.
ideas.why_now: In 2026, deepfake candidates are ranked among the top fraud threats by Experian, and hiring teams are openly adding in-person checks. Meanwhile mortgage volume is still well below its 2021 peak, so tens of thousands of trained loan-signing agents have idle capacity and already know how to verify identity and witness a signature. Remote notarization and gig onboarding tools make a distributed 1099 witness network cheap to stand up.
ideas.revenue_model: Employers pay $150-250 per attested session (witness keeps roughly 55%). Subscription tiers for volume hirers ($500-2,000 per month with session credits). Enterprise and staffing-agency contracts with bulk pricing. Later: per-exam fees from education and credentialing bodies.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not better deepfake detection but a cheap, trusted, physical human at a known place, and the law already has an institution for that: the notary. A loan-signing workforce is already trained, insured and idle. The purchase also gets filed under fraud and insider-risk compliance (nation-state fake-IT-worker schemes, SOC 2 evidence) rather than HR, which means bigger budgets and faster approval.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 signing agents in three metros through notary Facebook groups and NotaryCafe-type forums, with a simple 1099 onboarding. Write the session protocol and attestation PDF in a week; run booking and payment with Airtable and Stripe. Cold-email 100 remote-heavy startups and staffing firms with the offer 'we will send a human to sit with your finalist, first 3 sessions at $99'. Aim for 10 paid sessions by day 30. Publish an anonymized case study of the first mismatch or coached-answer catch.

ideas.title: Human Callback Line Sold Through Credit Unions
ideas.one_liner: A staffed 'is this really my grandson?' phone line and call-screening kit for members over 70, paid for per enrolled member by community credit unions whose deposits walk out the door in voice-clone scams.
ideas.customer: Community banks and credit unions with $300M-$5B in assets and an older membership, paying about $3-6 per enrolled member per month. A secondary direct-to-family tier is $12 per month paid by adult children.
ideas.problem: Voice cloning needs only a few seconds of audio, and older adults are losing large sums to family-emergency and impersonation scams. The FBI reportedly counted about $352M in AI-linked fraud losses among people over 60 in 2025, and the FTC estimates most fraud goes unreported. Victims are shamed and rushed, and the scam's whole design is to prevent a pause. Most transfers are authorized, so banks are usually not liable, but the member's savings leave the institution and often end up in a crypto ATM.
ideas.solution: A screen-free service: one memorable number on a fridge magnet and phone sticker. Whenever anyone calls asking for money or urgency, the member hangs up and calls the line. A trained human (retired tellers, 911 dispatchers, nurses) runs a slow 5-minute out-of-band check: pre-registered family safe word, a call-back to the real relative through their stored circle, and a plain-language 'this matches a known scam script' verdict. Members with large cash withdrawals or wires get a teller prompt that says 'want to call the line first?', with the credit union's flag visible to the desk. Enrollment happens at branches and senior centers with a 20-minute family safe-word ritual.
ideas.why_now: Voice-clone scams have moved from novelty to mainstream in 2025-26. Regulators, state elder-exploitation reporting duties and the UK's mandatory reimbursement rules for authorized push-payment fraud point the direction US institutions are heading. Credit unions are competing on trust and member service against fintech, and have no good product for the fraud they cannot block.
ideas.revenue_model: B2B2C per-enrolled-member fee ($3-6 per month) with a pilot flat fee of about $2,000 per month per credit union; overage for call volume; $12 per month direct-to-family plan; optional add-on to sell to insurers of members' homes and autos.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Against a perfect fake voice, the only durable defense is a slow, human, out-of-band ritual, and the buyer is not the senior but the institution holding the money. The scam is a deposit-flight event, and credit unions have the branch relationship, field-of-membership community ties and senior-center access to reach victims before the scammer does. Making the 'moment of doubt' land on a number people already trust is cheaper than any AI detector.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch one sub-$1B credit union through its CEO or member-experience lead (reach them via state credit union league events and CUNA meetups). Recruit 8 retired tellers and dispatchers to staff phone shifts from home using Twilio and a shared inbox, with no engineering needed. Enroll 60 seniors from a local senior center in a 60-day pilot and log every attempted scam reported. Sell the results as a member-perk pilot at $2,000 per month.

ideas.title: Staffed Junk Playgrounds as Apartment Amenity
ideas.one_liner: Adventure playgrounds with loose parts, dirt, tools and trained playworkers, installed on unused lots at family-heavy apartment communities and sold to landlords as a renewal lever.
ideas.customer: Owners and operators of garden-style, suburban and build-to-rent multifamily communities (200+ units, many households with children ages 5-12). Parents are the secondary payers via optional drop-in fees.
ideas.problem: Roughly 40 states now require schools to restrict phones, yet the 3-6pm window at home is where screen time actually happens. Australia's under-16 social media ban has reportedly changed daily use only slightly (about 58% still use daily vs about 60% before), a sign that removing a device without providing somewhere to go does little. Parents want unsupervised, physical, unstructured play but fear liability and have no safe place. Meanwhile landlords spend amenity budgets on gyms and coworking rooms nobody uses and lose family tenants to turnover that costs thousands of dollars per unit.
ideas.solution: A turnkey adventure playground service in the UK 'playwork' tradition: pallets, tires, rope, cardboard, sand, water, hammers and a supervised fire pit on an old parking lot or lawn, run 15-20 hours a week (after school and weekends) by trained playworkers who intervene as little as possible. The operator supplies the loose-parts kit, a written risk-benefit assessment, staff training, a background-check protocol and a specialty liability policy. The property signs a monthly contract, and families pay nothing or a small add-on. Tracked outcomes include tenant survey scores and renewal rates for families with school-age children.
ideas.why_now: Phone-free school laws spread across about 40 states by mid-2026 and the 'anxious generation' framing turned play-based childhood into a mainstream parenting goal. Free-range parenting statutes in a growing number of states reduce neglect-law fear. Build-to-rent operators are competing on amenities and retention. Nonprofit adventure playgrounds exist but cannot scale because of staffing and liability, which a landlord-funded model solves.
ideas.revenue_model: Service contract of about $3-5k per property per month (staff, materials, insurance, management), optional $15-20 per child drop-in for non-residents, and multi-property master agreements with regional operators. Ten properties gives roughly $400-600k in annual recurring revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real buyer of 'screen-free childhood' is the landlord, not the parent. One prevented move-out saves thousands of dollars in turnover, so a single retained family pays for a month of the program, and kids' friendships create lock-in that no gym can. The barrier to adventure playgrounds was never demand, it was insurance and staffing, and packaging them as a managed property service turns a nonprofit hobby into infrastructure.
ideas.first_30_days: Find one friendly 300-unit community and offer an 8-week free trial in exchange for data. Spend about $2k on pallets, tires, rope and tools, hire two playwork or early-childhood students, and get a liability quote from a specialty broker. Survey tenants with kids before and after, and track leasing-team feedback. Photograph everything and pitch 20 regional property managers through local apartment associations and LinkedIn. Aim to convert the trial and one more property to paid contracts within 4-5 months.

ideas.title: Off-Ramp Cohorts for AI-Companion Dependence
ideas.one_liner: Eight-week, in-person, non-shaming cohorts that help heavy AI-companion users rebuild human contact, sold to individuals and to employee assistance and counseling providers.
ideas.customer: Adults roughly 22-45 who spend two or more hours a day with AI companions (Replika, Character.AI, voice-mode chatbots), plus their worried partners and parents. Second wave: EAP vendors, university counseling centers and behavioral-health plans that have no protocol for this.
ideas.problem: Research suggests companions relieve loneliness in small doses but deepen it with heavy daily use; a two-year Aalto study of nearly 2,000 Replika users reportedly found heavy use raised the perceived cost of human relationships and tracked with more depression and loneliness. Lawsuits (Character.AI and Google settled the Garcia case in January 2026) and new laws (California SB 243 in effect since January 1, 2026, Washington HB 2225 signed in March) put the harm on the record, but clinicians have no playbook, users feel judged, and therapy waitlists are long.
ideas.solution: A harm-reduction curriculum, not abstinence. Week by week, participants audit what the companion provides (constant availability, validation, safe rehearsal), then re-home each need with a human equivalent: a weekly cohort dinner, a scheduled 'warm call' partner, rehearsal of hard conversations with a facilitator, and a graduated time-box on usage. Ten people per city per cohort, led by trained coaches with a licensed clinician supervising, screening for crisis, and referring out when needed. Pre/post measurement with a validated loneliness scale. Ends with a graduation dinner rather than a discharge.
ideas.why_now: Companion apps now have tens of millions of users, the APA flagged AI relationships as a major 2026 trend, and settlements and state laws have made 'what happens to heavy users' a public question. Operators under companion-chatbot laws need credible places to send users, and no incumbent exists. The EU AI Act provisions covering companion-style products are phasing in through 2026.
ideas.revenue_model: $395 per seat for an 8-week consumer cohort; $150-250 per seat through EAP and counseling partners; $1,200 curriculum license plus about $30 per participant for therapists and coaches who run their own cohorts; later, outcomes-based contracts with behavioral-health plans.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody pays to 'quit', but people pay to get more out of life, and the winning frame is nicotine-style harm reduction that meets the underlying need (low-stakes rehearsal, non-judgmental availability) with human structures. The competitor is not therapy, it is the AI, so the product has to be as easy to start as opening the app. Companion operators facing liability will eventually want a referral partner, which is a distribution channel nobody has built yet.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 12 participants from Replika, Character.AI and related communities with a screener asking who would try reducing use. Contract an LPC or clinical psychologist as supervising advisor and write a crisis-referral protocol. Run a 4-week pilot in one city in a cafe or coworking back room, charging $150. Collect pre/post loneliness scores and testimonials, then approach five EAP vendors and three university counseling centers with the data. Keep marketing to coaching and wellness, with no clinical claims.

ideas.title: Human Concierge for Phone-Free Adults
ideas.one_liner: A $29 per month phone number staffed by humans who handle the app-only chores of modern life (QR menus, parking, rides, boarding passes, 2FA migration) so people can keep their dumbphone.
ideas.customer: Adults 25-55 who switched to flip phones, a Light Phone or a stripped-down iPhone, or want to but keep failing; first found in dumbphone communities and among buyers of minimalist phone brands, then tech workers and parents who go phone-free alongside their teens.
ideas.problem: People do not abandon dumbphones from lack of willpower but from friction: authenticator-only two-factor logins, QR-code menus, parking and transit apps, rideshare, mobile boarding passes and app-only bank features. Then they buy the smartphone back. Device makers respond by adding features (cameras, maps, apps), which recreates the problem. As the flip-phone revival hits the mainstream in 2026, the failure rate is the business opportunity.
ideas.solution: Two products. First, a one-time 'Switch Day' ($99): a human sits with the customer for two hours, ports the number, migrates 2FA away from authenticator apps to hardware keys, voice codes or email, moves bank alerts to text and voice, prints backup codes and paper maps. Second, 'the Desk', a call/text line staffed by humans with a company smartphone and virtual cards: they book the ride to your address, pay the parking zone by plate, read you the QR menu, print or hand over the boarding pass, and make the reservation that only exists in an app. Fair-use unlimited requests on the subscription, with pay-per-errand for heavier tasks.
ideas.why_now: The dumbphone and analog movement hit mainstream press in 2026 (Fortune's Gen Z analog coverage in February, new flip-phone startups launching in September), while schools in about 40 states now restrict phones, pushing parents to model the behavior. Meanwhile, essential services keep going app-only. Cheap voice and workflow tools let a small human team serve dozens of subscribers per agent.
ideas.revenue_model: $29 per month subscription, $99 Switch Day setup fee, bundle and referral deals with dumbphone makers (a Desk membership included with each device), employer perk for 'focus' or wellness programs, and per-errand fees for premium requests.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce product in the anti-screen economy is not another device but human proxies for the smartphone-shaped holes in society. The business grows every time a restaurant or city makes something QR-only, and every new mandate is a marketing lead. Abstainers are also a tight, vocal community, so each retained customer is an ambassador, and the manufacturers gain from a service that reduces returns.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer 20 people in dumbphone communities a free Switch Day in exchange for interviews and permission to log every request. Run the Desk by hand from one shared iPhone, a Google Voice number and an Airtable. Categorize the first 300 requests to find the top 10 that drive 80% of the pain. Convert users to $29 per month and approach two minimalist phone brands about bundling. Target 100 paying members by month 5.

ideas.title: Blinded Self-Trials for Your Supplement Stack
ideas.one_liner: Mail-order double-blind crossover kits that tell you which of your own supplements move your own labs and wearable data, and which you can stop paying for.
ideas.customer: Adults 35-65 spending $60-300 per month on vitamins, longevity stacks and nootropics. About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, per a Pew survey published in September 2026. First reached through biohacker communities and health podcasts; later through functional-medicine and longevity practitioners who want evidence for their patients.
ideas.problem: Nobody knows whether magnesium, ashwagandha, creatine, NMN or fish oil does anything for them. Population trials show small average effects, but individual responders exist, and without blinding the placebo effect swamps everything. People keep stacks running indefinitely out of subscription inertia and spend hundreds to thousands of dollars per year with no feedback loop.
ideas.solution: The customer sends the product they already take. A partner packer or compounding pharmacist repackages it and a matched placebo into coded weekly pouches on a randomized ABAB crossover schedule with washout. Outcomes are chosen per compound: sleep and HRV from the customer's own wearable, glucose from an over-the-counter CGM (Stelo or Lingo), and fingerstick or lab draws for ApoB, hs-CRP, ferritin or vitamin D. Pre-registered Bayesian analysis returns 'keep, drop or inconclusive' with the confidence. Offered for supplements only (never prescription drugs), as self-experimentation, not medical advice. An annual 'Stack Audit' rotates one compound every six weeks.
ideas.why_now: Over-the-counter CGMs and consumer wearables now supply continuous, cheap outcome data for healthy people; fingerstick lab kits and direct-to-consumer lab ordering are cheap; supplement use is near-universal and skepticism is rising in coverage of 'mostly useless' supplements; and longevity stack culture gives buyers a natural stack to audit.
ideas.revenue_model: $129-199 per compound trial plus lab costs at cost; $349 per year Stack Audit; $60 per patient white-label for practitioners; aggregated, consented responder data licensed to academic researchers (never sold to supplement brands, to protect independence).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The most valuable longevity product for the middle class is subtraction. The average effect of most supplements is tiny but individuals differ, and 'proven for me' is the only evidence class people trust. Unlike the industry, this business makes money when people buy less: every dropped supplement saves $20-40 per month, so the service pays for itself in months and the buyer's own spending is the marketing.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 40 volunteers from biohacking and supplement communities for a $49 pilot on two popular compounds (for example magnesium glycinate for sleep and creatine for energy). Have a local compounding pharmacist or contract packer prepare coded pouches and placebo. Pre-register the analysis in a public spreadsheet, run the trial, and publish an honest 'what we found, including nulls' post. Pitch five functional-medicine practices on white-labeling the kits at $60 per patient.

ideas.title: Workup Cover: Insurance for Scan Findings
ideas.one_liner: A prepaid guarantee sold at checkout for $800-$1,000 whole-body MRIs and $949 cancer blood tests that covers the second read, the guideline triage and pre-priced follow-up when a scan finds something.
ideas.customer: Cash-pay screening buyers 45-70 (whole-body MRI, multi-cancer blood tests, coronary calcium, low-dose CT). First, people who already hold a frightening PDF; second, imaging centers and screening brands that want higher conversion and fewer angry customers; third, concierge doctors and employers.
ideas.problem: Screening has gotten cheap enough for the middle class (Function Health's Ezra scan lists at $999 or $799 for members, SimonMed at $899 promotional). The FDA advisory panel voted on September 23, 2026 to back Grail's Galleri blood test, and a new law lets Medicare cover such tests starting in 2028. But the tail is unpriced and unmanaged: in one large study about one in three whole-body MRI participants had an incidental finding and 62% of those biopsied had no malignancy, and the American College of Radiology does not recommend total-body MRI for average-risk adults. The follow-up (specialist visits, repeat imaging, biopsy) is stressful, uncoordinated and can run into the thousands.
ideas.solution: An add-on with three layers. (1) A subspecialty radiologist second read within 48 hours. (2) Guideline-based triage (Bosniak, TI-RADS, Fleischner, LI-RADS) that turns the majority of low-risk findings into 'do nothing or repeat in 12 months' with a written explanation. (3) A nurse navigator who books any needed follow-up at pre-negotiated cash prices and, once loss data exist, a financial cap on follow-up costs underwritten with a reinsurer or managing general agent. Phase 1 has no underwriting: sell 'Second Read and Triage' for $149 standalone; Phase 2 adds the guarantee.
ideas.why_now: Three things converged in 2025-26: scan prices fell below $1,000 through Function Health and others, the first FDA advisory-panel endorsement of a multi-cancer blood test arrived, and Medicare coverage is scheduled for 2028. Volume of consumer screening is climbing while incidental-finding anxiety is a top complaint in patient communities.
ideas.revenue_model: $149-249 attach fee at time of scan purchase (screening seller keeps 20-30% revenue share), $199 standalone second reads, and reinsured guarantee margin: most findings resolve with a read, so expected follow-up payout per member is a small fraction of the fee. Later: protocol licensing to health systems and imaging chains.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to mass preventive screening is not the price of the test but the unpriced tail. Pricing the tail like an extended warranty turns screening's biggest ethical objection (cascades of follow-up) into a product feature, and it lets cheap scans sell without the seller being blamed for the aftermath. A radiology-native underwriter also prices this risk better than a generic insurer.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit three moonlighting subspecialty teleradiologists licensed in target states and one RN navigator. Set up secure image upload with an off-the-shelf DICOM-sharing platform. Launch a $149 'Scary PDF Second Read' in the patient communities around Prenuvo and Function, and sign referral agreements with two independent imaging centers selling $899 MRIs. Log every finding and outcome to price the guarantee. Target 100 second reads in 60 days.

ideas.title: Executive Physicals for Union Trades Members
ideas.one_liner: Mobile 'Physical Days' at union halls and apprenticeship centers that give tradespeople the CEO-style cardiometabolic checkup, sold to the multiemployer health funds that pay their claims.
ideas.customer: Trustees and administrators of Taft-Hartley multiemployer health and welfare funds (building trades, Teamsters, food and commercial workers) and self-insured municipal and transit plans. First buyer: the fund of a 2,000-member electricians' or pipefitters' local.
ideas.problem: Workers 45-64 in the trades carry high rates of hypertension, sleep apnea, hearing loss, silica or dust lung exposure and undetected heart disease, yet they work 6am shifts and cannot make weekday clinic hours. Funds face rising costs (employers say GLP-1 drug costs loom large in the 2026 Business Group on Health survey) but their prevention is a voucher for an annual physical with low uptake. Corporate wellness vendors are built for white-collar campuses, not job sites.
ideas.solution: A 45-minute station circuit at the union hall or training center: validated blood pressure, fingerstick lipids and A1c (ApoB by send-out), single-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation, spirometry for dusty trades, audiogram, a STOP-BANG screen with a hand-off home sleep test, grip and gait, and FIT kits. A physician or NP reviews results the same day. Intermediate-risk members get a pre-booked $75-150 coronary calcium scan at a partner imaging center, and members with findings get a fast lane through a care navigator. Occupation-specific add-ons: sleep apnea for drivers, hearing and silica for construction. Fixed-fee pricing with no referral kickbacks.
ideas.why_now: GLP-1 spending has made plan sponsors receptive to prevention offsets. Point-of-care devices are now small and cheap enough to run a full circuit from two suitcases. Skilled-trades labor is aging and scarce, so trustees have a genuine interest in keeping members working and healthy longer.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-250 per participant paid by the fund, quarterly repeat days, plus optional shared-savings on downstream claims after the first year; add-on family-member days for spouses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Unions and multiemployer funds are the last pooled buyer with a 30-year time horizon on each member, so they are among the few payers who can actually capture the return on prevention (a corporate employer loses the employee after three years). Trustees are elected by the workers, so 'the same physical executives pay $5,000 for' is politically powerful. Elite prevention has to be sold where the payer keeps the member long enough to profit.
ideas.first_30_days: Get an introduction through an apprenticeship training center director or a local business manager. Offer a free or at-cost Physical Day for 40 members, staffed by a physician partner and two techs (roughly $6k in costs). Collect anonymized data on undiagnosed hypertension, high ApoB, apnea risk and hearing loss. Bring a one-page summary to the trustees at their next quarterly meeting comparing the cost of 30 physicals to one avoided cardiac event. Aim to sign a recurring contract within 4-5 months.

ideas.title: Health-Check Weekends Abroad, Vetted by US Doctors
ideas.one_liner: Three- to four-day trips to Korean and Japanese comprehensive screening centers, with a US physician who prepares you before, translates results after, and coordinates follow-up back home.
ideas.customer: Americans 45-65 who pay cash for screening: self-employed, pre-Medicare early retirees, high-deductible households. The wedge is Korean-American and Japanese-American families who already fly to visit parents and trust the hospitals; the broader market follows.
ideas.problem: US preventive imaging and endoscopy are sold a la carte and priced for insurers: one whole-body MRI can cost $2,500, and an MRI plus CT plus endoscopy plus cardiac workup can run to several thousand dollars out of pocket. Korea and Japan built prevention into national habit, with one-day comprehensive packages (imaging, endoscopy, cardiac, labs) that reportedly cost 40-70% less than equivalent US screening, but US patients cannot navigate the language, the choice of package or the follow-up when they return.
ideas.solution: A packaged trip: (1) pre-trip telehealth visit with a US physician who picks an evidence-based subset of tests and avoids overkill; (2) land package with hotel, interpreter and escort at a vetted university hospital health-promotion center, results in days; (3) post-trip visit where the physician turns the translated report into a US action plan and books any follow-up at home. Group departures create cohorts and lower unit costs. Pair with the Workup Cover idea for the tail if a finding appears.
ideas.why_now: Consumers have shown in 2025-26 that they will pay $800-$2,500 cash for a single scan, and K-culture has made Korea an aspirational destination for Americans. Korean hospitals run international patient centers and take intermediary partners, and international screening packages are now marketed in English. US screening costs, high deductibles and the coming FDA and Medicare changes for blood-based tests are widening the gap.
ideas.revenue_model: Package margin of 15-25% (travel margin plus hospital partner commission where legal), $250 per physician consult (pre and post), and group or employer retreat pricing for early-retiree communities and small businesses. Optional membership for annual return trips.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The right pitch is not 'cheap surgery abroad', which has a bad reputation, but 'join a country where prevention is a national habit'. The unclaimed value is not the discount but de-risking the two ends of the trip: choosing tests that matter and handling the follow-up in the US. The diaspora is the natural wedge because trust, language and family visits already exist.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact the international health-screening centers of three Seoul hospitals and agree one standard package and one heart-focused package. Recruit a telehealth-licensed US physician for pre- and post-trip visits. Recruit 20 pilot travelers from Korean-American church and community groups and longevity forums, take $500 deposits for a first group departure four to five months out, and get six seats confirmed. Keep marketing to screening and prevention, not diagnosis or cure.

ideas.title: Member-Owned Healthspan Co-ops on the HSA Cap
ideas.one_liner: Affinity groups of 300-400 households co-own a small primary-care practice on a roughly $99-129 monthly membership that is now HSA-compatible, use group visits, and buy elite screening at pooled cash prices.
ideas.customer: Self-employed and small-business households aged 40-64 on bronze, catastrophic or high-deductible plans who already belong to a trusted group: a congregation, a 55+ community, a chamber of commerce or freelancers' guild, a farmers-market vendors' association, a large local gym.
ideas.problem: Elite prevention is sold item by item at retail prices ($200-$2,500 per test), by clinics whose upsell incentives people distrust. Direct primary care exists but rarely includes a preventive protocol and does not pool purchasing power. High deductibles leave the middle class with either a rushed annual physical or nothing between that and an emergency.
ideas.solution: A consumer co-op that hires one physician, one NP or health coach and part-time admin on a fixed monthly fee under the direct-primary-care rules. Monthly group visits (60-90 minutes, about 12 members each) cover a rotating theme (blood pressure, lipids and ApoB, sleep, strength, metabolic health) with each member's numbers on a private dashboard, plus 1:1 visits, messaging and same-week appointments. The co-op negotiates cash prices for in-office and send-out labs, coronary calcium scans, DEXA and VO2 testing (paid separately as ordinary HSA-eligible medical expenses), and members vote on which tests the protocol includes, so there is no upsell incentive. The startup provides the co-op in a box: legal templates, protocol, software, physician recruiting and a shared purchasing agreement.
ideas.why_now: Since January 1, 2026, direct primary care fees of up to $150 per month for an individual ($300 for a family) no longer disqualify someone from an HSA, and bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans became HSA-eligible, opening HSAs to roughly 7.3 million more Americans. That creates a tax-advantaged price point for exactly this product. DPC statutes exist in most states, and cash-price transparency for imaging and labs is improving.
ideas.revenue_model: Members pay the co-op $99-129 per month; the startup earns a platform and management fee of about 12-15% (roughly $15-20 per member per month) plus a $10-15k organizing fee per launch. Group purchasing agreements are structured as flat fees to stay clear of anti-kickback problems.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The HSA rule sets a $150 ceiling that is roughly enough to fund a physician and coach if 400 households pool their membership, and the cooperative form solves the two things that block middle-class longevity medicine: trust (members own the practice and vote on the protocol) and price (pooled buying power). Group visits will not improve outcomes by themselves, as the evidence shows they are roughly equivalent to usual care, but they stretch physician time across more patients. Affinity groups already hold the trust and distribution; one founding meeting is the sales cycle.
ideas.first_30_days: Pair a burned-out primary-care physician or existing DPC doctor with one affinity group (a 400-member gym or 55+ community works). Hold a 60-minute founding meeting and collect pledge cards for 150 founding members at $99 per month. Get a state-specific legal and HSA-compliance memo on DPC and cooperative structure. Line up wholesale lab accounts and cash-price quotes from two imaging centers. Open in shared space with the first cohort within about 3-4 months.

ideas.title: Certified Raw Milk: Testing, Herdshares, Insurance
ideas.one_liner: The neutral assurance layer for the gray-legal raw milk market: weekly pathogen and H5N1 testing, herdshare paperwork, and the first insurable 'tested farm' program.
ideas.customer: Small dairies (roughly 5-100 cows) that sell raw milk through herdshares or state-permitted on-farm sales. Later, surplus-lines insurers and MGAs, and consumers who scan a batch QR code.
ideas.problem: Demand for raw milk is rising with the wellness and MAHA-era food politics, but farms run with no shared safety standard, no liability coverage, and thin legal paperwork. Herdshares are a legal workaround that state attorneys general and FDA (on interstate sales) increasingly scrutinize as disguised retail. H5N1 in dairy herds since 2024 and USDA's national milk-testing strategy raised the stakes. One sick customer can end a farm.
ideas.solution: A subscription with four parts. (1) Scheduled bulk-tank sampling, with a partner state-accredited lab running a pathogen panel (Salmonella, Listeria, STEC, Campylobacter) plus H5N1 PCR. (2) A public farm page and batch QR code that show results, including failures. (3) State-specific herdshare agreements and an incident-response protocol, reviewed by counsel. (4) After 6-12 months of data, a group liability policy priced off each farm's test history.
ideas.why_now: H5N1 in US dairy cattle (2024-26) made pathogen testing a mainstream topic. Federal and state milk-testing programs are expanding. Raw milk politics are at a high, and 2026 reporting shows FDA pressure on interstate sales and closer AG review of herdshare contracts. Farms now need a defensible paper trail, and insurers have no data to price this risk.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per farm per month for testing and certification, with lab costs around 40%. Per-batch certificate fees. A 10-15% commission or MGA fee on group liability premiums once claims data exists. Optional $5/month 'verified member' fee paid by herdshare customers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Raw milk's growth is capped by trust and insurability, not demand. Insurers, retailers and regulators won't touch it because nobody can prove anything. The winner is not a milk brand but the certifier (think UL or organic certification) that publishes failures. Believers and skeptics can both trust that, and the test history becomes the underwriting dataset that unlocks insurance, which is the real moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with a strong raw-milk farmer network and clear legal footing (for example Pennsylvania or Utah). Recruit 10-15 farms through state raw-milk associations and Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund events. Sign a wholesale rate with an accredited lab. Sell a $199/month 'weekly test plus public results page' pilot. Show 3 months of data to 2 surplus-lines brokers to scope a group liability program.

ideas.title: Private Road Associations in a Box
ideas.one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
ideas.customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
ideas.problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
ideas.solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
ideas.why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.

ideas.title: Amnesty Desk: Legalizing Unpermitted Backyard Units
ideas.one_liner: Fixed-fee 'legalize your existing unit' service that is paid at closing, turning unpermitted ADUs and garage conversions into appraisable, financeable, insurable square footage.
ideas.customer: Homeowners (and heirs) with unpermitted ADUs, basement apartments or garage conversions built before the amnesty cutoff, plus listing agents who need the unit legal before it sells.
ideas.problem: Huge numbers of homes contain units built without permits. They can't be appraised as living area, financed, insured properly, or sold without discounts and buyer fear. Owners assume legalization means demolition or a full code retrofit, and city permit counters are unfamiliar with the new amnesty rules.
ideas.solution: Productized legalization. A paid feasibility scan (measured as-built drawing, life-safety checklist), then a fixed-price package covering plans, permit filing under the amnesty rules, inspection coordination and any minimal safety fixes. Offer a contingent, paid-at-escrow version for listing agents, and an appraiser-ready package that unlocks HELOCs or refinancing once legal.
ideas.why_now: California's AB 2533 took effect January 1, 2025. Cities generally must accept applications for eligible pre-2020 unpermitted ADUs and JADUs without retroactive penalties or full code upgrades, unless the unit is unsafe. Regional guidance was still being issued in March 2026. Some estimates say tens of thousands of additional units are now eligible. Local planning staff are still learning the process. More states are loosening ADU rules.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 feasibility and as-built fee, then an $8-15K legalization package. Alternatively a contingent fee of roughly 1% of the sale price paid at close for agent-referred listings. Referral fees from lenders and insurers once units are legal.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is city-by-city procedural knowledge, not architecture: how each of the roughly 500 California jurisdictions actually processes amnesty applications. The buyer of the outcome is often the next buyer, lender or insurer, so price and pitch it as a sale-price unlock ('an extra $80-150K of appraised value') rather than a permit fee. A database of how each city behaves is the compounding moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 3 adjacent cities in one region (for example Bay Area or LA basin). Partner with a licensed architect or expediter and a measurement scanner. Build a one-page eligibility checker. Reach out to listing agents and to homeowners who have advertised unpermitted units on rental sites. Close the first 5 feasibility scans at $2,000 each and offer the first 2 legalizations at a discount for case studies.

ideas.title: Certification-Ready OS for Sober Living Operators
ideas.one_liner: Software and audit-readiness for independent recovery residences, so the good operators become visible, certified and eligible for opioid-settlement and referral funding.
ideas.customer: Independent sober living and recovery residence operators (8-40 beds), who pay a monthly subscription. Counties, states and treatment programs later pay for verified-quality dashboards.
ideas.problem: Sober living is a largely informal industry with a few notorious bad actors. States are moving to certification, and funding streams increasingly require it. Good small operators run on spreadsheets and can't prove house rules, incident handling, naloxone logs, drug-testing policies and fair-housing compliance. Funders and hospital discharge planners can't tell who is real.
ideas.solution: A recovery-residence operating system built around the NARR standard and each state's certification rules. It covers rent and bed management, house-rule acknowledgments, incident and naloxone logs, drug-test policy records, complaint handling and resident outcomes. It has a gap assessment and mock certification audit, and generates an audit binder. A separate funder dashboard reports verified occupancy and quality metrics.
ideas.why_now: Ohio made certification mandatory in January 2025, and Virginia followed in July 2025. New York launched its first recovery residence certification program in early 2025. Certification has become a gatekeeper for state opioid-response subawards, opioid-settlement contracts and Medicaid reimbursement in some states. The SUPPORT reauthorization signed December 1, 2025 extended HUD's Recovery Housing Program and SAMHSA grants through FY2030.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-499 per house per month for the operating system. $1,500-3,000 certification-prep packages. Annual license fees from counties, health plans or opioid-settlement administrators for verified-bed and quality dashboards. Do not take pay-per-referral fees: federal and state patient-brokering laws (such as EKRA) make that dangerous.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The gray market's problem is invisibility as much as bad operators: funders have no cheap way to tell good houses from bad. The trusted data trail is the product. The business model rule is to sell software to operators and dashboards to funders, and never take referral commissions. That keeps the network legally clean and trusted by courts, hospitals and families, which is what makes it hard to copy.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with a new certification mandate (Ohio or Virginia). Offer 10 operators a free gap assessment against the NARR standard through state recovery-housing associations. Convert them to a $199/month readiness plan. Meet the state certifying body to align templates. Pitch one county opioid-settlement administrator on a pilot verified-bed dashboard.

ideas.title: Cash Caregiver Rails: Deductible, Reimbursable, Legal
ideas.one_liner: Payroll plus clinician plan-of-care paperwork that turns cash-paid family and neighbor caregivers into tax-deductible, insurance-reimbursable, workers'-comp-covered employment.
ideas.customer: Adult children and spouses who pay $15-30 an hour in cash to informal home aides for a parent with dementia, frailty or serious illness. The households spend $20-60K a year, and some have long-term care insurance.
ideas.problem: A large slice of elder home care runs on cash, word of mouth and no paperwork. Families lose tax deductions and long-term care insurance benefits that require documentation. They carry unlimited liability for injuries in their home and owe unpaid household-employer taxes. The aide has no wage record, comp cover, or path to benefits. Agencies solve this at $35+ an hour, which many families can't afford.
ideas.solution: An employer-of-record service for family-hired caregivers. It provides payroll, tax filing (household employer) and workers' comp or injury cover. A telehealth nurse practitioner certifies chronic illness and writes a plan of care, which are the tax and long-term care insurance requirements for 'qualified long-term care services'. A claims-ready packet is generated for long-term care insurers and the family's tax preparer, and a shift-check-in log is kept. Optional backup-aide pool for absences.
ideas.why_now: Boomers are in their 80s. Agency costs keep rising, and 2025-26 Medicaid funding cuts push more families toward informal care. Telehealth nurse practitioner visits make chronic-illness certification cheap. Household payroll rails and workers'-comp programs for single-worker households are now easy to embed through APIs.
ideas.revenue_model: $99-149 per household per month platform fee plus payroll processing. An annual $150-250 clinician certification fee. An insurer-paid fee, or employer benefit contract, for claim-ready documentation that reduces fraud and denial disputes. Backup-aide shifts at a margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Families don't pay for compliance. They pay when the paperwork unlocks money that is currently being left on the table: deductions and insurance benefits that are only available to a documented, plan-of-care relationship. The clinician certification is the wedge, and payroll is just plumbing. Selling it as 'get reimbursed' rather than 'stay legal' changes conversion completely. It also builds a data asset that insurers will pay for.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a tax-preparer network or elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers who see cash caregivers daily. Contract a telehealth nurse practitioner group for plan-of-care certifications. Use an existing household payroll provider under white-label. Sign 15 families at $99/month with a money-back guarantee tied to documented reimbursements. Measure recovered dollars per household as the headline metric.

ideas.title: Landowner-Side Broker for Data-Center Land
ideas.one_liner: A conflict-free advocate that scores your parcel's power value and runs a competitive process, so the family farm isn't sold cheap to an anonymous LLC.
ideas.customer: Family landowners with 100-2,000 acres near high-voltage transmission lines or substations, in data-center-active counties, who are getting unsolicited offers. Each deal is worth $5-50M or more.
ideas.problem: Developers approach landowners through shell LLCs and landmen, with NDAs and options that lock the land up cheaply. Landowners can't tell whether $30K or $300K an acre is fair, because value now depends on grid interconnection position, water and fiber rather than acreage. Regional brokers don't know how to value power, so owners either sell too low or refuse offers that are actually good.
ideas.solution: A licensed landowner-side brokerage. A Parcel Power Score built from public transmission and substation data, utility large-load tariffs, zoning and moratorium status, water and fiber proximity, and an independent power engineer's review. It runs a competitive process to many site-selection teams and developers, negotiates terms (sale, option, lease, JV, decommissioning bonds), and represents only the seller.
ideas.why_now: Land purchases for future data centers reached about $6B in the first half of 2026, up roughly 79% from a year earlier (Avison Young), and sale offers in some places run up to 10 times agricultural value. Sept 2026 coverage shows farmers getting huge offers alongside a local backlash and moratoria that make timing and zoning risk decisive. The seller-side infrastructure has not caught up.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-15K representation retainer that is credited against a 1-2% success fee. On $10-50M deals this is $100-500K per closing. Optional fee for a second-opinion review of an existing offer.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Land in this market is priced on power queue position, not soil. Buyers know it and sellers don't, and that information gap is the fee pool. Being seller-only and publishing the methodology makes you the trusted party for landowners and gives hyperscalers a pre-assembled, pre-screened pipeline they will actually prefer. The parcel data is a compounding asset.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick a cluster of counties around a substation or 345kV corridor in a data-center-active area (for example Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Texas or Pennsylvania). Build parcel maps with public HIFLD and county data. Mail or door-knock 300 landowners with a free Parcel Power Score. Partner with a rural land attorney and an independent power engineer, get a broker license or partner with a licensed broker, and aim to sign 3 exclusive representation agreements. Send a one-page buyer package to 20 site-selection teams.

ideas.title: Verified Colony-Strength Ledger for Commercial Beekeepers
ideas.one_liner: Third-party hive-strength verification and escrowed pollination contracts, turning bees into a gradeable, financeable commodity after record die-offs.
ideas.customer: Migratory commercial beekeepers running 1,000+ hives who truck colonies to California almonds and other crops. Almond and fruit growers are the counterparties.
ideas.problem: Surveys found commercial operations lost an average of about 62% of colonies between June 2024 and February 2025, and estimated the lost almond pollination income at more than $400M. Pollination is sold by phone brokers on 'frames of bees' standards that are verified by spot manual inspection, so disputes and 'strength laundering' are common. Growers can't be sure what they get, beekeepers can't prove what they have, and lenders and insurers can't underwrite either.
ideas.solution: An inspector network using thermal imaging and frame-count sampling to grade colony strength before loading, with results stored in a tamper-evident ledger tied to each yard and hive. Strength-tiered pollination contracts with escrowed payments released on verified counts. Later, hive collateral reports for ag lenders, and parametric or indemnity cover for winter losses.
ideas.why_now: The 2024-25 losses were the worst on record, and 2025-26 survey and industry reports show continuing stress. Almond growers are paying about $181 per colony (2023 figure) for strong hives and demand certainty. Thermal and camera-based frame counting is now cheap. Almond bloom in February 2027 is about five months away, so a working pilot can earn first revenue this winter.
ideas.revenue_model: $4-8 per hive inspected, paid by the beekeeper and often co-paid by growers. A 2-3% fee on escrowed contract value. Later: data fees from ag lenders and insurance commissions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A beekeeper's scarcest asset is now the healthy colony, and the trade runs on trust and handshake grading. A neutral, standardized 'strength certificate' does three things at once: it lets strong operators charge more, it lets growers verify what they bought, and it creates the collateral data that lets banks lend against bees. The verifier becomes the exchange.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact 5-10 mid-size migratory beekeepers and 2-3 pollination brokers now (before winter loading). Hire or contract 2-3 experienced bee inspectors, and pilot thermal frame counting on 2,000 hives. Offer growers a paid 'verified load' program for the January-February 2027 loading window. Publish a strength-grade standard and get 2 growers to commit to tiered pricing.

ideas.title: MFP Cash Bridge for Independent Pharmacies
ideas.one_liner: Reconciliation plus short-term financing for the cash gap independent pharmacies now carry between dispensing at Medicare's negotiated price and getting the manufacturer refund.
ideas.customer: Independent pharmacy owners (about 18,000 US stores) with heavy Medicare Part D volume, who are being asked to float thousands of dollars a week.
ideas.problem: The first ten Medicare-negotiated 'maximum fair prices' took effect January 1, 2026. Pharmacies buy at wholesale acquisition cost, dispense at the lower MFP and are refunded later through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator, with refunds due within 14 days but the clock starting only when manufacturers receive the data. An analysis for NCPA estimated weekly cash-flow shortfalls above $10K per pharmacy, and a member survey found over 90% of independents are considering not stocking or have stopped stocking one or more of the drugs.
ideas.solution: Step one is software: read pharmacy-management system exports and MTF remittance data, reconcile every MFP claim against refunds received, flag underpayments and late refunds, and forecast next week's cash gap. Step two is an advance product: fund verified pending MFP refunds at a small fee, repaid automatically when the MTF payment lands.
ideas.why_now: MFP has been live since January 2026, and cash-flow strain is documented. The second negotiation cycle, effective January 2027, adds 15 more drugs (including semaglutide products), so volume and float will grow sharply. Independent pharmacies are already squeezed by PBM reimbursement and store closures, and wholesalers and PBMs have little incentive to solve this.
ideas.revenue_model: $149-299 per pharmacy per month for reconciliation and alerts. 0.5-1.5% fee per advance, with a short 14-30 day duration. Warehouse-line financing spread as volume grows.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is receivables finance in disguise. Refunds owed by big manufacturers through a federal facilitator are among the best-quality, most verifiable small-business receivables in healthcare. The reconciliation software is the underwriting engine, so a small team can start with software, prove default rates are near zero, and then raise a cheap credit line. Being the trusted data layer also positions you for the 2027 and 2028 waves.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a state pharmacy association or NCPA-affiliated buying group. Recruit 10-15 pharmacies and ingest exports from PioneerRx, Rx30 or QS/1. Sell a $149/month MFP reconciliation dashboard that finds unpaid refunds. Run a free 'cash gap audit' to generate leads. After 60-90 days of clean data, approach a specialty lender for a small advance pilot.

ideas.title: Audit-Proof Records for CDL Training Schools
ideas.one_liner: A compliance layer that captures entry-level driver training records as training happens, so legitimate CDL school owners survive FMCSA registry purges and audits.
ideas.customer: Owners of independent CDL and truck driving schools (roughly 10-500 students a year), whose business depends on staying on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry.
ideas.problem: FMCSA has removed thousands of training providers from the registry, put thousands more on notice, and is running in-person audits of roughly 1,500 providers, with Justice Department and DHS attention to fraud in the CDL pipeline. Legitimate small schools with sloppy paperwork (instructor qualifications, curriculum hours, facility and vehicle documentation, timely completion uploads) can lose registration overnight. Students can't test, and the business dies.
ideas.solution: A mobile-first record system used on the range and in the classroom. QR or biometric check-in per session, driving-hour and behind-the-wheel logs, instructor qualification and expiry tracking, curriculum completion mapped to the ELDT requirements, and automatic, timely uploads to the registry. It produces an audit binder on demand, runs a mock audit, and offers an audit-day support line.
ideas.why_now: The FMCSA crackdown on training providers escalated through 2025-26, and 2026 in-person audits give failing providers about 30 days to fix problems before removal. Owners are frightened, and law firms and generic compliance tools aren't built for a 3-truck school in a strip mall. Carriers increasingly ask where new hires trained.
ideas.revenue_model: $299-799 per school per month depending on size. $1,500-3,000 for a one-time audit-readiness package or mock audit. A carrier-paid fee to verify graduates from a 'clean records' school network.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: An audit is a documentation exercise, and most schools that fail are honest but disorganized. The registry is a public, scrapeable list, so you can sell to every provider directly by name. Over time the audit-clean data lets you build a trusted graduate-verification network that carriers pay to hire from, which is a bigger business than compliance software alone.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape the public Training Provider Registry list for two or three states. Cold-call and email owners with a free 20-point audit-readiness checklist. Sell a $1,500 audit-readiness package to the first 10 schools. Use their pain points to specify the mobile check-in and logging MVP.

ideas.title: Fire-Line Readiness Passport for Contract Wildfire Crews
ideas.one_liner: A qualifications, equipment-inspection and shift-ticket system for private wildland fire engine and crew owners, built so they are never rejected at check-in or paid late.
ideas.customer: Owners of private wildland fire engines, hand crews and water tenders contracted by federal and state agencies (the national association alone represents 300+ contractors). A single rig or crew can gross six figures in a season.
ideas.problem: Contract fire resources are dispatched from agency lists and must show current qualifications, red cards, fitness tests, insurance, vehicle and pump inspections and correct rate documentation. A missing or expired item gets the rig rejected or sent home at check-in. Payment then depends on shift tickets being filled out and reconciled correctly. Errors mean holds and weeks of waiting while the owner fronts payroll, fuel and insurance. Most operators run this on paper and text messages.
ideas.solution: A mobile passport per crew member and rig. It tracks qualification and training expiry, physical and medical dates, insurance certificates and equipment checklists against the specific contract's rules. It flags what will fail at check-in, generates GPS-and-time-stamped shift tickets in agency format with automated checks against contract rates, and packages payment documents. Later it adds accelerated payment.
ideas.why_now: Agencies are leaning heavily on contractors, the national Type 2-IA crew contract cycle continues through 2026-27, and the wildfire workforce and pay rules are shifting. It is late September, so the off-season sales window for 2027 contracts is open and there is time to build an MVP before next season.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per engine or crew per month. A 1-2% fee on accelerated payment advances against verified, error-free packets, once the record system proves low rejection rates. Insurance and training referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In fire contracting, the paperwork is the collateral. The rig-days lost to rejection and the payment delays from ticket errors are the real costs. A system that pre-validates packets against the contract's own rules is trusted by agencies, insurers and factoring companies alike, so it can become the data layer for everything financial in the niche. The market looks small (roughly a thousand firms), but each firm has an unusually high willingness to pay.
ideas.first_30_days: Join the national contractor association's conversations and contact owners on state preseason contract lists in Oregon, Idaho, Montana and California. Offer a $750-1,500 'pre-season readiness audit' per rig, mapping each contract's checklist. Use the audits to design the MVP. Sell subscriptions from February for the 2027 season.

ideas.title: Harvest-Season Fab Van for Farm Machinery
ideas.one_liner: A trailer with industrial printers, a small mill and lathe, and a 3D scanner that parks at grain co-ops during harvest and planting and fabricates the broken part while the farmer waits.
ideas.customer: Row-crop and specialty farms, custom harvesters and independent ag-repair shops (Midwest, Plains, Central Valley), plus farm co-ops that host the van.
ideas.problem: A combine or planter is worth thousands of dollars a day inside a 10-day weather window. The dealer's part is backordered, discontinued or priced like a ransom. The failed item is usually a $3 plastic or steel piece: a latch, bracket, sensor mount, cab trim, bushing, pin, wear pad or knob.
ideas.solution: Two things. First, a mobile print-and-machine unit (carbon-fiber nylon printing, benchtop CNC mill and lathe, handheld scanner) that turns a broken part into a fabricated one in hours. Second, a growing digital parts library indexed by machine make, model and serial number, where every repaired part becomes a reusable file. Farmers can also buy a 'Season Pass' per machine that guarantees fabricated-part turnaround inside 24 hours.
ideas.why_now: The FTC and five states settled with Deere on July 8, 2026. For 10 years Deere must give farmers and independent shops the same repair software and resources it gives dealers, and it separately agreed to a $99M class settlement. That will grow independent repair shops, and parts are the next bottleneck. Crop margins are tight, so cheaper aftermarket parts sell, and harvest is happening right now.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-part fabrication ($40 to $600, with a rush premium), Season Pass subscriptions ($1k to $2.5k per machine per season), wholesale to independent repair shops, and a co-op hosting fee or revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Farmers don't buy parts. They buy hours inside a weather window, so price against downtime avoided, not material cost. The scanned-part library by machine serial number is the compounding moat. Every emergency job builds the catalog that later lets you ship parts remotely, and the van is really a data-acquisition vehicle.
ideas.first_30_days: Borrow or rent a machine shop and start with two industrial printers, a benchtop mill and a scanner (about $40k to $60k), or begin with a used trailer. Sign two independent ag-repair shops and one co-op as hosts. Run a 'we fix it while you wait' pilot through the rest of this harvest, charging from job one. Post before/after photos in local farm Facebook groups and to elevator and co-op newsletters. Log every part as a file.

ideas.title: IEP-Ready Adaptive Hardware, Printed to Order
ideas.one_liner: A micro-manufacturer that acts as the approved vendor for special-education adaptive hardware, starting with custom AAC keyguards for tablets and expanding to OT-prescribed grips, switch mounts and positioning aids.
ideas.customer: School district special-ed and assistive-technology coordinators, school SLPs and OTs, and private pediatric therapy clinics, paid through district purchase orders funded by IEP obligations.
ideas.problem: Free keyguard designs exist, and Etsy sellers make standard ones. But an SLP has no time to print, a district can't pay an Etsy seller by purchase order, and a custom AAC grid on a specific tablet and case needs an exact fit. Legally required AT then arrives weeks late. Every tablet or case refresh orphans last year's keyguards.
