ideas.solution: A catalog and a 48-hour custom service. The SLP uploads a screenshot of the AAC layout and the tablet and case model. We return a fit-verified keyguard with an IEP-friendly quote and invoice. Then expand to OT-prescribed items (pencil grips, adaptive handles, switch and tablet mounts, tactile schedule boards) using a clinician-approved parametric library. Paperwork arrives ready for the file: W-9, liability insurance, net-30 terms and cooperative-purchasing listings.
ideas.why_now: Consumer-grade printing is now reliable enough for small runs of durable parts. Tablet-based AAC is now standard practice, and app grid layouts are standardized enough to parametrize. Districts are under pressure to meet AT obligations with tight budgets. Open-source designs prove the demand but leave the procurement gap wide open.
ideas.revenue_model: Per item ($35 to $95 for keyguards; $10 to $150 for other adaptive items), plus an annual district 'AT Bench' subscription ($3k to $8k covering a set number of custom items and a design consult).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing isn't the printing or even the design, since clinicians will share designs for free. It's the procurement wrapper: being a vendor a district can legally and easily pay. Whoever holds 'approved vendor' status with a few purchasing cooperatives gets pulled into every district's AT budget. Print cost is $4 against a $80 to $150 price because the customer is paying for zero-friction compliance and clinical fit.
ideas.first_30_days: Take the open-source keyguard parametric files and verify fit against the five most common tablet and case combinations. Post in SLP and AT groups: 'send a screenshot of your layout, first keyguard at cost, PO accepted.' Complete vendor registration with two districts and apply to one purchasing cooperative. Target 15 paid orders and one district relationship.

ideas.title: Supply-Continuity Escrow for Hardware Startups
ideas.one_liner: Software-style source-code escrow, but for physical products: startups deposit CAD, BOMs and tooling data, and a pre-qualified micro-factory network is contractually obligated to keep making parts for buyers if the startup dies.
ideas.customer: Hardware startups selling to risk-averse institutional buyers (hospitals, cities, universities, fleet operators, utilities) who pay the fee, plus the buyers themselves as beneficiaries of an activation right.
ideas.problem: Procurement teams fear vendor death more than defects. A city buying 200 startup e-scooters or chargers, or a hospital buying a startup's carts or robots, has no continuity plan, so deals stall or die. When a hardware company collapses, its fleet is orphaned. The roughly 11,000 Fisker Ocean owners spent two years building their own parts supply chain through a nonprofit.
ideas.solution: A continuity package. Startups deposit CAD, drawings, BOM, supplier list, firmware build environment and key tooling data. We validate it by making trial 'trigger-ready' proof parts on printers, CNC and short-run PCB partners so that the plan is real and tested. A contract gives named buyers release rights on defined triggers (bankruptcy, 90 days with no shipments, end-of-life). Result: a one-page Continuity Letter the startup attaches to bids.
ideas.why_now: Hardware failures have piled up (Fisker, Canoo, Nikola and other consumer and mobility failures), so procurement officers have fresh horror stories. Low-cost printing, CNC and small-batch PCB fabrication now make it plausible to reproduce a wide range of parts locally without the original supply chain. Cities and health systems are buying more startup hardware in robotics, mobility and charging.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual escrow and validation fee from the vendor ($5k to $25k based on complexity), a paid proof-of-manufacturability audit, an activation fee (10% to 20% of fabricated-parts value) when triggered, and optional buyer-side monitoring of vendor health.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: It sells like insurance with a tiny loss ratio. The physical network is only activated a few percent of the time, but the deposit and the tested proof are what unlock enterprise deals for the startup. Because the startup pays to close a sale, the network is funded by growth spend rather than by rare disaster events. The hard part is proving manufacturability in advance, and that proof is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Talk to 10 hardware founders who are stuck in enterprise procurement and to 3 procurement or biomed managers who have been burned before. Offer a fixed-price $2,500 Continuity Letter (checklist audit plus one proof part) to the first five. Draft a simple template agreement with a startup-friendly law firm and line up two machine shops and a PCB house as network partners.

ideas.title: Identical Object Kits for Robot Data Farms
ideas.one_liner: Manufacture and ship standardized kits of hundreds of everyday-object variants, panels of handles, hinges and knobs, and task fixtures, so that every home and lab collecting robot training data uses the same physical objects.
ideas.customer: Robot-learning startups and university labs, and the data-collection vendors that run gig-worker networks who record household demonstrations for humanoid and manipulation models.
ideas.problem: At-home robot data collection is booming, but contributors use whatever cups, jars and cabinet handles they own. That makes data hard to compare, hard to control for variation and impossible to replicate across sites. A robot learning to open a drawer needs the same drawer types in 500 places.
ideas.solution: A 'Kitchen-100' kit: 100 standardized, individually scanned objects (cups, lids, jars, tongs, utensils, packages), plus modular handle, hinge, latch and knob panels and drawer or door fixtures with known mass, friction and geometry. Ship to thousands of contributors and to labs. Sell new object sets monthly so datasets keep growing coherently, and bundle the digital twins (scans and physics parameters) for simulation.
ideas.why_now: Humanoid and robot-foundation-model companies are competing for training data in 2026, and coverage such as MIT Technology Review's April 2026 report on gig workers training humanoids at home shows the supply chain for that data is still improvised. Only a handful of vendors can collect at scale, and none owns the standardized physical layer.
ideas.revenue_model: Kit sales ($150 to $600 each in batches of hundreds or thousands), monthly new-object subscriptions, custom fixture builds for labs ($5k to $50k) and licensing of scan and physics data.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for physical AI is not only more demonstrations but controlled, comparable ones. Whoever ships the same 100 objects to 5,000 kitchens gets a natural experiment in robot learning, and the kit sets the de facto benchmark. Old benchmarks (like a single reference set of household objects) are small and dated, so a manufacturing-scale, refreshable standard can become infrastructure.
ideas.first_30_days: Design and print or source a v0 kit of 50 to 100 objects and a set of handle panels. Scan each object and publish a free open dataset as marketing. Pitch 15 labs and 5 data-collection vendors with a pilot offer: 20 kits at cost plus a custom object of their choice. Target one vendor pilot of 200 kits.

ideas.title: Idle Brewery Tanks as Biotech Pilot Plants
ideas.one_liner: Retrofit closing or underused craft breweries into shared 200 to 2,000 liter fermentation pilot plants for food-ingredient, cosmetic-ingredient and biomaterial startups.
ideas.customer: Pre-seed to Series A synthetic-biology and food-tech startups that need samples, regulatory batches and customer trials at pilot scale, plus struggling brewery owners who get rent or revenue share.
ideas.problem: Startups can make grams in the lab but face a valley before contract manufacturers will touch them: schedules booked, minimums high, and building their own plant is slow. Pilot-scale fermentation capacity is a widely reported gap. Meanwhile craft brewers are closing: 481 closures against 300 openings in 2025, and 9,344 breweries operating in June 2026, down 1.8% year over year.
ideas.solution: A 'bio-foundry co-op'. Lease off-hours tank time from 1 to 3 breweries. Add a portable sterile-air skid, in-place cleaning and sterilization protocols, a single-use inoculum train, and harvest and dewatering equipment (decanter or centrifuge, with drying done through mobile partners). Start with well-characterized yeast (Saccharomyces, Pichia) and other low-risk hosts. Sell fixed-price run packages, with brewer-trained operators supervised by a process scientist.
ideas.why_now: Breweries are stranded with stainless tanks, utilities, trade-waste permits and skilled operators, while beer volume keeps shrinking. Food and materials biotech has more strains than pilot capacity. The gap is at 500 to 2,000 liters, not 100,000, and that is exactly brewery scale.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-run fees ($8k to $25k), tech-transfer and process-development fees, a rent or revenue share to the brewery, and later a multi-year reserved-capacity subscription for repeat customers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The moat isn't the tank, it's the permitting: zoning, industrial wastewater discharge capacity for high-BOD effluent, food-grade utilities and a building already approved for fermentation take biotech companies years to secure. Breweries have all of it. Brewers are also the biggest pool of people who instinctively know how to keep yeast at scale contamination-free.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one distressed brewery on an off-hours share. Recruit 3 startups from synbio and food-tech directories and sell a paid $5k to $10k feasibility run at 200 liters. Prepare a biosafety plan and speak to the local wastewater authority early. Line up a part-time process scientist.

ideas.title: Glasses-Free Zone: Smart-Glasses Detection Kits
ideas.one_liner: A detection-plus-policy kit for rooms where camera glasses cannot be allowed (exam centers, courtrooms, medical rooms, locker rooms, poker rooms), with logged, defensible procedures.
ideas.customer: Independent test centers, licensing and language-test operators, court administrators, casinos and poker rooms, med-spas, therapy and medical offices, gyms and locker-room operators.
ideas.problem: Camera and AI glasses look like ordinary eyewear and are now cheap and everywhere. Venues have bans on paper but no way to enforce or prove violations. In May 2026 two TOEIC test-takers were caught with AI glasses and banned for four years. The College Board banned smart glasses (even prescription ones) at the SAT starting March 2026, and New York State courts banned them across all courthouses in 2026.
ideas.solution: A door-frame or desk unit combining Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signature scanning for known glasses families, plus an optional optical check for camera lenses. It ships with a written policy pack, non-accusatory staff scripts, signage, a tamper-evident event log usable in score-invalidation or eviction disputes, and a short staff certification. The software updates as new glasses launch.
ideas.why_now: Camera-and-AI glasses went mainstream in 2025 to 2026, and other brands are launching. Institutions responded with bans in months, but incumbents (exam vendors, courts, gyms) have no tooling or procedures. The 18-month gap is between glasses in millions of faces and venue-grade controls. Consumer detector apps exist, but no one owns the evidence-grade, staff-friendly layer.
ideas.revenue_model: $299 to $999 policy and training kit, $1,500 to $5,000 per site for hardware install, then $49 to $149 per month for signature updates, incident logging and re-certification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer's problem isn't detection accuracy, it's defensibility. A test center that cancels a score or a court that ejects a spectator needs a repeatable, logged, non-accusatory process to survive an appeal or a complaint. Sell the paper trail and the staff script, and treat the sensor as an accessory. False accusations, not misses, are what scare institutions.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a prototype scanner on an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi with known Bluetooth signatures from Ray-Ban Meta and other glasses, and test on real devices. Write the policy kit with an ex-proctor or court-security advisor. Offer paid pilots to 10 independent test-prep and test centers, one poker room and two med-spas. Charge for the kit from the start.

ideas.title: Data Center Deal Desk for Rural Counties
ideas.one_liner: An independent negotiating desk that gives county and township boards a benchmark of every comparable data-center abatement and community-benefit contract, a counter term sheet and a fiscal model, paid for by the developer's review escrow.
ideas.customer: County commissions, township boards, school boards and local economic-development authorities facing data-center proposals, plus state associations of counties and resident coalitions.
ideas.problem: Developers have negotiated dozens of deals and arrive with NDAs and shell LLCs. Counties have negotiated none, and commissioners vote on abatements they can't benchmark. Leverage disappears once approvals are granted. Terms on water use, noise, diesel backup hours, decommissioning bonds, grid-cost protection and clawbacks vary wildly.
ideas.solution: Parse every signed abatement, PILOT, host-community and large-load utility agreement obtainable (the Federation of American Scientists started collecting signed agreements in early 2026, and public records requests fill gaps) into a comparable clause database. Deliver a two-week Deal Review: where each term falls against the median and best deals, a counter term sheet, fiscal, water and power impact modeling, and a 'second chair' during meetings. Fees are typically recoverable from the applicant through a third-party review escrow.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 data-center land rush has local governments scrambling: most local ordinances and ballot measures tracked in 2026 passed, many deals sit behind NDAs, and counties from Texas to Ohio are tabling or denying abatements while others approve blind. LLMs make reading hundreds of messy contracts cheap. Incumbent consultants and county attorneys don't have a comparables dataset.
ideas.revenue_model: $12k to $40k per deal review (billed to the developer's review escrow where the county allows it), annual data license for state county associations ($30k to $100k) and, later, a pre-vetted 'fast-lane' term sheet that developers pay to use.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry, not law, is the county's problem, and the cheapest fix is a set of comparables. Commissioners also fear being first or being fleeced, so 'we asked for what the median county got' gives political cover. Charging the applicant through the review escrow means the buyer, a cash-strapped county, doesn't need a budget line.
ideas.first_30_days: Collect 100 signed agreements from the FAS repository, Texas Chapter 312 filings and records requests, and code them into a comparison table. Publish free state scorecards. Email commissioners in counties with pending abatement votes and offer a $5k rapid clause redline, asking the county to request that the developer pay under its review-fee ordinance.

ideas.title: 48-Hour Patent Troll Response Desk for SMBs
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee service that answers patent-troll demand letters within 48 hours with an AI-built claim chart, prior art, the assertion entity's litigation history and an attorney-signed response.
ideas.customer: Small e-commerce, restaurant-tech, app and SaaS companies (under about $20M revenue) receiving non-practicing-entity demand letters or complaints, plus IP insurers and trade associations that want a member benefit.
ideas.problem: Trolls price demands just below the cost of defense ($50k to $150k+), betting small targets will settle. Hourly-billing law firms can't respond cheaply, and the patent office's post-grant review path has gotten harder since 2025 with rising discretionary denials, though a March 2026 USPTO memo added small-business and domestic-manufacturing factors.
ideas.solution: 24-hour intake. LLM-assisted claim mapping of the patent to the target's product, a prior-art sweep, the patent's history (past invalidations, review petitions, family members, assignment chain), and the plaintiff's prior settlement pattern from court dockets. A partner patent attorney reviews and signs a response letter. Options: a shared 'campaign file' for other targets of the same troll, and an insured defense fund via membership.
ideas.why_now: Modern models can chart claims and search prior art in hours rather than billable weeks. Incumbent firms, paid by the hour, have little incentive to compress. The patent office's shifting policies make cheap district-court leverage more valuable.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed $2.5k to $6k per response package, $99 to $299 monthly membership with pooled defense credits, and referral or insurance partnerships.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The troll's model relies on low-cost, repeated assertion against many small targets, so it is undermined by a cheap, credible response and by a memory of it. Every response feeds a campaign file, and the second, third and hundredth target of the same entity get better and cheaper defense. That flips the network effect from the troll to the defenders, and word spreads fast that a target is not a soft settle.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one patent litigator on a flat-fee arrangement. Pull the top 20 active NPE campaigns from court dockets and pre-build claim-chart templates. Announce free 24-hour triage in small-business, Shopify and app-developer communities. Charge $3k for the first five full response packages.

ideas.title: Pooled Tariff-Surcharge Refund Claims for Small Buyers
ideas.one_liner: Connect to small businesses' accounting data, find tariff surcharges they paid distributors, and pool their claims against the same suppliers now receiving IEEPA refunds.
ideas.customer: Restaurants and restaurant groups, contractors, small manufacturers and retailers that bought through distributors who added tariff surcharge lines in 2025, paying on contingency.
ideas.problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and CBP began taking refund claims through its CAPE portal on April 20, 2026, with roughly $175B owed to about 330,000 importers. Suppliers who passed the tariff through on itemized surcharges are now collecting refunds. Small buyers who paid those lines have claims but no visibility and no lawyer, since a $3k claim is uneconomic to pursue alone.
ideas.solution: Read 24 months of AP data (QuickBooks, Bill.com, email invoices) with an LLM to isolate itemized surcharges and post-tariff price jumps by supplier. Aggregate each supplier's small-buyer claims into one pooled demand or arbitration or class action through a partner consumer-protection firm. Track which suppliers have filed for refunds. Later, add econometric analysis of 'embedded' non-itemized price increases.
ideas.why_now: Refunds are being issued now (typically 60 to 90 days after acceptance), so the window for suppliers to hold and spend the money is short. Pass-through disputes have begun to appear in courts, but law firms focus on large B2B claimants. Litigation and CBP timing remains uncertain (the government appealed the refund order), which favors moving fast.
ideas.revenue_model: 20% to 30% contingency on recovered amounts, plus a fixed fee to run the AP analysis for larger buyers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Claims are tiny individually but concentrated by supplier. Two hundred restaurants that all bought from the same three distributors are a multimillion-dollar claim against three defendants. The supplier-level dataset (who added surcharges, when, how much, who filed) is the moat, and it is built one small customer at a time.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a free 'surcharge finder' that scans an uploaded invoice export or QuickBooks connection and shows what was paid. Recruit through restaurant and contractor associations and bookkeepers. Sign 50 claimants on contingency and target the 10 distributors whose surcharges show up most often. Line up a partner litigation firm.

ideas.title: Satellite Settlement Radar for Condo Buildings
ideas.one_liner: Use free satellite radar archives to give condo boards a 10-year movement history of their building, and turn it into litigation-grade evidence when a neighboring construction project caused the settlement.
ideas.customer: Florida condo associations and property managers (3+ story buildings under post-Surfside milestone and reserve-study rules), structural engineers doing milestone inspections (white-label), buyers' agents, lenders and insurers.
ideas.problem: Milestone inspections and reserve studies are snapshots, while settlement is a trend. Boards face assessments of $30k to $100k+ per unit and don't know whether nearby construction is moving their building. A University of Miami-led study of Sentinel-1 data found subsidence of up to 8 cm in the Sunny Isles and Surfside area between 2016 and 2023 and linked it to nearby construction, yet no local product turns that into building-level reports for boards.
ideas.solution: A six-page Settlement Screening Report per building. Run open-source InSAR pipelines on Sentinel-1 (and newer radar sources) for large-footprint or tall buildings, overlay neighboring construction permits and pile-driving dates, and flag movement trends and differential settlement. Engineers can rely on it as a screening input. Optional monthly monitoring, and a litigation package with a geodesy expert declaration for claims against adjacent developers.
ideas.why_now: Post-Surfside laws now force inspections and funded reserves, so boards are spending on engineers. Free multi-year radar archives and mature open-source processing (ASF HyP3, MintPy) mean a two-person team can process buildings retroactively. Incumbents (engineers, inspectors, insurers) have not integrated satellite evidence.
ideas.revenue_model: $750 to $2,500 per building per year, $300 wholesale per building for engineering partners, monitoring subscriptions, and contingency or expert fees on construction-damage claims.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The archive already recorded the history, so on day one you can hand a board a decade of movement. The money is in the claim, not the report: construction-induced settlement is an insurable, litigable harm, and radar time series with permit overlays date the cause. Sell the report as the intake funnel for claim work with construction-defect counsel.
ideas.first_30_days: Process 50 buildings along the Miami Beach to Sunny Isles corridor with open tools and publish a free hotspot map. Contact 100 condo boards and 10 structural engineering firms. Sell five reports at $750 and sign one construction-defect litigator as a partner. Note the limits (resolution favors large buildings) in every report.

ideas.title: Knowledge Trusts That Pay Heirs From AI Licensing
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A fiduciary licensing shop that records a retiring or terminally ill master practitioner's judgment, holds the rights in an estate-friendly trust, sells non-exclusive licenses to AI buyers, and pays royalties to the expert and later the heirs.
ideas.customer: Two payers. First, employers and trade associations with an irreplaceable expert aged 62-75 about to retire, who pay for a knowledge-capture sprint. Second, AI labs, vertical AI vendors and professional-training firms that license the corpus. Beneficiaries are the expert and heirs. Channel: estate attorneys and wealth managers, who want an heir-engagement hook (Cerulli says 89% of firms treat family meetings as essential).
ideas.problem: The scarcest input for AI is long-tail, high-stakes tacit judgment (how a 40-year surety underwriter smells a bad bond, how a master electrician diagnoses an odd fault). It sits in the heads of people near retirement or death. Hourly expert-gig marketplaces pay by the hour with no royalties. They rarely reach 65+ specialists, and nobody structures who owns the recordings, annotations or persona rights after death, so it all falls into probate limbo. Meanwhile 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are about 19% below trend (Stanford) and have no path to learn from these people.
ideas.solution: 1) Structured elicitation: 30-40 hours of rubric-guided sessions (case walk-throughs, 'what would you do and why not that', annotated redacted real work). Junior apprentice-interviewers from the same field, meaning recent grads or displaced mid-career people, run them. They are paid and earn a verifiable co-credit. 2) Rights go into a knowledge trust drafted with the client's estate attorney: consent controls, approved-buyer list, sunset dates, and no voice, likeness or persona cloning unless explicitly opted in. 3) Non-exclusive licensing of the corpus to labs and enterprise vendors. Royalties go to the expert while alive and to heirs afterward.
ideas.why_now: Mercor's $10B valuation (Oct 2025) and reported ~$2B gross run-rate (Jun 2026, lower-tier source, verify) proved frontier labs pay heavily for expert judgment, while contractors complain about pay and lack of protection. Roughly 4M Americans turn 65 each year, and Cerulli projects $124T in transfers through 2048. Postmortem publicity and digital-replica laws are maturing (for example California's 70-year postmortem term). The junior hiring freeze creates a cheap, motivated interviewer pool.
ideas.revenue_model: Employer-funded capture sprints at $15-40K per expert (a succession-planning budget line). License revenue share, roughly 40% to expert/estate, 40% to us, 20% to an apprentice pool. Trust administration fee of about 1% of royalties per year. Optional per-client fee from advisors or attorneys who bundle it into estate plans.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The estate, not the living person, is the natural licensor of a lifetime of judgment. Postmortem and IP rights live in probate, and royalty streams fit inheritance planning better than hourly gigs do. Retirees who would never take a gig will happily fund grandchildren with a legacy asset. The demand is a fixed-time resource (a retirement wave) that becomes unavailable once experts are gone.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two narrow, lab-relevant, high-liability trades (for example construction surety adjusters and commercial roofing estimators). Recruit 8-10 retiring experts via trade-association newsletters and five friendly estate attorneys. Pitch each expert's employer a $20K 'retirement capture sprint' as the cash-generating wedge, with licensing rights reserved for the expert's trust. Hire 3 laid-off or junior domain grads as interviewers. Run two pilots. Send redacted sample corpora to 10 human-data teams and vertical AI startups to pre-sell licenses.

ideas.title: Advancement Ledger for Parents Funding Jobless Kids
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A living ledger plus a state-specific estate addendum that records what Boomer parents advance to struggling adult children, so the inheritance later comes out fair and siblings do not end up in court.
ideas.customer: Parents aged 65-80 with $500K-$5M estates and two or more adult children, at least one of whom is unemployed or underemployed. Channel: estate attorneys, elder-law firms and RIAs, who white-label it. Payers: parents ($199 setup plus $12-20/mo), firms ($500/mo white label) or RIAs (per-household fee).
ideas.problem: The AI hiring freeze (NY Fed: recent-grad underemployment about 42%) turns Mom and Dad into the bank of last resort. Rent, tuition, car and 'bridge loans' flow unevenly to siblings, undocumented and undecided as gift, loan or advancement against inheritance. Decades later, executors and trustees face contested history and estate litigation, and families break. Wealth advisors say family meetings are essential, yet nobody tracks advances.
ideas.solution: Parents log each advance in a simple app and tag it as gift, loan or advancement. The child e-acknowledges it. Optional interest at the AFR turns it into a formal promissory note. The system flags amounts near gift-tax-return thresholds (annual exclusion about $19K). It produces a running equalization statement the attorney can attach to a will or trust with a state-specific 'hotchpot' clause. An annual sibling-transparent 'family statement' replaces secrecy. Repayment or forgiveness schedules kick in when a child gets re-employed.
ideas.why_now: Millions of 22-35-year-olds face a low-hire market while Gen X and Millennial heirs are about to receive trillions (Cerulli: Gen X about $14T in the next decade). Federal student-loan caps reportedly tightened from July 2026 (verify), pushing more tuition onto family money. With a higher federal estate exemption (reportedly about $15M per person from 2026, verify), fewer estates are tax-driven and more are conflict-driven, so fairness documentation is now the main planning value.
ideas.revenue_model: $199 'Fair Share Package' (memo, ledger, 45-minute attorney review). $12-20/mo subscription. Attorney and RIA white label at $500/mo per firm or a per-household fee. Later: paid mediation add-on when siblings disagree.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The AI jobs shock will show up in probate court a decade before it shows up in most statistics. Unequal parental support is the seed of the next generation of estate fights, and equalization is a data problem (a ledger), not a legal one. Parents will pay real money to keep their kids from fighting after they die.
ideas.first_30_days: With two friendly estate attorneys, draft an advancement memo and equalization clause for two states. Put up a landing page aimed at parents searching 'paying rent for my 26-year-old' and post in personal-finance and parenting communities. Sell the $199 package with a manual spreadsheet ledger to the first 25 families, then build the app around what they actually log. Ask 10 elder-law attorneys to co-present at seminars.

ideas.title: Flat-Fee Estate Close-Out Pods for Middle-Class Heirs
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A retired probate attorney supervises 2-3 junior associates and an AI workflow to close $200K-$2M estates for a flat fee, filling the gap between a $400/hr attorney and nothing while giving locked-out grads a paid apprenticeship.
ideas.customer: Executors and heirs of middle-class estates (a house plus retirement accounts), often a grieving widow or an adult child. Channels: funeral homes, hospice social workers, credit unions and elder-law referral networks. Flat fee of about $3,500-6,500.
ideas.problem: Wealth managers chase the top 2% of households who hold $62T of the wealth transfer. Middle-class estates get either a $400/hr lawyer or an overwhelmed amateur executor, and probate takes 9-18 months (unverified practitioner claim). Online will sellers treat probate as an add-on. Meanwhile entry-level paralegal, analyst and ops roles that used to train juniors are vanishing (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend).
ideas.solution: A 'pod' is one supervising attorney (owning the firm, or operating in a jurisdiction that allows non-lawyer ownership such as Arizona ABS or the Utah sandbox), 2-3 estate associates (laid-off analysts, HR, bank-ops people or grads), and AI workflows for asset discovery, creditor notices, date-of-death valuations, account-closure kits and the final accounting. Each pod runs about 25 estates at once. The heir gets one coordinator, a weekly 15-minute call and one checklist. Associates keep a verifiable log of completed estate steps that ladders to paralegal or licensed-paraprofessional status (AZ, UT, WA, OR, MN).
ideas.why_now: Deaths are flat (3.07M in 2024) but dollars per estate are rising, and the first wave of transfers is spousal (about $40T heads to widowed women). AI now handles document drudgery well enough to cut hours per estate from a couple hundred to a few dozen, which turns a not-worth-a-lawyer's-time market into a viable flat-fee product. State regulatory sandboxes are more open to new legal service models than ever.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fee, median about $3,900 with tiers by complexity and state. Target 60%+ gross margin at 25 concurrent estates per pod. Channel partners get flat, bar-compliant marketing fees or co-branded membership benefits (not per-referral fees, which most states bar for lawyers).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in estates is not legal knowledge. It is 100-200 hours of tedious, deadline-driven admin that nobody will pay $400/hr for and no algorithm can be trusted with alone. AI collapses the hours enough to make flat pricing work, and the supervised junior is the feature, not a cost, because employers now refuse to train them.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one retired probate attorney in one county (probate is local). Hire two laid-off analysts. Get 3 funeral homes and 2 hospice social-work teams to hand out a one-page 'first 30 days after a death' checklist with a booking link. Price at $3,900, run 10 estates in 90 days on a manual playbook, then automate the steps that repeat.

ideas.title: Laid-Off Managers Buy Retiring Owners' Funeral Homes
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: A matchmaker, training cohort and SBA-loan packager that pairs displaced mid-career operators with retiring owners of independent funeral homes, so local homes stay local and the buyers get AI-proof, trust-based work.
ideas.customer: Buyers: laid-off director- and VP-level ops, HR, finance and customer-experience people aged 38-55 with severance, savings or a 401(k) rollover for a down payment. Sellers: independent funeral-home owners aged 60+ with no child taking over (NFDA counts 15,401 US funeral homes, about 75% family or privately owned).
ideas.problem: Owners have no succession plan, and their realistic exit is a consolidator (SCI, Everstory and others) that dissolves the local name and pushes preneed. White-collar workers hit by the hiring freeze (Amazon cut about 16,000 corporate roles in Jan 2026; information-sector jobs fell 23K in Aug) cannot find durable human-presence work. Licensing rules and deal mechanics make the path opaque.
ideas.solution: A 10-week 'Director-Owner Program': state-by-state licensing roadmap (many states let an unlicensed owner run a home if a licensed director-in-charge is employed, but verify each state), a 6-12 month paid apprenticeship placement inside a partner home before closing, FTC Funeral Rule and preneed-trust training, and SBA 7(a) plus seller-note structuring. Add confidential seller listings and matching. After closing, a shared ops kit (software, price-list compliance, vendor rates) and a peer board of owner-operators.
ideas.why_now: SCI's Q2'26 results (preneed sales +7%, operating cash flow +43%, volume -1.4%) show value is in pricing and preneed, not volume, so well-run independents are valuable. Cremation is heading to about 82% by 2045, which lowers facility needs. Consumer interest in green options (61.4%) gives new owners a differentiator that legacy owners ignore. Displaced managers are abundant now.
ideas.revenue_model: Buyer tuition of about $4,500 (partly deferred to close). Seller-side success fee of 1.5-3% or $15-25K. Deal-packaging fee of about $5K. Owner-community subscription of $199/mo. Later: software and preneed-admin services.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The funeral-home succession gap and the mid-career white-collar glut are the same problem seen from two ends. The best buyer is a people-good operator, not a financier, and consolidators structurally cannot serve either side: they overpay for scale and cannot preserve local identity. It is the ultimate trust job, and AI cannot hold a widow's hand.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose two states with friendly licensing and many rural homes. Phone 100 owners aged 60+ via the state funeral-directors association, aiming for 5 signed no-cost 12-month 'successor search' agreements. Recruit the first 10 buyers from laid-off-manager communities (ex-Amazon alumni groups, LinkedIn, Blind) with a $500 refundable screening deposit. Pre-qualify with one SBA lender. Start 1-2 apprenticeships at partner homes.

ideas.title: Break-Glass Interim Operators for Deceased Owners' Businesses
ideas.angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
ideas.one_liner: An on-call bench of laid-off COOs and ops directors who step in within 48 hours when the sole owner of a small business dies, keeping it alive until the heirs can sell or close it.
ideas.customer: Estate attorneys, CPAs, SBA lenders and key-person insurers who need the business to keep its value, plus the widow or heirs. The estate ultimately pays from business cash flow or sale proceeds. Target businesses: HVAC and trades firms, machine shops, independent insurance agencies, restaurants and other 5-50 employee owner-dependent companies.
ideas.problem: Probate treats assets as inert (houses, accounts), but a running business melts within 90 days when the owner dies: bank signing authority, payroll, licenses, customer relationships and key employees all hinge on one person. Executors are grieving family. Attorneys cannot run a company. Brokers cannot sell one in freefall. Boomers still own a large share of employer businesses, so this is a huge, mostly invisible transfer.
ideas.solution: A vetted bench of interim managers with a 72-hour playbook: secure bank and payroll access via letters testamentary or a special administrator, notify customers and vendors, fund key-employee retention from the estate, arrange licensing 'qualifier' coverage where required, stabilize for 60-90 days, prep a data room, then hand off to a broker or buyer. AI tools (contract abstraction, bookkeeping analysis, KPI dashboards) let a newcomer understand the business in about a week. Owners can pre-buy a 'continuity plan' retainer.
ideas.why_now: The largest generational transfer of small businesses is under way (Cerulli: $124T through 2048, about 81% from Boomers and older), while the 2026 labor market is full of experienced ops leaders who cannot find roles. Cheap AI document and finance tooling makes fast onboarding of an unfamiliar business feasible for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: Interim GM day rate of $900-1,500 billed to the estate, with the bench member keeping about 65%. Pre-need continuity retainer of about $1,200/yr for solo owners. Success fee on a sale, in coordination with brokers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The estate needs a verb, not a noun. The legal system has a process for distributing what a person owned but none for continuing what a person did. Unemployed senior operators are the perfect supply for that verb, and their downside is only the awkwardness of arriving during grief.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 15 laid-off ops and finance leaders. Write the 72-hour playbook. Offer a free 'owner-death readiness check' at bar association and CPA society events for 30 attorneys and accountants. Sell a $1,200/yr continuity retainer to 20 solo-owner businesses through one insurance agency or SBA lender's client list. The first at-need engagements will come from those attorneys' existing clients.

ideas.title: After-School Care Inside Senior Living Communities
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
ideas.one_liner: Turn senior living's empty afternoon dining rooms into licensed school-age programs where residents are reading, repair and garden 'buddies', funded by parent tuition, operator economics and loneliness-intervention budgets.
ideas.customer: Working parents of K-5 kids near independent- and assisted-living communities (dependent-care FSA eligible, cap $7,500). Secondary payers: senior living operators seeking occupancy and retention, and Medicare Advantage plans or Area Agencies on Aging funding loneliness programs.
ideas.problem: The 3-6pm care gap is where parents lose work hours, and average US childcare costs $13,128 (35% of income for single parents). Older adults are the least-served, highest-need loneliness segment, and 40-46% of adults 65+ are 'unsure' about AI companions (Pew, Aug 2026), so a human alternative has open ground. Operators have empty spaces between lunch and dinner and no scalable, reimbursable engagement model.
ideas.solution: 'Bridge Clubs': the community lends the room 2:30-6pm. We run a licensed school-age program (1:12 ratio, bus drop from the elementary school). Residents opt into structured 30-minute roles ('Reading Elders', 'Tinkerers', 'Garden Crew'). We track participation and a loneliness scale (UCLA-3) monthly and package the data for MA plans and AAAs so they can fund resident engagement. Parents pay less than typical after-school rates because space and volunteer time subsidize it.
ideas.why_now: The dependent-care FSA cap rose to $7,500 and the 45F employer childcare credit rose to 40% (50% for small businesses) in 2026, opening employer and parent budgets. WHO's 2025 Commission put loneliness on the health agenda. Payers are hunting for measurable loneliness interventions, and school-age licensing is lighter than infant care in many states.
ideas.revenue_model: Parent tuition of about $325-475/mo. Operator rent-share or management fee. Engagement-based fees from MA plans or AAAs. Employer sponsorship of slots via the 45F credit.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is two 'deserts' each holding the other's unused capacity. 'Intergenerational programming' usually fails as charity. It works when the payer stack (tuition, operator occupancy, and loneliness reimbursement) makes it profitable and the resident role is a job, not a photo op.
ideas.first_30_days: Find three independent-living operators within a mile of Title I elementary schools with after-school waitlists. Run a 6-week pilot with 12 kids in one dining room using a licensed partner provider. Charge $99 registration plus $349/mo. Collect resident participation and UCLA-3 scores. Take the data to one regional MA plan's community benefits team.

ideas.title: Continuity and Goodbye Service for Kids' AI Companions
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
ideas.one_liner: Escrowed hosting plus child-psychologist-designed transitions so that when an AI toy or companion is shut down, retired or swapped out, kids do not lose a 'friend' overnight.
ideas.customer: Parents of children attached to an AI companion (rescue subscription), AI-toy and companion makers and retailers who want a 'Continuity Pledge' for retailer, insurer and regulator confidence, and later schools and pediatric practices.
ideas.problem: Kids form real attachments to AI voices (Common Sense: 72% of US teens have used AI companions; Pew: 12% of teens got emotional support from chatbots). When companies shut down or change models, the loss is bereavement-like: the Moxie robot shutdown (Dec 2024, background knowledge) left kids and parents devastated, GPT-4o's retirement (Feb 13, 2026) triggered #Keep4o grief, and Character.ai's under-18 ban (Nov 25, 2025) cut teens off overnight. There is no norm or product for sunsetting. A wave of small-maker AI toys for holiday 2026 guarantees more orphans in 2027.
ideas.solution: 1) 'Lifeboat': a hosted or local-runtime fallback compatible with the toy's API, using maker-escrowed firmware and cloud credentials or community forks (OpenMoxie-style) with the maker's consent. 2) 'Goodbye Kit': pediatric-psychologist-designed scripts, rituals, a parent guide and a final 'graduation' message. 3) 'Off-Ramp': an optional 6-week parent-coached program that moves a child from AI-companion dependence to human connection. 4) B2B 'Continuity Pledge': makers deposit 12-36 months of hosting cost plus source or weights into escrow, get a seal for retailers, and we give parents 90 days' notice.
ideas.why_now: California SB 243 and New York's companion-chatbot law, the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) inquiry into minors and companions, Pennsylvania's May 2026 suit over bots posing as clinicians, and Raine-style litigation have made kids' AI a liability topic. Holiday 2026 will flood retail with AI plush and robots from small makers with short runways, and their sunset problem arrives in 2027.
ideas.revenue_model: B2C 'Keep-Alive' at about $7/mo. B2B pledge of $10-50K upfront escrow fee plus $0.50-2 per unit. Off-Ramp program at about $249 per family. Referral partnerships with pediatric practices.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The safety debate is about what companions say. The next scandal is what happens when they go silent. Escrow plus ritual is cheap insurance for makers, retailers and parents alike, and the first company to make 'we won't kill your child's friend' a standard owns the retail seal. It is the GPT-4o grief problem, but for 7-year-olds.
ideas.first_30_days: Find owners of discontinued companions in Reddit and Facebook groups and offer a hosted keep-alive at $8/mo, ideally partnering with the maintainers of the open-source Moxie stack. Interview 15 parents to build the Goodbye Kit with a child psychologist advisor. Approach 10 small AI-toy makers heading into Q4, via Amazon and Kickstarter listings, with a low-cost pledge. Pitch one mid-size retailer's product-safety team.

ideas.title: Co-op Childcare Kits That Also Make Parent Friends
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
ideas.one_liner: Modern rails (licensing map, insurance, shift scheduling, lead-teacher placement) that let 12-20 neighbor families launch a parent-participation preschool or aftercare co-op in a few months, cutting tuition and curing parent isolation at the same time.
ideas.customer: Groups of 10-20 families in childcare deserts: new-parent groups, neighborhood and church parent groups, remote-work households, employer resource groups. Later: employers and HOAs that sponsor co-ops.
ideas.problem: Childcare averages $13,128 a year and the labor inside that price is the reason. Parents are lonely (friendship is now a measured health metric), and post-2020 new parents often have few local friends. Parent co-ops once made childcare 30-50% cheaper, but they withered because launching one requires legal, licensing, insurance and payroll expertise that volunteer boards lack.
ideas.solution: 'Co-op OS': a state-by-state navigator showing where parent-participation programs are exempt or lightly licensed (verify per state), template bylaws, an insurance bundle (general liability plus abuse-and-molestation), background checks and mandated-reporter training, a shift scheduler that assigns parent duty days and keeps a credit ledger, payroll for one paid lead teacher, and a lead-teacher matching service for displaced educators. Friendship is designed in: monthly parent-only dinners, a crisis buddy system and meal trains.
ideas.why_now: Dependent-care FSAs now reach $7,500 and the 45F credit lets sponsoring employers offset 40-50% of childcare costs. Hybrid schedules and AI-driven job churn have left many parents with flexible hours to trade for tuition. Parents are already organizing collectively on phones and schools, so collective action is normalized.
ideas.revenue_model: About $1,500 setup, $149/mo per co-op for software and payroll, insurance commissions, a lead-teacher placement fee of about $2,000, and employer sponsorship of co-op slots.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Time is the new money. Childcare is expensive because it is labor, and co-ops swap parent hours for tuition. Nobody does it because of coordination and compliance, not desire. Parent friendship is the retention engine, not a nice-to-have, and lonely parents recruit each other for you.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two states with clear parent-participation rules. Recruit 3 existing neighbor or parent Facebook groups into a 4-week 'Co-op Launch Sprint' with a $299 deposit per family. Engage an early-childhood attorney for templates and an insurance MGA for the bundle. Place one lead teacher and aim to have three co-ops running by January 2027.

ideas.title: Driver's Ed for Smartphones, Sold to Parent Groups
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
ideas.one_liner: Ten-week, cohort-based 'phone license' programs where a whole grade's parents and kids pledge together, kids earn tiered device access through in-person challenges, and the finish is a coming-of-age ceremony.
ideas.customer: Parent groups for one grade at one school (PTA/PTO, church youth groups, scout troops, neighborhoods) with kids aged 9-13 facing the first-smartphone decision. Parents pay about $249 per child. PTAs get a rev-share. Later: device partners and employers offering parent benefits.
ideas.problem: The first smartphone is a collective-action problem ('everyone else has one'). Parental-control software fails technically (7 in 10 Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts) and socially. The first phone has become an unguided adolescent initiation with no ritual, no community and no meaning, while loneliness among the young is rising.
ideas.solution: 1) A Parent Pact night to agree shared rules. 2) Ten weekly 90-minute kid sessions with trained youth facilitators covering boredom, friendship, spotting manipulative design, AI-companion literacy and group-chat etiquette, with badges earned in person. 3) Tiered device 'licenses': none, then dumbphone or watch, then a filtered smartphone using OS-level age signals, then full access, each unlocked at cohort milestones with parent sign-off. 4) A License Ceremony with families. 5) An alumni circle with monthly meetups and a parent forum.
ideas.why_now: Under-16 bans (Australia Dec 2025, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Florida) and app-store or OS-level age-assurance laws (California's Digital Age Assurance Act, Texas) are tiering the internet by age. Roblox now tiers by age (Kids, Select, standard). Support for Australia's ban has fallen to 57% and enforcement is leaky, so parents need a home-side complement. Twelve US states have school phone bans.
ideas.revenue_model: About $249 per child per cohort, a 15% rev-share to PTAs, bounties on tier-appropriate device or plan activations (verify what partners will pay), a $600 facilitator certification for teachers and youth workers, and later employer-paid parent benefits.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The first smartphone fails as a family decision but works as a class decision. Because the product synchronizes a social graph, its moat is the cohort, not code. And a secular rite of passage supplies the 'meaning' that makes kids willing, which content-filtering apps cannot provide.
ideas.first_30_days: Pilot with two elementary schools' 4th- and 5th-grade parent groups through PTA presidents and 'Wait Until 8th' pledge lists. Recruit four facilitators (education or psychology students and retired coaches). Charge $249, run cohorts October-December so graduation lands before holiday phone gifting, and track how many kids stay phone-free until 13.

ideas.title: Same-Day Sub and Coach Bench for Home Daycares
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
ideas.one_liner: A membership that guarantees a licensed home daycare a vetted substitute within hours and, when a child's behavior threatens expulsion, an on-call early-childhood coach, so licensed slots stay open and parents keep their jobs.
ideas.customer: Licensed family child care providers (solo operators; start with about 300 in one metro or state). Co-payers: state agencies and child-care resource and referral (CCR&R) organizations with workforce-support funds, employers buying backup-care value, and Head Start partners.
ideas.problem: Childcare deserts are as much a retention problem as a construction problem. Family homes were the fastest-growing supply (+4.3% in 2024, versus +1.5% for centers), but one sick day closes a solo business, providers work 50-60 hour weeks, and average childcare worker pay is $33,140. Behavior challenges lead to expulsions, and few early-childhood mental health consultants exist to help. Each lost slot means a parent leaves work.
ideas.solution: 1) 'Slot Guarantee': a bench of background-checked, trained substitutes (retired teachers, early-education students, displaced parents) dispatched via app on a 2-hour target. 2) 'Calm Team': early-childhood coaches supervised by an infant-mental-health-endorsed clinician, deployed for observation and a behavior plan before expulsion. 3) Monthly Provider Circles of about 8 providers for peer support and reflective supervision. 4) Light back-office (attendance, billing).
ideas.why_now: Employer and family demand for childcare is rising with the 45F credit (40-50%) and the $7,500 dependent-care FSA, but supply is thin and fragile. Family homes are the growth segment, so protecting them is the cheapest new capacity. States are already funding workforce supports and early-childhood mental health consultation.
ideas.revenue_model: Provider membership of $79-129/mo including a few sub days per quarter, with extra sub hours billed at about $22/hr plus a fee. State or CCR&R contracts per provider. Behavior-coach visits at about $150 each or covered by state mental health consultation funds. Employer backup-care pools.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every desert plan builds new slots. The cheaper win is stopping existing slots from closing over sick days, burnout and expulsions. The real unit of childcare supply is a provider's mental state, and support for it is a bench of people, not an app.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 providers in one metro through Facebook groups and a CCR&R newsletter with a $59 founding-member rate. Assemble 15 substitutes from retired teachers and early-education students. Partner with one infant-mental-health clinician to lead the first Provider Circles. Approach the local CCR&R or county for a pilot fund, and track closures avoided as the headline metric.

ideas.title: Training-Day School Inside Youth Sports Facilities
ideas.one_liner: Turn the empty weekday hours of club-sports facilities into ESA- and scholarship-funded microschools for serious young athletes.
ideas.customer: Owners of independent indoor youth-sports facilities (volleyball, gymnastics, basketball, hockey, tennis/pickleball, swim) in ESA and voucher states such as AZ, FL, TX and UT. Tuition is paid by families out of ESA, voucher or (from 2027) scholarship-granting-organization funds.
ideas.problem: Facilities carry rent and HVAC costs but sit idle roughly 8am-3pm on weekdays, because their revenue is concentrated in evenings and weekends. Families spending thousands a year on club sports fight school schedules, travel and early mornings. Microschool compliance (registration, occupancy, insurance, ESA vendor status) is daunting for a gym owner. School status also matters financially: in Texas, registered private-school kids get about $10,474 in ESA money while homeschoolers get about $2,000.
ideas.solution: A turnkey 'training-day school' kit. It includes state-specific school registration and a change-of-occupancy checklist, a low-screen paper-based mastery curriculum from a partner, hiring and training of a credentialed lead teacher plus coach-guides, insurance, ESA/SGO vendor enrollment and tuition billing. The daily schedule is 3 hours of academics plus 3 hours of training. Opt-in wearable sleep and load data decides when the hard academic blocks and the hard training blocks fall. The facility fills 20-40 seats at ESA-level tuition during dead hours.
ideas.why_now: ESA money is scaling (Texas had 200k+ applicants). The federal $1,700 scholarship tax credit starts in 2027 with 31 states opted in, yet about 1,000 microschools are in limbo awaiting Treasury rules, so operators want ready-made compliance. Alpha School (about 50 campuses, heart-rate monitors) has shown parents will pay for short academics plus afternoon workshops. 61% of teachers now want less device use, and homeschooling is transient (about 30% do it for 1-2 years), so hybrid products fit.
ideas.revenue_model: $12-20k setup fee per facility plus 8-10% of tuition, or $1.5k/month SaaS plus billing fees. A site with 25 students at $8-10k is about $200-250k of tuition a year, so roughly $20k a year recurring to us per site. Add referral fees on curriculum and insurance.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Alpha School sells a schedule, not a building. The scarcest inputs (a big safe space, coaches, motivated kids, parents with athletic budgets) already exist in every metro at sports facilities that lose money on weekdays. Boarding sports academies cost $70k+; the mid-market, ESA-priced version does not exist yet, and the gating constraint is building code, so the wedge is a compliance kit for the friendliest states.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with microschool-friendly occupancy rules (for example Arizona or Florida). Contact 40 facility owners through club-owner groups and facility trade associations and sign 2-3 letters of intent. Pre-enroll 10-15 athlete families with $500 deposits for a January semester. Hire a part-time certified teacher as head of school, and use an existing curriculum partner plus a lawyer-reviewed compliance template.

ideas.title: Referee Pathway: Officiating as a School Credential
ideas.one_liner: A semester-long, credit-bearing officiating course that puts teens in mentored cohorts on paid youth games, fixing the referee shortage by fixing retention.
ideas.customer: District CTE directors and state high-school athletic associations are the buyers. Youth leagues and game assignors are paying placement partners. Students (14+ where state rules allow) are the beneficiaries.
ideas.problem: Youth and high-school games are shortened or cancelled for lack of officials. Widely cited surveys say most new officials quit within two years, largely because of abuse from parents and fans. Meanwhile teens lack decent first jobs, entry-level white-collar hiring has cracked, and districts are chasing CTE pathways that lead to real work.
ideas.solution: A CTE elective, 'Officiating and Conflict Management'. Students learn rules, mechanics, film review and de-escalation role-play. They then work mentored, paid assignments as a cohort (never alone) at rec-league games, with body-worn cameras or comms for protection. The output is a portable 'Registered Official' credential aligned with the state association's licensing. We sell curriculum, assignment scheduling and an insurance wrapper.
ideas.why_now: The officials shortage has persisted since COVID and many states have passed laws penalizing assault on officials. CTE enrollment is rising (vocational-heavy public two-years grew 11.7% in Spring 2025). After the entry-level AI job shock, schools and parents want credentials tied to human judgment. Sports is one of the few settings where judgment under pressure is the actual job.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-300 per student license paid by districts from CTE budgets. An 8-10% platform fee on paid assignments (typically $40-80 per game). State-association sponsorships and body-cam/insurance partner rebates. A 40-student district cohort is roughly $8-12k plus assignment fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a retention problem caused by isolation and abuse in an official's first 20 games, not a recruiting problem. A school cohort is the only structure that gives new officials a team, a mentor and institutional backing. De-escalating under hostile scrutiny is also a transferable credential for security, hospitality, HR and healthcare jobs.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch 2-3 CTE directors and the local officials' association. Run a 10-12 week after-school pilot for 30 students, funded by a rec league or booster at about $99 per student. Track how many are still officiating a season later against the roughly 20% baseline. Use the retention data and a league letter of support to pitch the state association.

ideas.title: Apprentice Athlete: Injury-Proofing the Skilled Trades
ideas.one_liner: An 8-week pre-apprenticeship that conditions and movement-screens new electricians, plumbers and pipefitters so they survive the first two years.
ideas.customer: Joint apprenticeship training centers (IBEW/NECA, UA, IEC, ABC), community-college trade programs, and the workers' comp carriers and brokers behind contractors. Contractors pay per placed apprentice.
ideas.problem: Electricians have about 72.7k openings a year (data-center demand) and plumbers about 42k, but the 4-5 year apprenticeship path is bottlenecked by employer sponsors and weak pre-apprenticeship screening. Overexertion and strain injuries are consistently a leading cause of lost-time injuries and feed early attrition. Many entrants are sedentary career-changers, including displaced white-collar grads (42% of recent grads are underemployed).
ideas.solution: 'Apprentice Athlete' runs 3 sessions a week for 8 weeks in existing gyms, taught by athletic trainers and strength coaches. It uses trade-specific drills (overhead conduit work, ladder and pipe carries, crawlspace mobility, grip endurance), phone-video or cheap-wearable movement screens, and an injury-prevention curriculum. Completion, not a fitness score, earns JATC pre-apprenticeship credit and can slot in as a short program eligible for Workforce Pell where approved. It is structured as training rather than a hiring screen, to stay clear of ADA limits.
ideas.why_now: Workforce Pell launched July 1, 2026 but only 5 programs are approved. Apprenticeship-linked programs get a fast lane, and up to 49% of instruction can be delivered by employers or unions. Data-center demand is pulling electricians, and AI-exposed grads are pivoting to trades. Phone pose-estimation and cheap wearables are now good enough to measure movement quality.
ideas.revenue_model: $400-800 per apprentice per cohort paid by contractor, JATC or Pell/WIOA funds. A $100-200k pilot contract with a comp carrier tied to premium credits. Then per-seat licensing to gyms and trainers who run the program (they keep 60-70%).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The trades treat the body as a consumable, while sports treat it as an appreciating asset. Comp carriers already have loss runs showing injuries cluster in the first 24 months, so a $600 conditioning program pays back if it prevents one strain claim per few dozen apprentices. Trade schools cannot have that ROI conversation, but insurers can.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one IEC/ABC chapter or a community-college trades program. Run a 6-week pilot for 20 career-changers using phone-video screening and a $50 tracker. Log attendance, attrition and minor injuries against the prior cohort. Take the numbers to the contractors' workers' comp broker to negotiate a premium-credit pilot.

ideas.title: Wearable-Verified PE Credit for ESA Families
ideas.one_liner: Turn any kid's fitness tracker into an audit-proof PE transcript line and an ESA service receipt.
ideas.customer: Homeschool and microschool families, co-ops and umbrella schools (about $10-15 per student per month). ESA administrators and clearinghouses (compliance contracts). Gyms and studios that want to bill ESA funds.
ideas.problem: PE is the least-supported homeschool subject. ESA homeschoolers get a fraction of what private-school kids do (about $2,000 versus $10,474 in Texas) and must spend in a closed vendor marketplace. ESA programs are audit-anxious. Local climbing gyms, swim schools and martial-arts studios cannot clear vendor onboarding. Screen-fatigued parents want real movement documented.
ideas.solution: An app plus a $40-60 band, or existing Garmin/Apple/Polar data shared with parent consent. It logs moderate-to-vigorous minutes and coach-attested skill milestones. It converts them into Carnegie-unit PE credit on a transcript issued through a partner accredited umbrella school. It also generates tamper-evident 'service delivered' receipts for ESA reimbursement. A vendor-of-record wrapper handles W-9, insurance and background-check attestations so a local gym can bill ESA funds. Parents control the data and only summaries leave the family account.
ideas.why_now: With 31 states opted into the 2027 federal scholarship credit and ESAs expanding, auditors and SGOs will demand evidence that services were actually delivered. Homeschool ESA marketplaces are closed and clunky. Alpha School has normalized heart-rate monitoring of kids, consumer wearables are ubiquitous, and 61% of teachers want less screen time.
ideas.revenue_model: $12 per student per month from families or co-ops. $2-5 per verified session or receipt from ESA clearinghouses. A 5-8% vendor-of-record fee on gym and studio ESA billings.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: As tens of billions of public scholarship dollars start to flow, the winning tools will be the ones that produce evidence of delivered service as a byproduct. A heart-rate trace is a hard-to-fake delivery receipt, and PE is the one subject where wearables give clean proof. Fitness providers' idle daytime hours are the supply, and education compliance is the demand.
ideas.first_30_days: In one ESA state (AZ or FL), recruit 8-10 homeschool co-ops and 3-5 climbing, martial-arts or swim studios. Sign an accredited umbrella school to issue the PE credit. Enroll about 100 kids for a semester at $12 a month. Ship a minimal web app that ingests Garmin/Apple Health exports plus coach attestation. Take the pilot data to one ESA clearinghouse.

ideas.title: Clinic-Sponsored Tuition for Loan-Capped PT Students
ideas.one_liner: Sports-medicine PT and athletic-training employers fund tuition for students shut out of federal loans, in return for a structured work commitment.
ideas.customer: Multi-site outpatient orthopedic and sports PT groups, performance-rehab clinics and athletic-training staffing contractors pay the fee. The beneficiaries are DPT and athletic-training students facing the new loan caps.
ideas.problem: Since July 1, 2026, grad loans are capped at $20.5k a year and $100k total, and PT, OT, nursing and counseling were left out of the 'professional' tier ($50k a year, $200k total). A $100-150k DPT can no longer be financed federally. Private lenders are tightening, some loans reach 16% APR, and disbursements ran up to 6 weeks late. Meanwhile clinics have chronic PT vacancies and pay recruiters roughly 15-25% of first-year salary per hire.
ideas.solution: A sponsored-seat platform. The clinic pledges tuition support paid directly to the school, using tax-free employer educational assistance (up to $5,250 a year under Section 127) plus scholarship funds. The student signs a transparent 3-year post-licensure commitment with pro-rated forgiveness, structured around state limits on stay-or-pay clauses. We handle matching, contracts, compliance and servicing. Any remaining gap routes to a CDFI or credit-union partner that underwrites on the employer's offer.
ideas.why_now: The caps went live with the fall 2026 semester, so the first affected cohorts are hitting the gap now. A healthcare-association lawsuit (suspension deadline December 2026) adds uncertainty, so students and programs want a hedge whichever way it goes. Recruiting costs are high, and the tax-free employer student-loan-repayment exclusion was made permanent in 2025.
ideas.revenue_model: A success fee of 8-12% of first-year salary (about $9-13k per seat), below the recruiter benchmark: one third at contract signing, the rest at licensure start. Plus a servicing fee of 0.5-1% on managed balances and a referral fee from the partner lender.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Federal caps have made employers the only underwriter that can price DPT risk, because salary, licensure pass rates and vacancy cost are all known. For a clinic group, tuition-for-service is a cheaper and stickier recruiting channel than a 20% recruiter fee. It also locks in local talent in the years when the pipeline shrinks.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 PT-group owners through APTA state chapters and practice-owner communities. Sign 10 sponsored seats for the Jan/Aug 2027 cohorts. Ask 3-4 DPT programs' financial-aid offices to introduce enrolled students with funding gaps. Use a counsel-drafted contract template. No lending is needed at first; the launch product is a paid placement plus a contract.

ideas.title: Second-Life Studio: Shelved Human Drugs for Dogs
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
ideas.one_liner: Mine the wreckage of failed human biotechs for safe, clinical-stage molecules that make viable dog and cat drugs, and broker them to animal-health companies.
ideas.customer: Animal-health business-development teams (Zoetis, Elanco, Dechra, Boehringer AH, Merck AH, Ceva, Virbac) and venture-backed vet-drug startups pay for screening and deal flow. Sellers (liquidating biotechs, bankruptcy trustees, pharma pruning portfolios) pay success fees.
ideas.problem: Roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs exist, and 2026 has brought 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies. Their clinical-stage compounds, with human safety and PK data in hand, are being abandoned because human markets need $300M+ peak sales. Meanwhile animal health has few new molecules for canine lymphoma and osteosarcoma, feline CKD, IBD or chronic pain, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo.
ideas.solution: A scouting and licensing studio. It uses AI to mine ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC filings, layoff and bankruptcy trackers for discontinued assets that were not stopped for safety. It scores each for target conservation in dogs and cats, allometric dosing, market size and eligibility for FDA CVM expanded conditional approval. It packages dossiers with a vet development plan and KOL letters, then brokers options, licenses or asset purchases, keeping a finder's fee plus equity or royalty in each spun-out newco.
ideas.why_now: The supply of stranded assets is at a peak (layoff tracker, 300 zombies, wobbling software-only AI-drug shops like Schrodinger). Precedents are proven: verdinexor, a human-oncology-origin XPO1 inhibitor, became the first oral canine lymphoma drug, and anti-NGF antibodies moved from human programs into dogs and cats. Pet owners increasingly want oncology and chronic-pain options, while roll-ups (GoodVets, Mars) create channels that can absorb new products.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-25k 'Vet Opportunity Screen' reports per target class. $25-100k option fees. Finder's fees of 2-5% of deal value, plus 5-10% equity or royalty in spun-out veterinary newcos.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The human 'failure' threshold is a commercial threshold, not a biology threshold. A $50M-peak product is a rounding error to human pharma but a real business in companion animals, where the target biology is often the same. Zombie boards will sell for pennies, so a tiny studio can option assets that incumbents ignore.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a database of about 500 clinical-stage assets terminated since 2019 for non-safety reasons, and shortlist 30 with plausible vet indications. Email 15 liquidating boards and 10 animal-health BD leads. Sell the first two $15-25k target-class screens as paid retainers. Aim for the first option agreement within 4-6 months.

ideas.title: Sponsor-Paid Care Network for Canine Trials
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
ideas.one_liner: Biotechs pay for dogs' cancer care in exchange for clean, immune-competent efficacy data, solving pet-owner affordability and drug-developer validation at once.
ideas.customer: Clinical-stage biotechs (including AI-drug-discovery companies) and animal-health developers that need cheap in vivo efficacy and safety signals pay per enrolled dog. General-practice and specialty clinics are site partners. Foundations can co-fund.
ideas.problem: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never receive IV chemo. On the other side, AI-designed drugs are bottlenecked by assays and validation, mouse models predict poorly, and FDA's Sept 21, 2026 rule makes sponsors show that non-animal methods are 'adequately validated'. Spontaneous tumors in pet dogs (lymphoma, osteosarcoma, mast cell, bladder cancer) are well-established human-relevant models, yet trials struggle to recruit because the dogs are first seen in general practices.
ideas.solution: A network of 30-60 general practices plus a few specialty centers. AI trial-matching runs over practice-management data and an owner-facing trial finder. Sponsors fund a standard-of-care baseline (diagnostics and supportive care) so owners get treatment free. The studio handles owner consent, GCP-style data capture, INAD/CVM paperwork, and opt-in blood and tissue banking. Start with observational registries and PK/PD window studies of oral and repurposed generic drugs, then move to sponsor-funded interventional studies.
ideas.why_now: AI-biotech funding is over $6B in 2026 and sponsors are hunting for validation evidence. FDA's Sept 2026 rule and its 25-use-case NAM database push developers away from lab animals without banning them. Duffield ($250M) and PetSmart Charities are funding 'access to care', so grant co-funding for clinics is available. Oral options like Laverdia now make community-level oncology treatable.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-30k per enrolled dog (treatment, site fees, monitoring, data), at roughly 30% gross margin. $100-250k per observational registry or PK window study. Foundation grants subsidize owner-side costs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Pet trials fail on recruitment and owner cost, not on science. The general-practice vet is where 90% of cases first appear, and no one connects them to sponsors. Turning a sponsor's development budget into owners' treatment budgets solves the affordability crisis and delivers a data product for drug developers.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and one board-certified oncologist as scientific lead. Pitch 10 biotechs on a $100-200k canine lymphoma real-world-outcomes registry or a dog PK window study of a repurposed oral drug. Co-apply for a foundation grant to cover owner costs. Keep the first studies observational or extra-label to stay clear of the heavier INAD requirements. First revenue in about 4-6 months.

ideas.title: Kennel Canary: Outbreak Surveillance for Dog Daycares
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
ideas.one_liner: Monthly environmental PCR swabs that give dog daycares, boarders and shelters an early-warning system and proof of due diligence.
ideas.customer: Dog daycare, boarding, grooming and training facilities (independents and franchise systems), animal shelters, and the specialty insurers that cover pet-care businesses.
ideas.problem: Canine influenza, kennel-cough pathogens and parvo outbreaks force closures, trigger owner lawsuits and tarnish reputation, and a facility can lose 20-30% of a month's revenue in one event. Facilities rely on vaccination records and owner honesty, and testing individual dogs means a vet visit ($150-300) after symptoms appear, which is hard when vets are scarce and 85% of clients decline care above $1,000.
ideas.solution: Subscription sentinel kits: pooled air-filter and surface swabs shipped to a partner lab that runs automated multiplex qPCR (CIV, CPIV, CRCoV, Bordetella, Mycoplasma cynos, Strep zooepidemicus, parvo, distemper) with 24-48 hour turnaround. Facilities get a traffic-light dashboard, outbreak playbooks (isolate, sanitize, boost vaccination), and a 'verified-clean' badge for marketing. Insurers receive premium-credit pilots. Aggregated data becomes a regional canine disease early-warning map.
ideas.why_now: Post-COVID pet ownership and return-to-office have grown daycare and boarding. Human wastewater and airborne surveillance have matured, and automated extraction plus multiplex PCR have driven per-sample costs down. Regional canine flu and respiratory outbreaks recur, and clinics have less capacity to triage.
ideas.revenue_model: $149 per month for a small facility (bi-weekly swabs), $399 per month for multi-room sites, and $50-150k per year for franchise systems. Sample cost is $20-30 at scale. Insurer-paid pilots per insured location and a $10-30k per year data subscription for vaccine makers and veterinary groups.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: What these buyers purchase is liability and reputation protection, not health testing. A sentinel result is a dated due-diligence log that insurers and lawyers value, and one avoided closure pays for a year. Pathogen surveillance built for airports and cities has never been priced for the roughly 100,000-plus US pet-care sites.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a university or commercial vet diagnostic lab that already has a validated respiratory multiplex PCR. Sign 5 daycares via one franchise owner or local trade group for an 8-week pilot at $99 per month. Interview two specialty insurers about credits. Publish a short 'what we found in the air' report to generate inbound interest.

ideas.title: Independent Safety Registry for Pet Medicines
ideas.angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
ideas.one_liner: A neutral post-market surveillance system for veterinary drugs and biologics, built on pet-insurance claims plus owner-reported outcomes.
ideas.customer: Animal-health drugmakers and biologics developers (safety and medical-affairs teams) pay subscriptions. Pet insurers and MGAs pay for cost-effectiveness analytics. Vet groups and foundations use the public lookup.
ideas.problem: Vet adverse-event reporting is voluntary and underreported, and after the 2025 controversy over reported adverse events with anti-NGF antibody injections for canine osteoarthritis, owners and vets have no independent way to weigh safety signals. Pharma-run surveillance is not trusted. Insurers hold the only longitudinal cross-clinic data, yet are pushing 19.7% premium increases on 9% more animals without knowing which treatments reduce downstream claims. New modalities (mAbs, CGMs, long-acting insulins, oral oncology, and possibly a canine longevity drug) are arriving with no owner for outcomes data.
ideas.solution: A data trust that ingests de-identified claims from partner insurers and MGAs, optional practice-management extracts, and owner-reported outcomes gathered by a QR code at the clinic. It runs disproportionality signal detection in the style of FDA Sentinel. Outputs are (a) a safety dashboard for drug makers, (b) formulary and cost-effectiveness reports for insurers, and (c) a public 'what happened to dogs like mine' lookup for vets and owners.
ideas.why_now: Premiums rose 19.7% against 9% more animals, so insurers need loss-control insight. Big biologics and Loyal's longevity program (1,317 dogs in the STAY study, FDA acceptance of efficacy and safety sections) mean a wave of new launches. IDEXX buying CoVet shows workflow data is becoming a strategic asset, and independent players need a neutral alternative.
